News.title: Biological mum accuses surrogate of ‘trying to steal her baby’ after refusing to have abortion as she breaks silence
News.content:
‘SHE’S TRYING TO TAKE HIM’

‘SHE’S TRYING TO TAKE HIM’ Biological mum accuses surrogate of ‘trying to steal her baby’ after refusing to have abortion as she breaks silence

THE biological mum has accused her surrogate of “trying to take” her baby as she breaks her silence in a multi-state custody battle.

It comes after the surrogate refused to abort the baby when the couple who hired her told her to end the pregnancy because of a heart defect.



Surrogate McKenna West, 28, gave birth to the child against the wishes of biological parents Nasheen Gilkar and Omar Ahmed.

The baby has a rare condition called hypoplastic left heart syndrome (HLHS) that means the heart does not develop properly.





It can be treated with surgery, but is life-threatening.

He was kept alive in the days after birth by doctors in Texas, but is now in critical condition.

The baby was diagnosed at a 20-week scan, when parents Nasheen and Omar decided they wanted to end the pregnancy because of the rare congenital condition.

Alaska surrogate McKenna refused to go through with the abortion and fled to Texas, where abortion is illegal.



The biological parents won custody of baby Rumi in California and are fighting in court to enforce a restraining order against the surrogate, as well as against a custody filing by McKenna in Texas.

Biological mum Nasheen tearfully told a Dallas court on Tuesday: “She’s making us run from doctor to doctor, state to state. With our baby – she’s trying to take him.”

She said she had been through eight unsuccessful rounds of IVF and had to have a hysterectomy, adding that surrogacy was her “only option” after her body “gave up”.



Nasheen said: “We’ve never wanted anything more than this baby.”

McKenna claimed she had agreed to give up any claim to the baby if the couple committed to lifesaving surgery.

She said: “I’m not fighting to try to take someone else’s baby.

“I’m fighting because this baby boy needs someone willing to advocate for and fight alongside him as he gets the ongoing treatment his fragile heart requires.”

“I have asked for only one thing from the very beginning: A commitment that this baby will be provided the life-saving treatment he needs. That is all it would take to end this.”



But biological mum Nasheen said she had already set up medical care in California, where they live, and claimed that McKenna had withheld the child’s medical records.

She told the court: “We didn’t even know if he was still alive for two months.”

Nasheen’s lawyer argued that surrogate McKenna had also refused to get an amniocentesis test that would have confirmed if the unborn baby would have been eligible for life-saving surgery.

The couple had previously agreed to pay McKenna £45,000 to carry their child, with a clause which stated that West must get an abortion if there were problems with the foetus.

Furious that she broke the terms of their contract, the couple sued the surrogate for at least $100,000 and cut off payments for the pregnancy.



Nasheen admits that she and her husband told the surrogate to have an abortion, but denied denying him any medical care.

Baby Rumi was born on August 12 and had to be resuscitated.

Nasheen told the court: “When they tried to give him medicine, the tube came out and he stopped breathing and chaplain was called.

“He’s suffering a lot.”

He has gone through a two-day open heart procedure, which lawyers said was delayed because McKenna had not got the amniocentesis test while pregnant.



Lawyers for the parents are asking the Texas court to dismiss McKenna’s claims for maternity, after a California court already declared Nasheen and Omar the sole parents.

Lawyers for McKenna, who filed for custody of the baby, argue she is the mother because she gave birth to the child.

She said on Tuesday: “I knew that he deserved to be protected and that he deserved a chance.”

McKenna is also suing the parents for breach of contract after they stopped paying her surrogate salary.

The temporary restraining order has been extended for two weeks as the judge considers the custody case.

News.title: ‘Intense’ thunderstorms sweep UK as Met Office warns of heavy hail, lightning and flash floods causing travel chaos
News.content:
FLOODY HELL ‘Intense’ thunderstorms sweep UK as Met Office warns of heavy hail, lightning and flash floods causing travel chaos

INTENSE thunderstorms are set to sweep across the UK with the Met Office warning of incoming flash floods, lightning and hail.

A yellow weather warning for thunderstorms has been issued across a large part of England with disruption to travel likely to follow.



The East Midlands, East of England and London and South East England, North West England, South West England, Wales, the West Midlands and Yorkshire and Humber are all covered by the warning.

It is in place from 3am this morning and will remain in place until around 10pm this evening.



A band of heavy rain and thunderstorms is expected to move northwards this morning before slackening slightly.

But there is a chance of further showers and thunderstorms breaking out again during the afternoon, the Met Office said.



Lightning, thunder, flash floods and hail could batter Britain today after weeks of sunshine.

Brits have been warned to expect some travel disruption as the storm rolls over the country.



Network Rail has instructed passengers to check ahead of travelling today with delays to its services likely.

Some 1.9inches of rainfall is expected in parts of the UK which is likely to lead to surface water building and poses a risk of flooding.

The Met Office said, large hail and frequent lightning are also possible throughout the day.

Rainfall will drift northwards and ease during the evening with the thunderstorm likely to subside tonight.

The Met Office has warned that some parts of the country may experience power cuts and damage to buildings from lightning strikes and hail.



In places, public transport services could be cancelled completely or delayed and driving could become difficult with a chance that some roads will be closed.

A similar yellow weather warning for thunderstorms is in place tomorrow, covering largely the same area.

Tomorrow’s warning comes into effect at 6am and will remain in place until 10pm.



Lightning, hail and heavy rainfall is also expected tomorrow as the country continues to be battered by thunderstorms.

A risk of flooding will persist with an estimated 2.9inches of rain falling over the course of 12 hours.

Met Office Chief Forecaster Steve Willington said: “As we move into Wednesday there is a growing risk of heavy rain and thunderstorms, with warm and humid air helping to trigger heavy showers and thunderstorms.

“Some places could see significant amounts of rain falling in a short period of time, bringing the potential for localised flooding, travel disruption and frequent lightning.

“On Thursday, slow-moving heavy and thundery rain may bring prolonged rainfall to some areas, increasing the risk of localised impacts.

“There remains some uncertainty around where the heaviest rain will fall, so it is important to keep up to date with the latest forecast and warnings”

News.title: Asylum seeker slashed woman 30 times with broken bottle in brutal unprovoked attack after lying in wait for lone victim
News.content:
SAVAGE ATTACK Asylum seeker slashed woman 30 times with broken bottle in brutal unprovoked attack after lying in wait for lone victim

A VIOLENT asylum seeker who slashed a woman 30 times with a broken bottle in an unprovoked attack has been jailed.

Ibrahim Albashir had lain in wait for a lone victim before pouncing on the woman as she walked home from a meal out with friends.



The 34-year-old grabbed her from behind in a stranglehold and stabbed her repeatedly with his spare hand.

One witness described the attack opposite the Original Oak pub in Leeds as “frenzied” and another “thought he was trying to kill her”.



A group of men, including nearby doormen, ran over to help after hearing the woman’s “blood-curdling screams”.

The horror only came to an end when one of the men punched Albashir so hard he was temporarily rendered unconscious.

Sudan national Albashir, who has catatonic schizophrenia, was given a 25-year prison sentence along with an indefinite hospital order after admitting attempted murder.

Judge Robin Mairs said “it is by good fortune alone that (the woman) escaped with relatively minor injuries”, but noted that the victim’s mental scars are “profound and lifelong”.

He told the court he was worried about concerns raised over the defendant’s sexual conduct – including a sexual assault in a hotel where he was staying in Birmingham.

He also abused a member of staff while detained in hospital, Leeds Crown Court heard.



The judge told the defendant: “It is of significance you chose to attack a lone female.

“The common sense conclusion is that there was a sexual element to the attack.”

Judge Mairs said Albashir told doctors he was born and lived in Sudan until he was 25 then travelled via Libya and Italy to France.

He spent some time in a mental hospital and was eventually refused asylum so went to the UK from Calais “using the services of people smugglers”.

Albashir lived in Luton, Coventry and Birmingham before ending up in a hostel in Barrow-in-Furness.



He was in Leeds near the time of the attack in March 2024 after being thrown off a Manchester to York train for having no ticket, the court heard.

Two days before the horror, Albashir was stopped by police in the area after he was found with his trousers round his ankles and in a “trance-like state” but he was released with no action taken.

Consultant forensic psychiatrist Lucy Bacon told the court that all doctors agree that Albashir has catatonic schizophrenia.

In a victim impact statement, the woman – now aged 32 – told how Albashir grabbed her as she walked home from a meal out by herself in a nearby restaurant.

She said her physical injuries may have been relatively minor but “my mental injuries are scars that will stay with me forever and will always affect me”.



The woman also revealed how when she is asked about it, she has to “relive the worst day of my life all over again” and described how the attack “completely changed the way I live my life”.

She added: “I still have no idea why he attacked me.

“It’s not knowing why he did this to me that makes it difficult to process.”

Albashir will be detained indefinitely in a secure mental hospital and, if he ever recovers, he will be transferred to prison to serve the remainder of his sentence.

He may be deported after serving his sentence.



Detective Inspector Richard James, of West Yorkshire Police, said: “Albashir has approached a lone woman and subjected her to a ferocious, sustained attack which has only stopped thanks to the intervention of these security staff.

“Thankfully they heard the victim’s screams and rushed to her aid, potentially putting themselves in harm’s way to protect her.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“They have not only detained Albashir but also treated the victim’s injuries until the attendance of paramedics.

“Without their actions, this could very easily have been a murder investigation.”

News.title: Irish couple, 45 & 50, found dead in jacuzzi by their teenage children in Spain as police launch investigation
News.content:
DEATH PROBE Irish couple, 45 & 50, found dead in jacuzzi by their teenage children in Spain as police launch investigation

POLICE are investigating the deaths of an Irish couple, aged 45 and 50, found lifeless in a jacuzzi at a Spanish coastal resort.

Their two children, aged 14 and 15, reportedly alerted the homeowner after finding their bodies inside the hot tub at their rented villa.

Police investigating the couple’s deaths have ruled out foul play.

The grim discovery was made yesterday afternoon on an upmarket residential estate called Cap Blanc in Cullera, a town of around 25,000 inhabitants 25 miles south of the east coast city of Valencia.





In a statement to The Irish Sun this morning, a spokesman for the Civil Guard in Valencia said: “The Civil Guard has confirmed the discovery yesterday of the bodies of an Irish couple, aged 45 and 50, in the town of Cullera (Valencia).

“They were found by their children, aged 14 and 15. Violent death has initially been ruled out. A police investigation is underway.”

The bodies of the Irish couple have been taken to a Forensic Medicine Institute in Valencia so autopsies can take place.

They were removed from the scene just before midnight last night.



A water sample was taken from the jacuzzi the couple were found dead in.

A source close to the investigation said today: “This is not necessarily going to have a quick resolution and the ongoing probe will take time to complete.

“It’s all very recent still and the autopsies which will help to determine how the couple died have not yet taken place.”

Cap Blanc is a popular golden-sand beach and residential neighbourhood in Cullera, situated near the resort’s lighthouse.

News.title: Huge fire erupts near Scots caravan park leaving 600 homes without power as locals warned to avoid area
News.content:
FIREFIGHTERS have been battling a huge blaze near a Scottish caravan park after it erupted yesterday afternoon.

Emergency crews were scrambled to a seaside village in Elgin, Moray, after the alarm was raised at around 4.30pm.



The Scottish Fire and Rescue Service (SFRS) initially deployed six appliances to the scene in Hopeman after recieving reports of grass and hedged alight.

A wildfire unit and specialist resources were also sent to help extinguish the massive inferno close to West Beach Caravan Park on West Beach.



Firefighters have remained at the scene this morning as they continue to try and dampen down hotspots from the blaze.

Last night, fire chiefs confirmed that the fire is around 250 metres x 100 metres.

READ MORE SCOTTISH NEWS IN CUFFS Brit 'kingpin' arrested in dawn swoop after feud with rival mob tore UK city apart

And the public has been urged to avoid the area as crews work to bring the blaze under control.

Locals have also been warned to keep windows and doors closed as plumes of smoke continues to billow into the air.

It’s understood that no one has been hurt as a result of the blaze, however, it caused mass powercuts in the area.



Around 1,000 homes were initally left without power last night after the blaze broke out.

This was then cut to around 647 homes by 10pm, with the rest expected to get power restored by around 4am today.

The power cut also affecetd businesses, with one staff member at a local Key Store annoucing that it forced to shop to shut early.

A post on Facebook read: “Due to the power cut caused by the fire, we have made the decision to temporarily close the shop early.

“This is to ensure our fridges and freezers remain closed and temperatures are maintained while the power is off, and also in the interest of safety without lights!



Wildfire warning THE massive inferno comes just ten days after West Beach Caravan Park blasted a vistor who tried to start a fire bythe gorse. In a “gutting” post on social media, site workers revealed that they discovered that someone had attempted to set the area alight. The team warned that this could have devastaing consequences for the park and could cause a massive wildfire “within seconds”. Staff pleaded with locals and visitors not to light fires, have bonfires, or use charcoal BBQs in the area. The post, on Facebook, read: “Please help us prevent a wildfire. “We are absolutely gutted to have found evidence that someone has actually been trying to start a fire by the gorse. “The ground is incredibly dry just now, and the gorse and grass around the beach and surrounding area are tinder dry. “A fire could spread unbelievably quickly – what might start as a small fire could become a serious wildfire within seconds. “We are urging everyone visiting the caravan park and the beach to please NOT light fires, have bonfires or use charcoal BBQs. “Please tell the youngsters among us too – help us protect our beautiful coastline, wildlife, homes and businesses. “One spark is all it could take. We love sharing this beautiful place with everyone, but please help us keep it safe. No fires, please.”

“We apologise for any inconvenience and thank you for your understanding. Stay safe everyone.”

Photos and videos from the scene show huge plumes of thick black smoke billowing into the sky after the blaze took hold.

Huge flames could also be seen tearing through the grass as firefighters descended on the scene.

The smoke soaring above houses in the town, with many claiming it could be seen for miles.



Massive flames have also been seen leaping from the ground as the fire spread near the caravan park.

Last night, a A SFRS spokesperson told the Daily Record: “We are currently in attendance at a large fire in the open in Hopeman, Elgin.

“We were alerted at 4.33pm this afternoon and Operations Control mobilised six fire appliances, a wildfire unit and specialist resources to the scene of the fire, which is approximately 250 metres x 100 metres.

“People are asked to avoid the area as crews work to extinguish the fire.

“Due to a large amount of smoke in the area, nearby residents should keep windows and doors closed as a precaution. Crews remain at the scene.”

The SFRS has been contacted for comment by The Scottish Sun.

News.title: UK towns hit by earthquake as 2.2 magnitude tremor rocks homes and residents feel ‘shake’ and ‘rumble’
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

QUAKE SHAKE UK towns hit by earthquake as 2.2 magnitude tremor rocks homes and residents feel ‘shake’ and ‘rumble’

AN EARTHQUAKE struck a UK town leaving homes “shaking and rumbling” as residents felt the ground suddenly jolt.

The 2.2-magnitude tremor hit just before 7.50pm yesterday, with people across Grimsby and nearby areas reporting a sudden bang.



Residents in Cleethorpes and surrounding areas also felt the earthquake, which struck at a depth of around 5km.

One resident described feeling a “really quick shake” inside their home.



They said: “I felt what felt like a really quick shake in my house, I thought something heavy had fallen down upstairs or in the loft.”

Another said they “felt a bang like the house being hit”.



A third resident wrote on Facebook: “Felt the house shake and rumble.”

Another said: “I heard a deep rumble, I thought it was thunder.”

The BGS said the epicentre was in the Scartho area of North East Lincolnshire.

A 2.2 magnitude earthquake is considered a minor tremor and would generally only be felt by people close to the epicentre.



BGS data shows around 200 to 300 earthquakes of this kind are recorded across the UK every year.

But the area has experienced much stronger quakes in the past.

A 3.9 magnitude earthquake struck Grimsby in June 2018, with reports of people feeling it up to 60 miles away.

That came ten years after the area’s most significant earthquake in decades struck shortly before 1am on February 27, 2008.

The huge tremor measured 5.2 on the Richter scale and was classed as a “moderate” earthquake.



Some damage to buildings was reported, while residents described substantial shaking lasting several seconds.

It remains the largest recent onshore earthquake recorded in the UK.

News.title: Mum-of-four, 37, died in house fire as husband saved kids before climbing drainpipe to desperate attempt to rescue her
News.content:
TRAGIC RESCUE Mum-of-four, 37, died in house fire as husband saved kids before climbing drainpipe to desperate attempt to rescue her

A MUM-of-four died in a “ferocious” house fire as her husband desperately tried to save her by scaling a drainpipe, an inquest heard.

Kate Mulcahy, 37, was found dead after the horror blaze broke out at a £1.2m property at Ramsden Farm in Middleton, Manchester, in November 2024.



Rochdale Coroners’ Court was told Mrs Mulcahy had attended a friend’s baby shower before returning home at around 1.30am on November 10.

Her husband, John Mulcahy, woke to the sound of a smoke alarm at 3.51am.



He safely evacuated their twin sons and two daughters, aged between one and nine, to a neighbouring property before making frantic attempts to rescue his wife.

The court heard the couple had been experiencing relationship difficulties and the property had recently been placed on the market.



Mrs Mulcahy was sleeping alone in an attic room on the top floor – where the blaze is believed to have originated – while Mr Mulcahy and the children slept on the floor below.

After finding himself unable to force entry into the top-floor room from inside the house, Mr Mulcahy scaled a drainpipe onto the roof, the court heard.

The desperate dad smashed a skylight, and pulled away tiles in a frantic attempt to reach her, the inquest was told.

He was ultimately driven back by the intensity of the flames.



Neighbour Tim Ainsworth described hearing loud bangs and dog barking before Mr Mulcahy arrived at his door in “sheer terror,” dropping off the children while screaming in panic.

Mr Ainsworth, whose hair and forehead were later singed by the heat, attempted to enter the property but was turned back by a “wall of fire,” concluding that no one inside could have survived.

Firefighters tackled the blaze and discovered Mrs Mulcahy’s body inside the property.



A post mortem concluded Mrs Mulcahy died as the result of “burns and the inhalation of fire fumes”,

Forensic pathologist Dr Jamie Robinson said he found no evidence of an assault, injury or underlying disease.

Dr Robinson said Mrs Mulcahy likely to have been rendered unconscious quickly and that there was no evidence of “a prolonged period of survival”.

Forensic scientist Martin Crookes said he believed the loud bangs would have been the result of “roof windows failing”.

He said the fact the front door and attic bedroom door were open would likely have created a “chimney effect”, with oxygen sucked in, fuelling the blaze.



He said he believed the “seat of the fire” was in the attic room but that he was unable to reliably determine the precise cause.

The entire room was engulfed in flames, he added, which made the investigation “very difficult”.

Detective Inspector Kim Tallis-Hines said she was satisfied there was no evidence of any suspicious circumstances or third-party involvement.

Coroner Mr Salt, concluding Mrs Mulcahy’s death was accidental, said: “These are circumstances that have been thoroughly investigated.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Sadly, for various reasons, we don’t know 100 percent what took place.”



A number of flowers and tributes were placed on the front lawn in honour of the mum-of-four at the time.

News.title: TikTok star, 39, dies after ‘courageous’ cancer battle as heartbreaking final message revealed
News.content:
A BELOVED mum and TikTok star has died after a long battle with cancer as her final heartbreaking message is revealed.

Andree Greig Baudoin, 39, pre-recorded a final video to be shared in the event of her death.



The mum and influencer passed away on August 22 at Calcutta House by Hospice of Acadiana in Lafayette, Louisiana.

In Andree’s last video, released after her death, she said: “Hi, my TikTok family. If you’re seeing this video, it just means that my time has come and I’ve crossed over.



“This TikTok account has become my diary. It has become my way to let things out. It has become something I turned to first.”

She initially created her TikTok account so that her children would have video clips of her after she died.

READ MORE TRAGIC STAR TikTok star mom dies of cancer aged just 30 after amassing 237k fans

Andree said: “I started it because I wanted my kids to be able to follow my journey. And for it to be able to be accessed at any time and all times if they wanted to see me or see a video of me.”

Under the name “Andreethegirl”, the TikToker posted content about her four-year battle against metastatic breast cancer.

Treatments, diets and different medications formed part of her struggle to beat back the cancer – all of which she posted about online.

She had multiple tumors in her breast and had previously said that “all of the chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and radiation have not successfully killed the cancer”.



More recently Andree revealed that her illness had deteriorated rapidly to the point where there was “just nothing we can do about it”.

Her greatest fear was leaving behind her husband and three children.

In a heartbreaking admission, she said: “I’m 39. I’ll never be able to see my son get married, my daughter get married.



“I’ll never be able to meet my grandchildren. I’ll never be able to grow old with my husband, who I love dearly.”

She thanked her followers for their love and support.

Her final plea to fans is to be grateful for the everyday.

“My biggest, biggest wish is that you don’t take your health and what’s in front of you for granted,” she said, adding: “Enjoy the day in front of you.”

News.title: The life of an iconic country singer
News.content:
Iconic country musician Dolly Parton has died at the age of 80, her family announced on her social media.

"Sadness lies with us, not with Dolly," Parton's nephew Brian Seaver said in a video announcement.

In a seven-decade career, Parton won 10 Grammy awards, sold more than 100 million records worldwide, and wrote in excess of 3,000 songs.

Parton took her writing seriously, and considered herself a songwriter over everything else. "It's my way of expressing myself," she said. "It's my therapy."

She was also a savvy businesswoman who wasn't afraid to make tough decisions. Armed with a quick wit and southern charm, she took control of her show business career that spanned more than 60 years.

Follow for live updates and read more about Dolly's life.

News.title: Household energy bills to hit three-year high as Ofgem announces 4% rise from October
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham acknowledged the increase would be "difficult for people" but highlighted his move to cut VAT from electricity bills, which he said would help from October.

He said the government would "continue to look... at how we get energy prices down in the long term".

As well as the VAT cut, the government said the warm homes discount would take Â£150 off bills for six million households this winter.

But analysts at the energy consultancy Cornwall Insight have forecast domestic energy prices may rise a further 9% in the new year, bringing renewed concern to households at the coldest time of the year.

Shadow energy secretary Claire Coutinho said the government must "put cheap energy first", saying while it had promised to cut bills by Â£300 they had "gone up by nearly Â£400 instead".

Liberal Democrat spokesperson for energy and net zero Pippa Heylings said Burnham needed to "wake up to the scale of the challenge" and make bold changes to lower bills.

Former Prime Minister Gordon Brown also weighed in, saying the government should introduce a "machine gaming tax" and use proceeds to help those struggling with bills.

Longer term, he said Burnham should look at a social tariff for energy.

"I think Andy Burnham, I know him well, will want to do something along the lines I'm suggesting," he said.

Neil Kenward, Ofgem's director general for markets, said while gas bills were rising by 8%, electricity bills were actually falling slightly due to the government's VAT cut.

He said the gap between gas and electricity bills meant it would be cheaper for households to transition to heat pumps.

News.title: Dad of woman who took her own life says Treasury failed in its duty of care
News.content:
The father of a civil service employee who took her own life the day after a meeting with her managers has said the lack of support given to her by the Treasury "beggars belief".

Chloe Moffat, 26, a personal assistant to a Treasury director, died on 20 May last year, after she was told of allegations she had shared sensitive confidential information about colleagues, which she denied.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, David Moffat said he did not feel the Treasury had taken responsibility for its part in her death.

He added that her loss was "devastating", and had "torn such a big hole in our lives".

The Treasury said "it will learn the lessons from this tragedy".

On 19 May 2025, Chloe went to what she thought was a routine one-to-one with her line manager, but a more senior manager was also present.

"Chloe's first comment was, 'Oh, this must be serious, there's two of you here'", David told Today's Emma Barnett. "So that's the first time that she was aware of anything [that] might be a to do."

"And then they worked through and put several allegations to her that she'd shared confidential information."

During the meeting, David said she had asked on several occasions if she would lose her job, and if she could have a friend there - both of which were refused.

A coroner found at an inquest earlier in August that the Treasury did not apply written disciplinary policy, which would have made clear that if the allegations against Chloe were proven, the likely penalty was a written warning, not dismissal.

"Even though she asked, they said they could not determine the outcome," David said.

Straight after the meeting, Chloe was locked out of her emails. "That was all part of the shock and awe of it all for Chloe," David said.

The coroner found that the meeting between Chloe and her managers "materially contributed" to her death.

News.title: Yellow warnings in force as rain and thunderstorms hit parts of UK
News.content:
Downpours and thunderstorms will continue to bring the risk of flooding to parts of the UK on Wednesday.

A Met Office yellow warning for thunderstorms is valid from 03:00 until 22:00 BST, covering much of the Midlands, parts of northern, eastern and southern England, as well as the far east of Wales.

The rain could be heavy enough to bring flash flooding and travel disruption, with lightning and large hail posing additional hazards.

A further Met Office yellow warning has been issued for Thursday with more thunderstorms expected.

For some areas that have seen barely any rain so far this August, the next few days could bring the wettest weather in many weeks.

News.title: Why Pride is facing a backlash - from inside and outside the LGBT community
News.content:
Matt left Crewe as soon as he could, aged 18, feeling that he wasn't accepted as a young gay man. The only LGBT scene to mention was a tiny, makeshift bar behind a curtain in the back of an out-of-town pub.

He left in 2015, but this June found himself returning home, for Crewe Pride.

For Matt, it was a significant homecoming. "It really took me back to when I was a kid growing up here, trying to navigate my identity. It felt so important to be there and see how a town that wasn't particularly welcomingâ¦ has changed and flourished."

For many, these small, community Pride events feel a world away from the huge celebrations in the UK's largest cities.

But Matt's happy weekend in Crewe masks a growing culture war over Pride. Over the last few years, a number of councils have withdrawn their support for Pride festivals, while some big brands - perhaps nervous about being seen as too "woke" - have become hesitant to associate themselves with them. On top of all that, there's a long-running complaint from some LGBT campaigners that Pride has become overly commercialised; while the argument over trans issues has also made matters more fraught.

It's leading some to ask: what future do Pride events have?

News.title: Ex-England footballer Sterling charged with dangerous driving after crashing Lamborghini
News.content:
Raheem Sterling will appear in court next month to face charges of dangerous driving and possessing nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation after crashing his car into motorway barriers in May.

The former England winger, who most recently played for Feyenoord in the Dutch Eredivisie, crashed his Lamborghini into barriers on the M3 in Hampshire on the morning of Thursday, 28 May.

The 31-year-old was arrested and then released on bail pending further enquiries.

A Hampshire & Isle of Wight Constabulary spokesman said: "A driver will appear in court next month to face charges following a collision on the M3.

"Raheem Sterling, 31, from Berkshire, has been charged for the following offences: dangerous driving, possession of nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation, failing to provide a specimen.

"The charges come following a single vehicle collision, involving a Lamborghini, on the M3 southbound, close to the Minley Interchange [Hampshire], on 28 May, 2026.

"No other vehicles were involved and no injuries were reported. Mr Sterling is due to appear at Basingstoke magistrates court on 15 September."

Police suspected Sterling of "driving a vehicle whilst unfit through drugs," but that has not been included in the charges.

In May a source close to Sterling told BBC Sport there was "no proof" of drugs in his system.

The source added the player had faced "an extremely tough couple of years" and had been made to "feel worthless" and "forgotten about".

Sterling has been without a club since leaving Dutch side Feyenoord at the end of last season.

He joined Feyenoord in February on a short-term contract after leaving Chelsea by mutual consent.

Chelsea paid Â£47.5m to sign Sterling from Manchester City in 2022, where he had won four Premier League titles, five League Cups and one FA Cup in seven years.

In 2024 the former Liverpool winger joined Arsenal on loan, but upon returning to Chelsea in 2025 was exiled from the first-team squad and made to train separately.

Sterling earned 82 England caps between 2012 and 2022, and appeared at three World Cups and two European Championships.

News.title: NHS failing child sexual abuse victims in adulthood, say psychiatrists
News.content:
People sexually abused as children who seek help in later life for mental health problems are being failed by the NHS, senior doctors have told the BBC.

The Royal College of Psychiatrists is issuing a public apology for what it says is decades of mismanagement and misdiagnosis in the UK.

For some, it has worsened their traumas, it said.

The college said mental health staff have been too focussed on treating symptoms rather than exploring how past traumatic experiences can still affect patients.

Support is improving, it said, but there must be better training and more investment - something NHS bosses have said is being introduced.

The apology has been included in a report, external by the college and given to the BBC.

Immediate past president of the college, Dr Lade Smith, said she was "sorry" that, too often, victims have suffered "avoidable harm when seeking help".

The report details how treatment has sometimes been inappropriate, while people have been re-traumatised by the experience of repeated assessments and history-taking and not always being believed.

Dr Smith told the BBC it was clear people were not getting the support they needed, and that this was not just a failing of psychiatrists, but the whole mental health system.

"Services are so fragmented. The system is set up to provide short, discrete episodes of care. Psychiatrists do not get the time to build up a relationship with patients so they can be properly supported.

"They are lucky if they get eight sessions of therapy, when it could take eight sessions for a person just to disclose the abuse.

"And these are just the people who get support â many don't even get seen by mental health services because services are so stretched," she said.

News.title: As Ukraine hits Russia's refineries, Russia targets Ukraine's petrol pumps
News.content:
"Fill up quickly and move on," Mayor Ihor Terekhov warns drivers in Ukraine's second largest city Kharkiv.

Two petrol stations in the city in Ukraine's north-east were hit by Russian drones on Monday, which local officials say wounded two people. In another attack on a petrol station outside the city of Kryvyi Rih last week, three people were killed.

Russia's campaign of targeting civilian filling stations with drones and missiles began in earnest in April, primarily in regions on the front line, and the attacks are steadily growing more frequent.

At the same time, Russia has endured two waves of severe fuel shortages across the country as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries.

In total, Russia has hit at least 246 filling stations across Ukraine so far, says Oleksandr Sirenko, an analyst with Ukrainian energy think-tank Nafto Rynok ("Oil Market").

In July alone, the Centre for Information Resilience, an open-source investigation non-profit group, verified 114 Russian strikes on filling stations, compared with 66 the month before.

Given the threat, police have issued special guidance urging motorists to leave petrol stations and, if necessary, to abandon their vehicles whenever air raid alerts sound.

"You can fix your car, but you won't get your life back," says one police force in the Dnipropetrovsk region.

The damage is highly disruptive and puts civilians at considerable risk.

According to Sirenko, initially the attacks were being carried out with smaller, remote-controlled drones, but then Russia started using bigger, more expensive and more destructive Iranian-made Shahed drones.

One Shahed drone is estimated to cost between $20,000 (Â£14,500) and $50,000 (Â£36,000).

"One petrol station took five Shahed hits," Sirenko tells the BBC. "These Shaheds cost more than the petrol station."

News.title: Father's house rammed before son died in A66 crash
News.content:
A house rammed by a car before the fatal A66 crash in Middlesbrough belonged to the father of a teenager who died in the incident.

Cole Worthy, 17, was one of five young men who died when a Volkswagen Passat travelling in the wrong direction hit a Cleveland Police armed response vehicle, also killing two police officers.

Before the crash at 03:39 BST on Saturday, police had received multiple reports of two cars driving dangerously around the town and a Volvo XC60 was seen ramming properties.

The BBC understands that, after his father's home was rammed, Worthy and the four others set out in the Passat. Police said they were linking the activities of the Volvo XC60 and the Passat.

There is no suggestion Worthy's father was involved in criminal activity.

PC Tom Clough, 38, and PC Matthew Blades, 37, died in the crash, as did Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18, Theo Rae, 17, and Worthy.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct said officers had been pursuing the Passat for almost seven minutes after it was connected to earlier alleged criminal activity, but the pursuit was abandoned 10 seconds before the crash when it turned on to the dual carriageway.

Both vehicles were operating with cloned number plates but were picked up by automated number plate recognition technology.

News.title: Nicotine vapes best chance to quit smoking, major review finds
News.content:
Smokers who want to quit have the best chance of doing so if they use nicotine e-cigarettes, a review has found.

The Cochrane team looked at 80 major trials involving nearly 30,000 people and found that nicotine vapes were more effective than traditional aids such as patches, gum and support plans - increasing the success rate by about 60%, from around six in every 100 managing to quit smoking to one in every 10.

They outperformed non-nicotine vapes too, although researchers say switching to these afterwards might help with weaning off nicotine.

And they could prove more effective than the new anti-smoking pill cytisine, external, which the NHS has started to roll out - although more research is needed.

News.title: Major gangland figure Steven Daniel arrested in organised crime raid
News.content:
One of Scotland's most high-profile gangland figures has been arrested during an early morning police raid.

Steven 'Bonzo' Daniel, 46 was taken into custody at around 06:00 from his home in Robroyston in the north of Glasgow.

Daniel is understood to be the head of the notorious Daniel crime family which has been engaged in a violent feud with the rival Lyons family for 25 years.

He was arrested in connection with serious and organised crime, firearms and drugs offences as part of Operation Ventetic, a major UK-wide operation which has dismantled several gangs.

News.title: Young care leavers dying early a 'national tragedy'
News.content:
Young adults who have left care have a death rate around four times higher than the general population, a new review, external shows.

Often left alone "with no safety net," the report says the consequences can be catastrophic.

On turning 18, people leaving care in England often lose "significant levers of support", the Government-commissioned report concluded, as it warned the so-called "care cliff" must be addressed.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4 Today, report co-author and broadcaster Ashley John-Baptiste, who grew up in care, called the deaths a national tragedy.

There were 112 deaths of care leavers aged 18 to 24 notified in 2025, which the review said equalled about 130 deaths per 100,000 care leavers.

John-Baptiste recalled his own experience of turning 18 and moving out of the last of four foster homes he'd lived in.

"I was made to live alone and work out how to be an adult," he said.

Unable to afford a bed frame, he says he slept on a mattress on the floor of his council flat and felt a deep sense of abandonment and isolation.

News.title: Libyan who was cleared after Lockerbie bombing trial dies aged 70
News.content:
A Libyan who was cleared after standing trial over the Lockerbie bombing has died aged 70.

Al Amin Khalifah Fhimah was accused of murdering 270 people in the attack on Pan Am Flight 103 in December 1988.

He was found not guilty but a second Libyan, Abdulbasset Al Megrahi, was convicted of playing a key role in the bombing of the American airliner.

A Facebook post by Libyan Airlines announced Fhimah's death and expressed the company's condolences to his family.

Fhimah worked for the carrier in Malta before the bombing of Pan Am 103.

His funeral is set to take place on Wednesday in Tripoli, the capital of Libya.

News.title: 'I'm still paying a mortgage for a home destroyed by a fire'
News.content:
Sarah Williams vividly remembers watching her home burn down on the news. On 26 August 2024, she was on holiday when a neighbour texted her to say the Spectrum Building in east London was on fire.

But two years on from the blaze in Dagenham, which left more than 80 people homeless, residents including Williams say they are still "in limbo".

The leaseholder said: "We're still just stuck waiting for other people to make decisions about our future."

She added that in a year's time, the money they were given through insurance to pay for alternative accommodation will run out, and she is still paying her mortgage for a home that does not exist.

At the time of the blaze, from which at least 20 people were rescued, work was under way to remove dangerous cladding. An investigation found the scaffolding around the building at the time had caused the fire to spread, although the exact cause of the blaze is unknown.

The government had provided almost Â£6m through its Building Safety fund to remediate the building - administered by the Greater London Authority (GLA) â with a clause stating that if the work was not completed, the money would have to be repaid.

The Spectrum Building was demolished in December 2024 after surveyor reports deemed it unsafe.

The building's freeholder, Arinium Ltd, has since gone into administration, leaving the administrators, FRP, in control of the company's assets, including the insurance proceeds.

The government says, external the GLA has told the building's administrators that the GLA may be owed money as part of the insolvency process.

The government says this is a standard procedural step and would not affect the money residents are owed, as the GLA would only receive any funds left after residents had been fully compensated.

The GLA said that, as is standard practice in insolvency law, it had informed the administrators of the government's interest as a potential creditor.

News.title: Calls for GPS monitoring of domestic abuse suspects after murder
News.content:
The campaign has been started by Lynne Mackenzie, herself a domestic abuse survivor, who lives a few miles from the isolated cottage where Stacy was killed in July.

Stacy's husband Jim Mair, 43, whose body was found beside her, had been charged with assaulting her but had reportedly been granted bail, external on condition that he did not approach her.

While Mackenzie did not know Stacy personally, she said she was shocked at her murder which happened just six days after the death of another domestic abuse victim, Vikki Soloman, in Edinburgh.

She told BBC Scotland News the killings led her to question whether enough was being done to protect women in Stacy's situation.

"Every time driving in and out of the village I was aware of the police at the end of the road," she said.

"And it really got me thinking what could we have done? What could have been put in place beforehand? What else do we need?"

She has been in contact with Stacy's family who have agreed for her name to be associated with the campaign.

News.title: 'We just want to get home' - dozens stranded in Tunisia after cancelled Belfast flight
News.content:
Dozens of people from Northern Ireland have been left stranded in Tunisia after their EasyJet flight home was cancelled, with the airline telling them it had no other flights available for another 10 days.

One man told BBC News NI he has spent Â£4,000 on travel home for his family-of-five, while another woman, Georgina Doherty, said she and her six children were trying to get home after the death of her mother-in-law.

Others described running out of medication for health issues, while EasyJet were also criticised over a lack of support and communication.

EasyJet has said it is operating an additional direct flight to Belfast on Tuesday night, and that it was "very sorry" for the inconvenience.

BBC News NI understands more than 100 people were booked onto the cancelled flight that was due to leave Enfidha-Hamamet Airport for Belfast International three days ago.

Stuart McCartney, from Dromore, County Down, said he had spent thousands on accommodation and flights to get his family home via a flight to Brussels.

"I'm willing to pay Â£4,000 to get us home, if needs be, and then battle for reimbursement if I have to after that," he said.

"But we shouldn't have to pay. My holiday was a fraction of what I'm paying to get home right now."

McCartney said EasyJet provided two nights of accommodation but then told the family to find alternative accommodation for the rest of the delay.

He said his mother Katherine, who accompanied his wife and children on the trip, relies on heart medication and they have had to keep a close eye on her remaining supply as the delay continued.

An EasyJet spokesperson said that the company "have been doing everything we can to support Mr McCartney, providing hotel accommodation and meals and we will be reimbursing expenses that may have been incurred".

Georgina Doherty, who is originally from Londonderry but now lives in County Donegal, told BBC News NI the last few days have been an "absolute nightmare" for her family.

Her husband returned home a day before they were due to fly back due to his mother taking ill. She has since died, with Doherty and her six children stranded in Tunisia.

News.content:

Patients have died or have been harmed because of care failures at an under-fire NHS trust which staff fear could become the next major health scandal, whistleblowers have claimed.

An investigation by The Independent and Channel 4 into Northern Care Alliance NHS Foundation Trust, which treats more than a million patients across Greater Manchester, has uncovered allegations that patients have died in surgery without adequate investigation, while others had their cancer diagnosis delayed.

Some patients are alleged to have been left dying or in pain in overcrowded A&E corridors or have been forced to undergo invasive treatments that might have been avoided if their care had not been delayed.

And some staff claim they have been encouraged not to submit reports to managers when safety issues arise, while others say their accounts of serious harm and death are shut down or not investigated properly.

Other allegations include:

Kidney patients being forced onto dialysis due to treatment delays

Wards so understaffed that nurses cannot care safely for patients

‘Unsafe’ cuts to appointment times from 30 to 15 minutes in a bid to drive down waiting lists

Retired consultant, Dr Glyn Smurthwaite, who blew the whistle over rogue spinal surgeon John Bradley Williamson, found to have harmed dozens of patients at the trust between 2009 and 2014, including some who had misplaced screws causing chronic pain, warned that the deterioration in patient care and the trust’s attitude to harm was not a recent development.

“I believe this is potentially bigger than the Mid Staffs scandal in terms of the magnitude of harm. For decades, Salford Royal [before the creation of the NCA] had seemingly executive-led and failing governance processes,” he said.

“The organisation has a malevolent intent to defocus from the true problem and just tick a box. We’ll do an investigation because the system forces us to generate an investigation… but they’ll close it, investigate it, file it, and no one will ever see it, and there’s probably no meaningful outcome from it.”

The Mid Staffordshire Hospital scandal was one of the worst care disasters in NHS history and saw between 400 and 1,200 people die due to care failures between January 2005 and March 2009, prompting calls for widespread culture change to put patients first.

Have you been impacted by this story? Email Rebecca.thomas@independent.co.uk

open image in gallery Retired consultant anaesthetist Dr Glyn Smurthwaite said the trust seemed reluctant to tackle the root cause of the problems ( Channel 4 News )

Senior consultant Dr Vanessa Lawton, who wrote to the Care Quality Commission watchdog to voice her concerns in April and is now speaking publicly for the first time, said she had retired earlier than planned because she could no longer work in the trust’s gynaecology department. She described it as “unstable and chaotic, with poor cultures, lacking safety for patients and psychological safety for staff”.

Another clinician working in the A&E medical team told The Independent: “I just feel that I’m gonna get involved with something or something’s gonna happen, and it will be career-ending, and it will be devastating, and it’s not something that I want to be associated with anymore.

“It’s worse than anything I’ve ever, ever experienced ever before, and something needs to be said. We can’t carry on like this.”

The warnings come months after this publication revealed the trust’s gynaecology department had to review the care of hundreds of women due to “administration delays” linked to one consultant, meaning some had their cancer diagnosis delayed. Now, the trust faces a new independent external review of gynaecology surgeries due to safety concerns.

Concerns about the trust’s culture were raised with local politicians and Andy Burnham’s mayoral office in at least 2024 and 2025. Emails, seen by The Independent, from a group of former staff, claim whistleblowers had been “bullied into life-altering illnesses, early retirement or a fearful silence”.

In a further email in 2025, they warned: “Trust-wide systems which permitted so many patients to be harmed for decades within the current NCA are probably unlikely to be due to an individual ‘rotten apeple’ or confined to just one department.”

‘Incidents downgraded’

According to multiple testimonies from NCA staff, Datix reports, which staff are required to submit when they believe a patient has been harmed, are often downgraded or closed without adequate investigation.

Dr Lawton, a consultant at Salford Royal Hospital for 20 years, said she felt obliged to blow the whistle after claiming she witnessed issues at Salford and Oldham Hospital.

She said: “Incidents that are being submitted through Datix are not being investigated appropriately or even honestly. Many are not investigated at all; they’re just closed down and left blank… there’s a real keenness to close [them down], even when patients have been harmed.”

Dr Lawton also raised concerns about the slashing of appointment times, which she said the trust introduced to increase the number of appointments.

open image in gallery Dr Vanessa Lawton, consultant gynaecologist at Northern Care Alliance NHS Foundation Trust ( Channel 4 News )

In one shocking example, Dr Lawton found a woman in her early fifties, who was seen for a 15-minute weekend appointment due to post-menopausal bleeding, was not examined as she should have been. She wasn’t examined during a second appointment either, and several months later, she returned to the hospital with advanced cervical cancer and died.

According to Dr Lawton, an investigation into the woman’s death did not consider the impact of the shorter appointments, and she alleges it “omits many of the important issues”.

Another consultant who left the trust earlier this year said the shorter appointments meant doctors have little time to complete the required tasks.

“Of course, you rush patients this way; this is not care. We used to see around eight patients in a clinic, and they pushed us to see 14 patients. It's not safe. Of course. There is no way not to miss things, you know? And these things can be important,” they said.

In a response to allegations about how it handles incident reports, the trust said it has established processes to learn from events and make improvements where needed and said it has brought in an independent senior nurse to ensure patient safety issues are acted on.

‘People lining the corridors’

The issues do not appear confined to the gynaecology department. In another example, a group of A&E clinicians complained about overcrowding and patients being cared for in corridors. It is understood managers recently asked the group to close the complaint, but they refused.

Andrea (not her real name), a member of the A&E medical team, said: “Overcrowding and poor care: people in corridors dying or people in corridors deteriorating on a hard trolley. They’re a fire risk. Lying there for days, I mean, the longest we’ve ever had somebody wait for a bed is four days in a corridor.”

“It’s definitely unsafe, and it’s inhumane,” she added.

Last year, hundreds of admin staff across the trust launched a grievance over unmanageable work demands and backlogs in patient care, as revealed by The Independent earlier this year.

Now, new documents show fresh allegations from the team, including claims that delays in care due to short staffing meant kidney patients ended up on dialysis, which might have been avoided if they had treatment sooner.

Another document summarising staff grievances alleged: “We reassert our members’ concern and view that the lack of ability to complete tasks directly caused by lack of staff, as an active decision of the organisation, is causing patient harm.”

open image in gallery Northern Care Alliance said it was working to address staff concerns ( Getty )

The NCA said it has to provide care for patients in corridors and other temporary spaces due to pressures on the hospital, but that it was committed to ending the practice.

‘It’s a shambles’

Former staff told The Independent that the trust’s attitude to investigating patient safety and harm has been going on for years.

Rebecca (not her real name), who retired in 2021, described the then-trust leadership’s approach to patient safety as “absolutely toxic" and claims her efforts to raise concerns were ignored.

She claimed: “I’d write a report every night warning of unsafe staffing levels… and nothing was done for it. In a few meetings, people spoke up, especially anaesthetists, and said, you know, this is another Mid Staffordshire waiting to happen. They were deemed then a troublemaker.”

She had submitted reports on incidents such as patients dying on the surgical table, that later got downgraded without investigation.

Kelly (not her real name), a senior nurse who left the trust in 2024, said: “It’s the next Mid Staffs, if we’re not already there, really.

“There was plenty of patient harm while I was there. There were plenty of Datix raised for patients that were stuck in corridors with no dignity, no respect. Staff walking through; they got no curtains. It was a shambles.”

The trust said sickness has had a significant impact on staffing levels and it was focused on trying to address this.

‘Malevolent intent’

NCA was formed in 2017 following a merger between the then “outstanding” rated Salford Royal Hospital NHS Foundation Trust and Pennine Acute NHS Foundation Trust, and it now runs Salford Royal Hospital, Fairfield General Hospital, Royal Oldham Hospital, and Rochdale Infirmary.

Nine years on, it is now rated as “requires improvement” and faces enforcement action from NHS England over care failings.

Responding to staff concerns, Northern Care Alliance NHS Foundation Trust said it had changed the way it runs the organisation, putting more clinicians into leadership positions and giving them a direct role in making decisions and driving improvements.

It added: “Like many NHS organisations, we’re facing challenges. We’re clear about what those challenges are and recognise the concerns colleagues have raised. We are working to address those concerns and will continue to listen when colleagues tell us we haven’t got something right, so that we can keep learning and improving.

“We have clear processes to investigate incidents and learning from these is an area we need to prioritise. By doing this, we can drive forward improvements and maintain our focus on safety.

“We’ll continue to work with our partners, including our local authorities and Integrated Care Board, as part of our ongoing commitment to making improvements.”

The Cabinet Office was approached for comment.

A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said patients at Royal Salford Hospital had been "severely let down".

They added: “NHS England is working at pace with the trust and Greater Manchester ICB to support rapid improvement, strengthen oversight and accountability.“

“We are also prioritising gynaecology services in surgical hubs, at community diagnostic centres, and in pathways for NHS Online. We know there is much more to do but we are determined to make sure the NHS is the safest in the world.”

Two pastors in South Korea have been fined 1m won (£230) each for disrupting a flight by preaching to passengers despite repeated warnings from the cabin crew.

The pastors, both in their 60s, were flying from Jeju to Gimpo on 12 March when they began preaching, standing in the aisle and getting into altercations with passengers who protested against the disruption they were causing.

“You will go to hell if you don’t believe in Jesus,” one of them shouted at passengers as the cabin crew attempted to stop him and make him sit down. The other pastor joined him, shouting “Hallelujah, you will go to hell” while walking up and down the aisle.

When a crew member approached the pastors with a warning, one of them yelled back: “Don’t try to lecture me.”

On 18 August, following a trial, the Seoul Southern District Court convicted the pastors of violating the Aviation Security Act over an incident aboard a flight. “Based on the lawfully collected evidence, both the defendants’ disruptive conduct and their intent to cause it have been established,” the court ruled.

The incident lasted 13 minutes as the pastors ignored repeated objections and warnings from crew members and passengers, the court was told.

The pastors rejected the charges, saying their conduct did not meet the legal definition of “disturbance” and that they never intended to cause a scene.

Under South Korea’s Aviation Security Act, unruly passengers can be restrained using stun guns and binding ropes and an investigation can be opened against them upon landing.

The UN’s International Civil Aviation Organisation defines a disruptive passenger as someone "who fails to respect the rules of conduct at an airport or onboard an aircraft or to follow the instructions of the airport staff or crew members and, thereby, disturbs the good order and discipline at an airport or on board the aircraft”.

According to the International Air Transport Association, there have been 93,107 incident reports of unruly behaviour from more than 140 operators worldwide so far in 2026.

The government will tell households to stock up on tinned food and bottled water to prepare for extreme weather or cyber attacks on the country, according to reports.

The Financial Times reports Andy Burnham’s government is focusing on national resilience in the wake of threats from Russia and this summer’s heatwaves.

Russia said there would be “consequences” for Britain providing Ukraine with blueprints for British components used in the French-produced Scalp missile as Paris looks at setting up assembly lines for the weapon in Ukraine.

The country’s foreign minister Sergei Lavrov said his country had a right to regard the “direct involvement of British missile forces” as “participation in the war, with all the ensuing consequences”.

Andy Burnham’s government is focusing on national resilience in the wake of threats from Russia and this summer’s heatwaves ( AFP/Getty )

But in a speech outside Kyiv’s St Sophia cathedral on Monday, Mr Burnham vowed he would not be deterred from providing aid to Ukraine.

According to the FT, the government is accelerating work on its “war book” – a manual for the defence of the nation against external threats – as well as planning a social media campaign with advice to help people to deal with the impacts of extreme weather, such as the heat waves which have hit the country this summer.

A source told the newspaper: “There will be practical advice on things you can do to improve domestic resilience, like having some bottled water and tinned food. It will be common sense, not scaremongering.”

The government’s national risk register was updated last month, with the risk of interference in the UK’s democratic process added to it.

The national risk register is the government’s assessment of the most significant risks facing the UK. It is a planning tool designed to help professionals prepare for risks and is not intended to be a prediction of future events.

Earlier this month, The Independent reported analysts warned extreme heat and ongoing droughts are putting Britain at risk of its “worst food security crisis in decades”.

The knock-on impact of five heatwaves and prolonged dry conditions could destroy farmers’ harvests, leading to food shortages later this year and increasing reliance on foreign imports, according to analysts from the investment bank Shore Capital.

The National Farmers Union (NFU) warned the situation is “increasingly concerning” and that dairy farmers are already using winter feed because grass has stopped growing.

Speaking to The Telegraph at the time, Shore Capital’s Akhil Patel and Clive Black said the recent extreme weather could ruin homegrown supplies and potentially drive up animal feed costs, leading to greater costs for consumers.

“The UK has not been so close to a food security challenge for many decades,” they said.

More than 40,000 people died of climate-related causes over the 38 years between 1988 and 2025 in England and Wales, according to new estimates by experts.

The figures, published by the Office for National Statistics (ONS) on Wednesday, show the the proportion of deaths associated with the hottest days has increased in recent years, and that the gap between heat and cold-related deaths is also closing.

London had the highest proportion of deaths attributable to both the hottest and coldest days, according to the research, and those over 65 were most at risk in both extremes.

The UK saw five back-to-back heatwaves this summer ( Getty )

The statistics do not include this year’s heatwaves, which have put the UK on track for its hottest summer on record as the country sweltered in five back-to-back heatwaves, with temperatures of up to 38.1C recorded in London.

Last year saw the warmest summer on record with four back-to-back heatwaves and a mean temperature of 16.12C across the UK.

The latest provisional Met Office data shows that in 2026, England has recorded a mean summer temperature of 18.19C so far meaning the remainder of August would need to be 1.41C below the summer average for England to equal its current warmest summer on record, also set in 2025.

Researchers looked at the daily mean temperatures from 38 years of climate and mortality data for England and Wales during the period 1988 to 2025 in order to make these new mortality estimates.

The analysis found that those aged 65 years and over in each region of England and Wales experienced at least a 50 per cent increased mortality risk at temperatures exceeding 24C when compared with optimal temperatures.

This is a breaking story. More to follow...

News.title: Ooni karu 2 vs Ninja artisan: I put two top garden pizza ovens to the test
News.content:
If you’re after truly authentic pizza, with blistered leopard spot crust and a slight smokiness that will make you feel like you’re in the back streets of Naples, then the Ooni karu 2 is the oven for you. This oven primarily runs on wood or charcoal, but there is an option to buy a gas burner, so it’s also a great choice if you want the flexibility of a multi-fuel oven.

Setting up the pizza oven was nice and easy, although I will admit that getting the fire going took me a little while, but that’s more down to my survival skills than the oven. That said, once I had got the hang of how to set an efficient fire, it was plain sailing from there on out. Because it uses wood, it does take longer to get to temperature than a gas-powered oven, but spoiler alert, it is certainly worth the wait.

The glass door to the front has a viewing window so you can keep an eye on the fire and when to turn the pizza (Rachael Penn/The Independent)

The karu 2 reaches temps of up to 500C and that means the pizza cooks fast – you can expect it to be in and out of the oven in less than two minutes. The base was perfectly crisp and properly cooked through, and there were no doughy spots that hadn’t quite risen. Speaking of which, the rise on the pizzas that came out of this oven were spectacular. The crusts also had that proper char and chewiness that you’d expect from a traditional wood-fired oven. I’m not exaggerating when I say that by using this oven, you’ll get pizza that feels like you’ve ordered from a restaurant.

The pizza oven gets up to a maximum temperature of 500C (Rachael Penn/The Independent)

Whilst the results are amazing, this isn’t a pizza oven you just walk away from. You need to make sure you stay close because in that two minutes that it takes to cook the pizza, you will need to rotate it at least every 30 seconds, as it’s very easy to go from slightly charred to burnt in just seconds. Also, with it being wood fired, you can’t just turn down the temperature like you could on a gas or electric oven.

If you’re serious about pizza, this oven is among the best options out there (Rachael Penn/The Independent)

The oven itself is solidly built. The glass door to the front has a viewing window so you can keep an eye on your fire and also when to turn the pizza. The door really makes a difference to keeping the temperature sealed in, so it’s ideal if you’re making back-to-back pizzas.

One notable downside about the wood fired cooking method, is that if you live in a smaller space or next to a lot of other gardens, it can get a little smoky. Therefore it may not be the best option if you are planning on doing a lot of lunchtime pizzas during the summer, as people who have their washing out or windows open may not appreciate it. But, that’s where the versatility of being able to use a gas burner really makes this oven stand out from the crowd.

If you’re serious about pizza and you like cooking with traditional methods then the Ooni karu 2 is one of the best options out there.

News.content:

Gavin and Stacey fans can now book a place to cwtch in Barry, South Wales – in Uncle Bryn’s actual house.

“Gone Fishin”, a two-bedroom Airbnb on Trinity Street, sleeps six on the set of Rob Brydon’s beloved character’s home.

According to the listing, guests can whip up an omelette inspired by Gwen, stage a workout like Bryn and Smithy in the home gym, play on Trevor’s Subbuteo table and spend time spotting hidden Easter eggs inspired by the series.

open image in gallery Guests can whip up an omelette inspired by Gwen ( Airbnb )

When Airbnb host Jaxx Nelson and her partner Tom spotted the familiar property up for sale, they didn’t even think they would get a viewing.

Nelson said: “I think we were among the first through the door. Talking afterwards, we thought how much we'd love to stay ourselves for an 'Uncle Bryn experience' of sorts – and then figured, if we'd love it, there must be other fans who would too. So we put an offer in that same day and were slightly stunned when it got accepted. Beyond excited, obviously!”

Prices to stay at the Airbnb start from £482 for a minimum of two nights.

Guests will have sole access to the full house during their stay as well as free street parking and a private patio.

open image in gallery The Airbnb features two bedrooms and a sofa bed ( Airbnb )

The Trinity Street accommodation is also within walking distance to several well-known filming locations in Barry Island and the beach.

Lisa Marçais, a general manager at Airbnb, said: “Airbnb is home to truly unique stays that let guests step into places with a story, and it doesn’t get much more iconic than Uncle Bryn’s house.

“We’re delighted that Gavin and Stacey fans can now experience a little piece of TV history for themselves, while exploring Barry and the nearby locations that provided the backdrop to the much-loved series.”

News.title: Raheem Sterling charged over Lamborghini crash and possession of nitrous oxide
News.content:
