Read our Privacy notice

Footballer Raheem Sterling has been charged with dangerous driving and possession of laughing gas after a car crash.

The 31-year-old was arrested after crashing his Lamborghini in May on the southbound carriageway of the M3.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary said the former England player had been charged with dangerous driving, possession of nitrous oxide for wrongful inhalation and failing to provide a specimen.

He is due to appear at at Basingstoke Magistrates Court on 15 September.

After he was initially arrested, his representative said that he had been made to feel “worthless” and “forgotten about” in recent years.

open image in gallery Raheem Sterling had scored 20 goals for England during his football career ( PA )

The player scored 20 goals in 82 appearances for England, helping Gareth Southgate’s side reach the 2018 World Cup semi-finals and the final of Euro 2020.

He came through the academy at QPR before joining Liverpool, where he made his senior debut.

Sterling moved to Manchester City in 2015 and won four Premier League titles, five League Cups and the FA Cup in 2019.

He left for Chelsea in 2022 but after falling out of favour spent the 2024-25 season on loan at Arsenal.

After leaving Stamford Bridge, Sterling joined Feyenoord on a short-term deal in February and played eight times in the Dutch top flight.

In the 2021 Queen’s Birthday Honours list, he was made an MBE for services to racial equality in sport amid controversy over England fans booing players taking the knee at matches as a gesture against intolerance.

News.title: China clamped down on exotic wildlife farms – now they’ve moved to Southeast Asia
News.content:
We hear the bamboo rats before we see them. At the bottom of almost 200 concrete containers are hundreds of chunky rodents – some squealing as they scurry in circles, others loudly gnawing corn, sugar cane and bamboo with their sharp protruding teeth.

“They’re very easy to keep,” says Suriyan Wanpakwaen, as he peers into one of the pits at the DIY breeding facility beside his home in Nakhon Ratchasima, a province roughly 150 miles northeast of Bangkok. “My favourite thing is how clean they are, there are no bad smells.”

For almost seven years, Mr Suriyan has been farming bamboo rats – and now, the business is booming. A single rodent can sell for as much as 4,000 baht (roughly £90), and there’s so much demand that Mr Suriyan and his wife can’t keep up.

They’re not the only ones cashing in. Since the coronavirus pandemic, backyard wildlife farms like this have proliferated across Southeast Asia.

While this industry long existed in the region, the mounting new additions are filling a vacuum created when, in the wake of Covid-19, China closed thousands of similar farms over bio-security concerns.

“There was obviously a void and therefore an opportunity,” said Dr Ross McEwing, a project officer focused on the illegal wildlife trade and emerging zoonotic diseases at the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) in Bangkok.

“There was a coordinated effort to set up these wildlife farms, led by people who could consolidate stock and move that stock illegally across multiple international borders,” he added.

News.title: Ten years after Brazil’s Zika epidemic, its children are still paying the price
News.content:
In the heated pool, ten-year-old Stephany Vitória Silva Costa is weightless. The water soothes her convulsing muscles, providing brief respite from constant pain, and she coos with delight, igniting smiles among everyone in the room.

Stephany is a “Zika baby”; one of more than 3,080 children born with Congenital Zika Syndrome (CZS) following a devastating outbreak of the mosquito borne virus that swept Brazil in 2015-16. At least 444 of those children have died, mainly from respiratory and infectious diseases.

Like most of the surviving children from the cohort, she has suffered from an array of symptoms including microcephaly, severe cognitive and motor impairment, vision and hearing loss and seizures – which can occur up to ten times a day.

But a decade after the outbreak, a second wave of complications are emerging in children like Stephany.

Stephany’s exposed back, showing the pronounced 120-degree curvature caused by rapid, severe scoliosis Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

As her therapist gently turns her in the pool, a pronounced bulge shows through the back of her pink and blue swim top. Over the last two years, her growing spine has been pulled 120-degrees into an S-shaped curve that is now crushing her lungs.

While many of the children born with microcephaly after the outbreak died in early infancy, a much-loved group including Stephany lived on. Now, however, mortality rates are again climbing as the children near adolescence.

An x-ray image showing a severe s-shaped spinal deformity threatening to compress a young patient’s lungs Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“It weighs heavily on my heart. After so many years of following these children, it is inevitable to form bonds – not only with them, but with their families,” says Dr Milena Cavalcanti, one of just 11 paediatric neurologists in the state.

“Every loss affects me deeply. It is very hard to say goodbye to them”.

At the Altino Ventura Foundation’s (FAV) hydrotherapy centre, steam clings to murals depicting ocean scenes – a smiling pink octopus swims around a silver painted shipwreck.

As Stephany coos, another girl in a brown swimsuit and rainbow coloured shorts smiles as her mother fills a cup with water and pours it over her black curls.

Originally an ophthalmology institute, FAV expanded into neuro-rehabilitation as the Zika crisis unfolded. It provides free therapy to children with CZS twice a week, with treatment plans reassessed every six months.

Some 230 children affected by the syndrome have had therapy at the foundation and 84 are currently being treated. Its clinicians are tracking the cohort's long-term development.

Physiotherapist Gustav Wagner assists a young patient in the hydrotherapy pool Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

None of the Zika children present can walk or hold themselves up, and the majority have already had at least one major surgery.

Nevertheless, Gustav Wagner, a physiotherapist, says installing the hydrotherapy pool – which increases blood flow and loosens muscles – was a major breakthrough.

The children can’t express pain verbally. Mr Wagner and his team instead use a visual scale from one to ten, based on reading their posture and expressions. The mothers, above all, learn to spot the smallest changes and the pool, they say, makes a huge difference.

“It’s a very peculiar disease,” says Amanda Rodrigues, a physiotherapist. “We have to learn with them how to get better – we have never treated something like this before”.

A silent invasion

First discovered in 1947 in Uganda’s Zika forest, the Zika virus is thought to have quietly reached Brazil in 2014.

Experts attribute its arrival to increased air travel; either carried by visitors landing for the 2014 FIFA World Cup or brought from active outbreaks in the South Pacific islands.

Either way, the virus spread unnoticed and unchecked in Brazil for over a year.

Most Zika infections are asymptomatic or easily mistaken for dengue, both cause a similar red rash and flu-like symptoms.

The alarm was finally raised in August 2015 when neuropaediatrician Dr Vanessa van der Linden identified an unprecedented surge in infants born with microcephaly across Pernambuco state.

“It was very chaotic at the beginning,” says Dr Milena Cavalcanti. She added that doctors frantically coordinated emergency responses over WhatsApp as the crisis unfolded.

“The physical toll on the children was devastating,” she said.

Paediatric neurologist Dr Milena Cavalcanti Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Infections early in pregnancy inflicted the worst damage. And in one of the side rooms of the hydrotherapy centre, it's evident that the disabilities are profound.

Five children sit motionless in their wheelchairs with blankets pulled up to their necks. One of them, Emily Sophia dos Santos Luna, weighed just six kilograms at age two before being given a feeding tube to enable her to survive.

The children are unable to swallow, causing mucus to pool in the back of their throats. To prevent choking, their wheelchairs are permanently tilted at a 45 degree angle.

Maria José da Silva wheels her granddaughter to specialist transport Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“In the beginning, we thought they would discover a treatment,” says Emily’s grandmother, Maria José da Silva, 43. “But now we understand she will always be this way”.

She added: “It’s a very difficult life, but God gave us the power to keep going. I will take care of her until the day God wants”.

In the therapeutic gym, a large room filled with foam mats, standing frames and slings hung from the ceiling, Allana Kauane perches on a large silver balance ball.

She wears a green skirt, shin-high pink socks, and a white T-shirt that has “be happy” printed in shimmery lettering.

Ms Rodrigues, her physiotherapist, supports her torso and bounces her gently to build core strength. With every movement, she patiently lifts Allana’s head back up as it falls onto her chest.

Thailene Maria uses a bright gold pompom to draw her daughter’s focus Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Thailene Maria, the child’s 28-year-old mother, waves a bright gold pompom in front of her eyes in an effort to draw her focus.

Down the corridor in a consultation room, Dr Cavalcanti examines another patient.

It’s a girl who has not had a seizure in six years, but her last one lasted thirty minutes – six times the length that defines a medical emergency in Brazil.

Manuelle does not like to be touched, her grandmother says. She used to bite herself, now she pulls at her own hair instead.

As Dr Cavalcanti taps gently at her knee with a reflex hammer, the girl tenses and struggles to lie flat. Fine dark hair has started to grow along the girl’s shins – a side effect, says Dr Cavalcanti, of the anticonvulsant medication she relies on to control her seizures.

It is one of several changes the clinic still cannot fully explain. Many patients entered puberty years earlier than expected, one as young as three. Most are treated with hormone-blocking injections.

Dr Cavalcanti gently tests the reflexes of a young patient’s knee Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“We don’t know,” says Dr Cavalcanti, when asked about the cause. “We are just following the cases”.

On the ground floor, past the therapy rooms, sits the Capela Santissima Trinidade, a small wood-pannelled chapel. Inside, there are rows of pews, and in the centre is a large stained glass window.

It’s a small reminder that the building was designed to cater for the spiritual needs of its patients alongside their medical care.

While infants with CZS initially received only basic motor stimulation, severe musculoskeletal issues are emerging as they reach adolescence.

Dr Epitácio Rolim, the top orthopaedic surgeon in the state, has tracked a cohort of 152 children since the outbreak.

By age 10, 98 per cent developed orthopaedic deformities – 70 per cent suffer hip deformities, and 64 per cent from spinal curvature.

Previously, the public health system did not offer corrective surgeries or have a structured waiting list.

Some 230 children affected by the syndrome have had therapy at the foundation Credit : Lucas Landau

Dr Zilda Cavalcanti, Health Secretary of Pernambuco state, told The Telegraph: “We know we have a lot to do yet. The needs are giant and the funds are not”.

The root problem is neurological, says Dr Rolim. Damaged brain pathways create severe muscle imbalances around major joints. Unable to reposition themselves, the children’s relentless muscle tightness pulls their hips out of their socket and twists their spines.

Delaying intervention drastically restricts surgical options, Dr Rolim warns.

In the worst cases, repairing the hip is no longer possible. Surgeons must instead remove the top of the thigh bone simply to stop it from grinding against the socket.

“I am not talking about surgery to make most of these children walk,” says Dr Rolim. “The realistic goal is quality of life… hope does not mean promising a cure that we do not have… it means living with as little pain as possible”.

Dr Zilda Cavalcanti, Health Secretary of Pernambuco State Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Only five to seven per cent of pregnant women exposed to Zika had babies with visible symptoms like microcephaly. For the rest, timing of the infection in pregnancy determined how destructive the virus was.

“The children you saw with microcephaly were at the extreme end of the spectrum,” says Dr Ernesto Marques, a senior researcher at Fiocruz in Recife. “As the others become teens, developmental delays are showing up more clearly”.

Dr Patricia Garcez, a neuroscientist at King’s College London who helped establish the link between Zika and brain defects in 2016, said that many of the “milder” CZS cases are now displaying severe autism and neurodevelopmental delay, or motor deficits caused by prenatal Zika exposure without severe microcephaly.

The perfect breeding ground

The night we arrive in Recife, known as the “Brazilian Venice”, heavy rains transform the city’s roads into rivers. Gesturing to the rising water outside, our taxi driver chuckles: “Here we say: When someone sneezes, the whole city floods”.

Centuries ago, the city was a low-lying landscape of tidal sandbanks, estuaries and mangroves. When Dutch colonisers arrived in the 1600s, they engineered canals, bridges and dikes to prevent flooding and make the swamplands habitable.

It is this geography that made Recife, the capital of Pernambuco, the epicentre of the 2015-16 Zika outbreak, its pools of still water proving the perfect breeding ground for mosquitoes.

The state recorded around 742 confirmed CZS cases – 24 per cent of cases nationwide, and 39 per cent of cases in the northeast.

In Recife’s hillside favelas – densely populated, self-built communities largely lacking basic public services – residents were forced to store tap water in open buckets and barrels due to intermittent water flow making the mosquito problem worse.

Joane da Silva Sena pushes her son Heytor up a steep hill to their home in Favela do Monte Credit : Lucas Landau

Halfway up a steep hill in Favela do Monte, Joane da Silva Sena lives in deep poverty, caring alone for her 10-year-son, Heytor, who was born with microcephaly in November 2015.

Ms Sena, 36, a thin, weary-looking woman with a kind face, is entirely on her own.

The father abandoned them at birth, and the neighbours refuse to even watch Heytor while she goes to the shop, instead watching her struggle up the hill from their homes.

Ms Sena rarely receives any help with her son Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“My family doesn’t help me, nobody cares,” she says. “People are afraid of Heytor, they say he’s ‘special’.”

Inside the house, only secured with metal bars on gaping door and window frames, Ms Sena frequently skips meals so Heytor can eat. There’s a shadow on the wall of the pink-painted kitchen where the fridge should be. She had to throw it out because it kept giving her electric shocks and was too expensive to repair.

Heytor’s specialised wheelchair broke months ago, leaving him only with an ill-fitting wicker chair that he constantly slumps on.

Ms Sena lifts her son roughly 10 times a day Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Ms Sena lifts his 54 kg frame roughly 10 times a day between the chair and the bed to soothe him when he gets agitated. She also carries him up the steep hill twice a week to reach physiotherapy classes.

“I will not abandon him,” Ms Sena says through tears. “I just ask God for health, because if I get sick, no one will look after him”.

In August 2025, Brazil’s Congress passed a bill – first floated in 2015 – to compensate the families of children born with microcephaly and other disabilities caused by Zika.

The package includes a one-off payment of 50,000 BRL (£7,150), and a tax-free monthly support payment of 8,150 BRL (£1,165), five times the previous allowance.

But despite the national law, Ms Sena receives very little support.

The hospital Heytor was born in did not provide official documentation linking Heytor’s condition to Zika, even though multiple experts say that it is the cause.

Ms Sena said she dreams about having access to the funds, adding that she would love to “buy a beautiful armchair that will be so comfortable for him”.

Ms Sena prays for her own robust health so that her son is not without a carer Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

After The Telegraph raised her case with the Pernambuco Health Department, state officials launched an investigation into Heytor’s birth records and admitted him to the hospital for a complete evaluation.

They also dropped off medication and nappies at the house and have arranged for a vehicle to transport them to therapy classes.

Acknowledging that Ms Sena’s struggles span housing, transportation, social support and caregiver mental health, the state told The Telegraph it would assemble a multi-agency task force to assist her.

Across Brazil, the mothers of children with Zika are renowned for their resilience.

Many were young and living in poverty when the outbreak hit. Fuelled by deep rooted stigma, most were then abandoned by their partners after their children were born with disabilities.

It took a decade of campaigning for these women – a movement known as the Mothers of Angels – to finally secure the social security breakthrough last year.

They proved that the state failed families twice over: by not containing the virus, and by under-compensating the children for years.

A new generation at risk

It remains unclear whether Brazil is vulnerable to another Zika outbreak.

In 2016, amid the original epidemic, the World Health Organization declared a public health emergency of international concern.

A few months later, cases began to drop and today the population is thought to be protected by herd immunity.

However, that immunity is unlikely to last forever.

A study in Salvador, the capital of nearby Bahia state, found antibody protection dropped from 59 per cent to under 39 per cent within two years of the first outbreak.

Dr Marques estimates Brazil could see another outbreak resulting in children born with CZS within 15 to 20 years.

Originally focused on eye care, the Altino Ventura Foundation expanded its operations during the 2015 outbreak Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

A new generation has grown up without having been exposed to the virus, creating a growing population vulnerable to infection, he says.

The root cause of poor water infrastructure and mosquito infestation also hasn’t been resolved.

“Almost everybody born after 2016 has not been exposed to Zika at all... they are naive, and that piles up with the older people who did not get infected,” he told The Telegraph.

“Once the population vulnerable to Zika reaches a critical threshold, the risk of another outbreak grows”.

The research that could prepare Brazil for that eventuality has stalled.

There is still no approved Zika vaccine or antibody treatment. The most advanced candidate has only just completed early-stage safety trials, and experts say a larger trial is nearly impossible without an active outbreak to test it.

Basic diagnostic tools also have major limitations. Standard antibody tests still cannot reliably distinguish Zika from dengue, and PCR testing – the only definitive testing method – is only effective for around five days at the peak of infections.

For Erika Silva Costa and her ten-year-old daughter Stephany, the child with severe scoliosis, the struggle to secure that necessary care has reached a standstill.

Ms Costa contracted Zika five months into her pregnancy. When doctors recommended that she terminate, she refused.

Erika Silva Costa, Stephany’s mother and full-time caregiver, is also a fierce campaigner Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

A former MRI technician, Ms Costa is now a full-time caregiver and a prominent campaigner for Zika children.

“My dedication to her is total, 24 hours a day… my brain is always awake,” she says, adding that she sleeps in the same bed facing Stephany in case she chokes during the night. “I feel like the umbilical cord was never cut”.

Despite the urgent need, Stephany’s position remains perilous.

Her doctors say she needs an operation costing 150,000 BRL (£21,400) on her spine but so far she has been refused coverage by medical insurers. Ms Costa is now mounting a legal battle to fight the decision in court.

“The authorities together with the health services aren’t tackling this properly,” said Dr Rolim.

“It’s so frustrating. The professionals know what needs to be done, but can’t do it because the system doesn’t provide the right conditions”.

With the public health system crippled by long waiting lists and a lack of specialised equipment, families like Ms Costa are waiting in limbo.

“Sometimes one of the children dies and we all fall apart,” she says. “We have to believe in God to wake up the next day and be strong”.

Protect yourself and your family by learning more about Global Health Security

On the ground floor, past the therapy rooms, sits the Capela Santissima Trinidade, a small wood-pannelled chapel. Inside, there are rows of pews, and in the centre is a large stained glass window.

It’s a small reminder that the building was designed to cater for the spiritual needs of its patients alongside their medical care.

While infants with CZS initially received only basic motor stimulation, severe musculoskeletal issues are emerging as they reach adolescence.

Dr Epitácio Rolim, the top orthopaedic surgeon in the state, has tracked a cohort of 152 children since the outbreak.

By age 10, 98 per cent developed orthopaedic deformities – 70 per cent suffer hip deformities, and 64 per cent from spinal curvature.

Previously, the public health system did not offer corrective surgeries or have a structured waiting list.

Some 230 children affected by the syndrome have had therapy at the foundation Credit : Lucas Landau

Dr Zilda Cavalcanti, Health Secretary of Pernambuco state, told The Telegraph: “We know we have a lot to do yet. The needs are giant and the funds are not”.

The root problem is neurological, says Dr Rolim. Damaged brain pathways create severe muscle imbalances around major joints. Unable to reposition themselves, the children’s relentless muscle tightness pulls their hips out of their socket and twists their spines.

Delaying intervention drastically restricts surgical options, Dr Rolim warns.

In the worst cases, repairing the hip is no longer possible. Surgeons must instead remove the top of the thigh bone simply to stop it from grinding against the socket.

“I am not talking about surgery to make most of these children walk,” says Dr Rolim. “The realistic goal is quality of life… hope does not mean promising a cure that we do not have… it means living with as little pain as possible”.

Dr Zilda Cavalcanti, Health Secretary of Pernambuco State Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Only five to seven per cent of pregnant women exposed to Zika had babies with visible symptoms like microcephaly. For the rest, timing of the infection in pregnancy determined how destructive the virus was.

“The children you saw with microcephaly were at the extreme end of the spectrum,” says Dr Ernesto Marques, a senior researcher at Fiocruz in Recife. “As the others become teens, developmental delays are showing up more clearly”.

Dr Patricia Garcez, a neuroscientist at King’s College London who helped establish the link between Zika and brain defects in 2016, said that many of the “milder” CZS cases are now displaying severe autism and neurodevelopmental delay, or motor deficits caused by prenatal Zika exposure without severe microcephaly.

The perfect breeding ground

The night we arrive in Recife, known as the “Brazilian Venice”, heavy rains transform the city’s roads into rivers. Gesturing to the rising water outside, our taxi driver chuckles: “Here we say: When someone sneezes, the whole city floods”.

Centuries ago, the city was a low-lying landscape of tidal sandbanks, estuaries and mangroves. When Dutch colonisers arrived in the 1600s, they engineered canals, bridges and dikes to prevent flooding and make the swamplands habitable.

It is this geography that made Recife, the capital of Pernambuco, the epicentre of the 2015-16 Zika outbreak, its pools of still water proving the perfect breeding ground for mosquitoes.

The state recorded around 742 confirmed CZS cases – 24 per cent of cases nationwide, and 39 per cent of cases in the northeast.

In Recife’s hillside favelas – densely populated, self-built communities largely lacking basic public services – residents were forced to store tap water in open buckets and barrels due to intermittent water flow making the mosquito problem worse.

Joane da Silva Sena pushes her son Heytor up a steep hill to their home in Favela do Monte Credit : Lucas Landau

Halfway up a steep hill in Favela do Monte, Joane da Silva Sena lives in deep poverty, caring alone for her 10-year-son, Heytor, who was born with microcephaly in November 2015.

Ms Sena, 36, a thin, weary-looking woman with a kind face, is entirely on her own.

The father abandoned them at birth, and the neighbours refuse to even watch Heytor while she goes to the shop, instead watching her struggle up the hill from their homes.

Ms Sena rarely receives any help with her son Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

“My family doesn’t help me, nobody cares,” she says. “People are afraid of Heytor, they say he’s ‘special’.”

Inside the house, only secured with metal bars on gaping door and window frames, Ms Sena frequently skips meals so Heytor can eat. There’s a shadow on the wall of the pink-painted kitchen where the fridge should be. She had to throw it out because it kept giving her electric shocks and was too expensive to repair.

Heytor’s specialised wheelchair broke months ago, leaving him only with an ill-fitting wicker chair that he constantly slumps on.

Ms Sena lifts her son roughly 10 times a day Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

Ms Sena lifts his 54 kg frame roughly 10 times a day between the chair and the bed to soothe him when he gets agitated. She also carries him up the steep hill twice a week to reach physiotherapy classes.

“I will not abandon him,” Ms Sena says through tears. “I just ask God for health, because if I get sick, no one will look after him”.

In August 2025, Brazil’s Congress passed a bill – first floated in 2015 – to compensate the families of children born with microcephaly and other disabilities caused by Zika.

The package includes a one-off payment of 50,000 BRL (£7,150), and a tax-free monthly support payment of 8,150 BRL (£1,165), five times the previous allowance.

But despite the national law, Ms Sena receives very little support.

The hospital Heytor was born in did not provide official documentation linking Heytor’s condition to Zika, even though multiple experts say that it is the cause.

Ms Sena said she dreams about having access to the funds, adding that she would love to “buy a beautiful armchair that will be so comfortable for him”.

Ms Sena prays for her own robust health so that her son is not without a carer Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

After The Telegraph raised her case with the Pernambuco Health Department, state officials launched an investigation into Heytor’s birth records and admitted him to the hospital for a complete evaluation.

They also dropped off medication and nappies at the house and have arranged for a vehicle to transport them to therapy classes.

Acknowledging that Ms Sena’s struggles span housing, transportation, social support and caregiver mental health, the state told The Telegraph it would assemble a multi-agency task force to assist her.

Across Brazil, the mothers of children with Zika are renowned for their resilience.

Many were young and living in poverty when the outbreak hit. Fuelled by deep rooted stigma, most were then abandoned by their partners after their children were born with disabilities.

It took a decade of campaigning for these women – a movement known as the Mothers of Angels – to finally secure the social security breakthrough last year.

They proved that the state failed families twice over: by not containing the virus, and by under-compensating the children for years.

A new generation at risk

It remains unclear whether Brazil is vulnerable to another Zika outbreak.

In 2016, amid the original epidemic, the World Health Organization declared a public health emergency of international concern.

A few months later, cases began to drop and today the population is thought to be protected by herd immunity.

However, that immunity is unlikely to last forever.

A study in Salvador, the capital of nearby Bahia state, found antibody protection dropped from 59 per cent to under 39 per cent within two years of the first outbreak.

Dr Marques estimates Brazil could see another outbreak resulting in children born with CZS within 15 to 20 years.

Originally focused on eye care, the Altino Ventura Foundation expanded its operations during the 2015 outbreak Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

A new generation has grown up without having been exposed to the virus, creating a growing population vulnerable to infection, he says.

The root cause of poor water infrastructure and mosquito infestation also hasn’t been resolved.

“Almost everybody born after 2016 has not been exposed to Zika at all... they are naive, and that piles up with the older people who did not get infected,” he told The Telegraph.

“Once the population vulnerable to Zika reaches a critical threshold, the risk of another outbreak grows”.

The research that could prepare Brazil for that eventuality has stalled.

There is still no approved Zika vaccine or antibody treatment. The most advanced candidate has only just completed early-stage safety trials, and experts say a larger trial is nearly impossible without an active outbreak to test it.

Basic diagnostic tools also have major limitations. Standard antibody tests still cannot reliably distinguish Zika from dengue, and PCR testing – the only definitive testing method – is only effective for around five days at the peak of infections.

For Erika Silva Costa and her ten-year-old daughter Stephany, the child with severe scoliosis, the struggle to secure that necessary care has reached a standstill.

Ms Costa contracted Zika five months into her pregnancy. When doctors recommended that she terminate, she refused.

Erika Silva Costa, Stephany’s mother and full-time caregiver, is also a fierce campaigner Credit : Lucas Landau/The Telegraph

A former MRI technician, Ms Costa is now a full-time caregiver and a prominent campaigner for Zika children.

“My dedication to her is total, 24 hours a day… my brain is always awake,” she says, adding that she sleeps in the same bed facing Stephany in case she chokes during the night. “I feel like the umbilical cord was never cut”.

Despite the urgent need, Stephany’s position remains perilous.

Her doctors say she needs an operation costing 150,000 BRL (£21,400) on her spine but so far she has been refused coverage by medical insurers. Ms Costa is now mounting a legal battle to fight the decision in court.

“The authorities together with the health services aren’t tackling this properly,” said Dr Rolim.

“It’s so frustrating. The professionals know what needs to be done, but can’t do it because the system doesn’t provide the right conditions”.

With the public health system crippled by long waiting lists and a lack of specialised equipment, families like Ms Costa are waiting in limbo.

“Sometimes one of the children dies and we all fall apart,” she says. “We have to believe in God to wake up the next day and be strong”.

News.title: Glasner made to wait for first win as Trafford thwarts Forest
News.content:
Leeds manager Daniel Farke said: “He has the potential to be one of the best goalkeepers in the Premier League and that is why Thomas Tuchel has picked him for England.

“I like his natural confidence and aura, he knows that he’s good and he will be outstanding one day.

“He has major chances to be under the spotlight and we are very pleased with him so far.”

Forest manager Oliver Glasner will be pleased to see the back of Leeds. He was appointed by Forest for the primary reason of winning trophies after successful tenures with Crystal Palace and Eintracht Frankfurt, but this particular avenue is now closed for this season.

Four-time League Cup winners, Forest endured a difficult evening following the pre-match news that they have agreed a £45m deal with Chelsea for striker Liam Delap.

Forest have established a reputation for noisy transfer windows but are determined to focus on quality over quantity this year. With Delap to undergo a medical on Wednesday, Forest will then focus on signing a new right wing-back before the deadline.

Newcastle’s Jacob Murphy has been discussed, though a move is now regarded as unlikely. There are understood to be other targets under consideration.

Glasner has insisted he does not want Forest to panic, and it remains to be seen whether they do spring into life on the final day. He said: “I am not a magician or the messiah and we cannot ignore the reality that Leeds are ahead of us at the moment.

News.title: Palmer and Rogers show promise of star double act for Chelsea
News.content:
“I am very happy for Cole,” Alonso said. “I have really enjoyed seeing him play with the dynamism and the freedom and the responsibility... when Cole feels this way we have a better team and a better Cole.”

Palmer makes it look very easy in this form, capable of switching the direction of play a beat before anyone else spots the opportunity. He and his old Manchester City academy friend Rogers came off before the end, Palmer having demonstrated some discomfort chasing a ball. Asked afterwards how ready he felt, Palmer responded in kind. “Did you not watch the game? I’m only joking, I’m ready... it was a difficult season with injuries and whatnot, but through the summer and since I’ve been back I’ve worked extra hard.”

If there was an attacker to compare with him on the other side it was King, who looks even better. The 19-year-old was way ahead of Arbeloa’s two young Real Madrid imports. García toiled away and took his chance, but César Palacios struggled for any impact in a position tucked in on the left. Oscar Bobb and King gave Fulham some edge but the concern, as ever, will be where Fulham get their goals.

Arbeloa pushed his full-backs high and encouraged Sander Berge to drop deep to get on the ball in the first passing phase. The Norwegian delayed too long in challenging João Pedro for Chelsea’s third – backing off and allowing Palmer to overlap to receive the pass.

Sánchez had not been the only concern for Chelsea. Back in the team, Levi Colwill misjudged a challenge on King in the first half and was relieved that the card was only yellow. Roméo Lavia took a wild swing at Calvin Bassey and was also booked. Moisés Caicedo was not fit to play. Enzo Fernández was on the bench and would come on in the second half to the kind of reception from opposition fans to which he will quickly become familiar.

There was a grin from the Argentine at those who berated him from the home stands when he returned at half-time. Fernández worked hard to transmit a general sense that the abuse did not land, although he will be relieved that the Chelsea fans were supportive. His future still feels very much in play.

It was Palmer’s subtle ball through that gave João Pedro the chance with 32 seconds of the game played. The ball came forward immediately from Lacroix’s firm header from defence. The Frenchman delivered a very accomplished assist for Rogers’s first-half goal. Before that King had equalised. There was an exchange with Timothy Castagne, and King looked up just inside the box and decided to have a swing at it. Sánchez was close enough to grasp the ball and somehow failed to do so.

Sánchez would later push a Castagne shot in the direction of García, who stooped and nodded the ball over the goalkeeper after Palmer had scored Chelsea’s third. This second error was unfortunate, but it is the kind of thing that happens to a goalkeeper as erratic as the one for whom Chelsea’s hierarchy seem to have such patience.

News.title: Help us test binoculars with the RSPB and birding experts
News.content:
At Telegraph Recommended, we test hundreds of products each year, and we rely on our community members to help verify our experts’ findings.

We currently have an upcoming opportunity for Telegraph readers to help test the latest binoculars for birdwatching with the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB).

Selected readers will be invited to RSPB’s The Lodge nature reserve in Sandy, Bedfordshire, where Jamie Wyver, editor of the RSPB magazine, and Tim Jones, otherwise known as ‘Begin Birding’ on Instagram, will host two binocular testing mornings.

Taking place on September 23 and 24, Jamie and Tim will lead each group on a morning ramble across the heathland, offering the chance to spot local bird species, including Nightjars, Hobbies and Spotted Flycatchers.

Sports.title: River Card and Cloud Forest clash at Newbury
Sports.content:
We have a busy day’s racing on Wednesday with flat action from Newbury and Wolverhampton, live on Sky Sports Racing...

6.30 Newbury - Cloud Forest and River Card headline feature handicap

Cloud Forest and River Card clash in an excellent renewal of the feature Gracelands Handicap at Newbury.

Saeed bin Suroor saddles Cloud Forest, who drops back to a mile as he makes his handicap debut after three starts this season. The form of his recent second at Kempton has been boosted and he can go well under Hector Crouch.

River Card claimed the notable scalp of Maltese Cross when winning an Ascot maiden last year but finished well beaten in a sales race over in Deauville next time. He makes appeal if fit enough on this seasonal return and handicap debut with Tom Marquand in the saddle for the first time.

Others to note include Haydock winner Home Hero, while the hat-trick seeking Accademia must be feared despite a six-pound penalty for her course and distance success last month.

3.30 Wolverhampton - In-form The Craftymaster faces Boilermaker

In-form The Craftymaster takes on six rivals in a trappy attheraces.com/Marketmovers Handicap at Wolverhampton.

Tony Carroll's charge has won three of his past four starts and seeks a hat-trick under new pilot Molly Gunn. A narrow winner at Lingfield and Newmarket the last twice, he switches back to the all-weather with obvious claims.

Boilermaker recorded a first career success at Sandown last month and, with confidence boosted, the sole three-year-old in the field ought to make his presence felt on just his third all-weather run.

Thomas Faulkner's V Power merits respect on the pick of his form, while Letmebetheboss and Fair Dinkum complete the shortlist.

5.55 Newbury - Somers Isles and Bidsta clash in hot fillies maiden

Somers Isles and Bidsta clash in a hot edition of this IRE Incentive, It Pays To Buy Irish Maiden Fillies' Stakes at 5.55pm.

The Andrew Balding-trained Somers Isle made a pleasing start to her career when runner-up at Newmarket last month and, with the yard in cracking form, she could go one better under Oisin Murphy.

Richard Spencer's Starburster showed ability when getting the hang of things late on debut at Windsor and granted natural progression she looks an each-way player.

George Boughey's Bidsta is a fascinating newcomer for Victorious Racing. A 380,000-guineas purchase at two, she is closely related to useful sprinter Ferrous and should be in the mix for a yard who have done well with juveniles this summer.

4.45 Newbury - Maiden with several interesting types including Yabreen, Solar Swing and Perfect Strike feature.

Sports.title: Mayer: I feel unbeatable - Cameron fight won't be close!
Sports.content:
Mikaela Mayer says she feels "unbeatable" and that her blockbuster unification fight against Chantelle Cameron for the world super welterweight titles won't be close.

British WBO title holder Cameron (22-1, 8 KOs) faces American Mayer (22-2, 5 KOs) at the bp pulse LIVE arena on Saturday - live on Sky Sports - with every bout on the MVPW-06 main card pitting a UK fighter against a US opponent.

WBA and WBC champion Mayer has no shortage of respect for Cameron - who has won her last four fights since a rematch defeat to Katie Taylor in 2023 - but has backed her own ability to unify the titles in front of what is set to be a hostile Birmingham crowd.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mikaela Mayer says she and Chantelle Cameron are at the peak of their powers and that the super welterweight showdown can only lead to 'an action-packed' fight.

"I feel better than ever," Mayer told Sky Sports. "I just know I just feel unbeatable right now. I feel in a great position and I can't wait to get out to the UK and do my thing.

"[Cameron] is good at what she does. She's an aggressive fighter. She lets her hands go.

"She fights at a fast pace and so do I. So that's going to make for a very exciting fight for the fans.

"But I just don't think it's going to be as close and as much of a war as everyone thinks.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Chantelle Cameron can't wait for her unified world super welterweight title fight with Mikaela Mayer in Birmingham on 29 August.

"There's probably a handful of people who think I'm stupid for coming to the UK and going onto Chantelle's turf, but I'm just confident in myself right now.

"I'm fighting better than I've ever fought, smarter than I've ever been. And I just believe in myself.

"I feel like no matter where I go, I'm still going to kick butt. So it could be here. It could be there. I'm taking the win."

Mayer pointed to her "versatility" as a defining factor come Saturday, insisting nothing can prepare Cameron for the new and improved version of the 36-year-old that awaits.

"I'm really hard to train for because I've developed so much these last 10 months of being in the gym," Mayer told Sky Sports.

"I know I haven't fought since last October but the things I'm doing now, it's really impossible for Chantelle to have trained for me at this point.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mikaela Mayer, Chantelle Cameron, Caroline Dubois and Amelia Moore face off ahead of their MVP 06 clashes on Saturday.

"I'm going to do everything I can to make it a very obvious win, maybe a stoppage, we'll see, but I know I'm coming out with my hand raised.

"I've worked on making sure that my inside game and when I do press forward that my defence is tighter and I'm the one landing my shots. I'll definitely be using a little bit of everything I've got, but knowing mine and Chantelle's styles there will definitely be moments where it will be a dog fight."

Mayer vs Cameron - fighter records

Mikaela Mayer Wins 22 Losses 2

Chantelle Cameron Wins 22 Losses 1

'A win would be one of the best moments of my career'

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mikaela Mayer is supremely confident she'll beat Chantelle Cameron when the pair clash on 29 August, live on Sky Sports.

The 35-year-old Cameron won the WBO super welterweight title - a belt Mayer had vacated just months after beating Mary Spencer for it - with a dominant victory over Michaela Kotaskova in April.

The significance of the chance to become unified world champion by reclaiming the WBO crown is not lost on Mayer, with the American describing the prospect of victory as a career-defining moment.

"[A win would be] definitely up there with one of the best [moments].

"I've had a pretty awesome career. Even though I've gone through some ups and downs, I think that's what makes my career even more special and what makes these big fights that are ahead of me extra special.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Chantelle Cameron says she has been waiting a long time for a big name clash with Mikaela Mayer and put their super welterweight world titles on the line.

"I've had to go through trials and tribulations - I've had to adjust, I've had to make changes in my team and keep continuing to get better - and I've done that.

"Going in there and having a dominating performance against someone like Chantelle Cameron, who is very highly respected - the only person to beat Katie Taylor - that's going to definitely be one of the best moments of my career thus far."

The upcoming bout may not be the last between the two, with Mayer revealing that a rematch clause has been included in the contract of both fighters:

"Well, Chantelle and I do have a rematch clause on both of our ends, which is unique, but if it's the type of fight that everyone expects, then why not do a rematch?

"Why not give it to the world again? I have no problem giving a rematch when it's, when it's justified.

"Do I want to kick her butt so bad that she doesn't even want to activate that rematch clause? Of course. But if she does, we can go again."

Watch MVPW-06 in Birmingham, headlined by Mikaela Mayer vs Chantelle Cameron and with Caroline Dubois also in action, live on August 29 on Sky Sports. Get Sky Sports or stream boxing with no contract.

Sports.title: Wolff 'not at all' disappointed by Verstappen's new Red Bull deal
Sports.content:
Mercedes chief Toto Wolff says he is "not at all" disappointed by Max Verstappen having committed to Red Bull with a new contract that runs until 2030.

Ahead of the Formula 1 season resuming with Verstappen's home Dutch Grand Prix over the weekend, Red Bull ended speculation over the four-time world champion's future by announcing the extension.

While Verstappen's previous deal was set to run until 2028, exit clauses in the agreement meant the 28-year-old would have been free to join another team in 2027, with possible switches to Mercedes and McLaren having been the subject of significant speculation.

Wolff made a very public pursuit of Verstappen after Lewis Hamilton announced in February 2024 that he was leaving Mercedes to join Ferrari in 2025, and the Mercedes boss appeared to still be interested in signing the Dutchman last season

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Verstappen admits that, with V8 engines' potential return in 2030, there may be another opportunity for him to reassess his future in F1

However, Wolff has insisted in recent months that he is happy with his driver pairing of Kimi Antonelli and George Russell, who sit first and second, respectively, at the top of the Drivers' Championship after Sunday's race in Zandvoort.

Asked about Verstappen's new contract in an interview with Sky Sports F1 on Saturday in Zandvoort, Wolff said: "Most important was that we had the clarity in the team since a long time.

"We're committed to George and Kimi, and in a way, that was just a logical consequence what happened now.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff had previously downplayed suggestions Verstappen could join his team

"Silly season is officially cancelled now, and everybody can concentrate on the racing."

Pushed on whether he felt any disappointment about the length of Verstappen's commitment to Red Bull, Wolff added: "No, not at all.

"We know each other well. With Kimi and George, it's the perfect set-up we have and the perfect line-up, so there is no disappointment."

Rosberg: I don't think Max had any options

The cooling of Wolff's interest in Verstappen appears as though it may have been influenced by the hugely impressive form that has put Antonelli in control of the championship.

The Italian, who turned 20 on Tuesday, has unexpectedly outperformed the far more experienced Russell to build a 59-point advantage over his team-mate at the top of the standings.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the 2026 Dutch Grand Prix

While Mercedes showed huge faith in Antonelli by fast-tracking him in as Hamilton's replacement as a teenager, an inconsistent rookie campaign left doubt over whether he would be able to live up to expectations.

However, his 2026 form, which saw him break countless records by winning five successive races after finishing second in the season opener, could potentially have made Wolff reconsider whether bringing Verstappen to Mercedes remained necessary.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player A 360-degree look at Verstappen’s race-ending crash at the Dutch Grand Prix on Sunday

McLaren appeared to be similarly content with their current driver line-up of reigning world champion Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri, who have combined to lead the Woking squad to successive constructors' titles.

Sky Sports F1 pundit Nico Rosberg, who won the 2016 world championship with Mercedes, said: "It's fantastic news for Formula 1 because Max Verstappen is the greatest driver at the moment, and we want him to stay here. He's a phenomenal driver!

"He was thinking about taking some time off, or stopping F1 for a while, so that's great.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Nico Rosberg discusses Verstappen's contract extension with Red Bull, saying it's a 'super important message' for the team

"I don't think he had any options. He was in talks with McLaren, but I think that was just to strengthen his position at Red Bull.

"Red Bull need stability so you offer him a bit more money, and the range is from £70-90m a year, so let's land on £80m - which is a lot of money!"

Sports.title: St Helens legend Lomax announces retirment at end of season
Sports.content:
St Helens legend Jonny Lomax is to retire at the end of the 2026 Super League season, he announced on Tuesday.

Lomax, who has not featured since fracturing his jaw in Saints' defeat by Warrington Wolves in June, has made 388 appearances for the club, winning five Grand Finals, one Challenge Cup and a World Club Challenge.

He won four caps for Great Britain and 11 for England, which included a World Cup final appearance against Australia in 2017.

Lomax confirmed the move with a post on his Instagram that read: "At the end of 2026, I will call time on my playing career. This was something I always planned, and those closest to me have always been aware of.

"Over the last 20 years [18 professionally], I have been able to live out a boyhood dream. Achieving far more than I could ever have imagined. Representing and captaining my hometown club and, of course, the pinnacle, representing England and Great Britain.

"I will retire at the age of 36, grateful for the life the game has given me, knowing I have given it everything I could, with the scars to prove it [19 operations, including 12 knee ops by the age of 26]. Despite this, I still feel lucky.

"For those that have supported me throughout it all... I hope I have been able to do you proud."

Saints are currently on 28 points and seventh in the Super League standings, one place outside of the play-off positions with three games to go.

They need to leapfrog one of Hull KR (sixth, 30 points), Leigh Leopards (fifth, 32 points) or Wakefield Trinity (fourth, 32 points) down the stretch.

Current Super League leaders Leeds Rhinos, as well as Wigan Warriors - tied on 38 points but with an inferior point differential - and Warrington Wolves, two back in third, have already qualified for the play-offs.

Sky Sports will show every game of the Super League live this season, including two matches each round exclusively live. The remaining five matches will be broadcast on Sky Sports+.

Sports.title: Serena and Alcaraz dazzle in mixed doubles before exit
Sports.content:
Star pairing Serena Williams and Carlos Alcaraz reached the quarter-finals of the US Open mixed doubles before being beaten by fourth seeds Belinda Bencic and Flavio Cobolli.

Williams - a 23-time Grand Slam singles champion - returned to tennis in June at the age of 44 and secured her first professional win since 2022 as she and Alcaraz beat Britain's Lloyd Glasspool and partner Erin Routliffe in their opening match.

It was also seven-time major winner Alcaraz's first match back on tour after a wrist injury sidelined the reigning men's singles champion since April. The 22-year-old was born five years after Williams won the 1998 mixed doubles title at Flushing Meadows.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the US Open Mixed Doubles match between Serena Williams & Carlos Alcaraz vs Erin Routliffe & LLoyd Glasspool

The dynamic pairing bounced back from a slow start to claim a 5-3 4-1 opening victory over Routliffe and Glasspool, much to the delight of fans inside Arthur Ashe Stadium.

"I never expected to be back on this court," Williams said. "I never thought this would happen."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Carlos Alcaraz and Serena Williams react to Mixed Doubles US Open victory

With their quarter-final match scheduled immediately afterwards, Williams and Alcaraz ultimately ran out of puff as Bencic and Cobolli triumphed 5-4 4-1, the latter then having hailed their opponents pre-match as "the queen of tennis and the king of now."

The question now is whether Williams will seek an encore performance in women's doubles alongside older sister Venus, having already ruled out a repeat of her singles appearance at Wimbledon.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Serena Williams and Carlos Alcaraz won the first set of their Mixed Doubles match at the US Open

Djokovic and Sabalenka suffer early exit

Top seeds Novak Djokovic and Aryna Sabalenka were bounced out of the tournament in the opening match on Arthur Ashe, falling to a 1-4 4-2 10-2 ‌defeat to Britain's Henry Patten and Katerina Siniakova.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the US Open Mixed Doubles match between Aryna Sabalenka & Novak Djokovic vs Katerina Siniakova & Henry Patten

Djokovic, a ​24-time Grand Slam singles champion, and four-time major winner Sabalenka made a strong start by ​taking the opening set, but doubles specialists Patten and ‌Siniakova hit back to claim the second before dominating the tiebreak ​to secure a place in the quarter-finals.

Siniakova sealed the upset in style with an ace out wide on match ​point, ending the tournament hopes of the ⁠star-studded pairing.

"It wasn't looking very ⁠good for a while, in this format we play one bad game and all ‌of a sudden the first set's gone," Patten said.

"We knew the same could happen in the second, and we played ‌an amazing tiebreak. Kat acing Novak on match point was great."

The mixed doubles championship is once again being staged in the week before the singles main draw, after organisers revamped ⁠the format last year to attract more ​leading singles players by reducing the field and ​giving the event a standalone slot on the ​calendar.

The revamped format proved a commercial success in its ⁠debut year, drawing sell-out crowds and attracting many of the sport's biggest singles names despite criticism from some doubles specialists, ⁠who argued it marginalised established pairings.

Defending champions dumped out in first round

Italian ​duo Sara Errani and Andrea Vavassori went on to ​retain the title by defeating Iga Swiatek and Casper Ruud in last year's final, but suffered a first-round exit this year.

Mirra Andreeva and Andrey Rublev beat the defending champions 1-4 4-1 11-9 in the opening round, before clinching a semi-final spot with a 4-1 4-5 10-5 victory over Diana Shnaider and Casper Ruud.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Gael Monfils hit an incredible shot during his mixed doubles match at the US Open

They next face Czech pair Karolína Muchova and Jakub Mensik in one of Wednesday's semi-finals, with Bencic and Cobolli facing husband and wife partnership Gael Monfils and Elina Svitolina in the other after they edged out Patten and Siniakova in the last eight.

The final two follow the two semis on Wednesday night will resemble a regular match, with traditional sets to six games.

Sports.title: Leeds earn second win at Forest in three days in Carabao Cup
Sports.content:
Leeds United registered a second win at Nottingham Forest in three days as they booked their spot in the Carabao Cup third round.

Daniel Farke's side took the three Premier League points home on Saturday and earned a 2-0 victory in the League Cup thanks to goals from Dan James and James Justin.

Having not won at the City Ground since 1972 before the weekend, they have now triumphed there twice in 72 hours as the Yorkshire club enjoy a winning start to the new campaign.

It is not the start new Forest boss Oliver Glasner was looking for as things are yet to click, though additions are on the way with a £50m deal agreed for Chelsea striker Liam Delap.

Neither side will have been jumping for joy at the prospect of a rematch so soon after Saturday's Premier League opener.

But Forest enjoyed some early promise as James Trafford was forced into a great save in the 10th minute when he had to fend away Ola Aina's cross-shot, which almost left him wrongfooted.

Then Justin was in the right place at the right time to stop Igor Jesus' header from going in.

Leeds came into it and should have gone in front midway through the first half when James got in down the right, but his pull-back was just behind Sean Longstaff, who shot straight at Matz Sels.

Image: James Justin scores Leeds' second goal at Forest

Both sides were going for it and Leeds defender Joe Rodon denied Chris Wood with a brilliant last-ditch tackle while Sels kept out James' low effort at the other end.

The Wales international showed the required composure five minutes after the restart.

Aina's wayward header allowed Longstaff to gallop forward and he played in James, who clipped home.

Forest almost hit straight back as Arnaud Kalimuendo's cutback was perfect for Wood, but Trafford did brilliantly to stop his effort from going into the bottom corner, before Noah Okafor sent an effort just wide as Leeds staged a rapid counter-attack.

Leeds sealed the victory with 15 minutes remaining but there was nothing pretty about it.

Lucas Nmecha tried to claim it as his bundled effort was blocked on the line by Williams, with Justin finally putting the ball into the back of the net.

The managers...

Nottingham Forest boss Oliver Glasner told Sky Sports

"This is a little bit the assessment after six weeks here, that maybe - and not just in the team, it's maybe in the club - that there's a little bit of ignoring the reality.

"Right now, we are far away from where we want to be, and what I'm really convinced in that where we will be.

"The fact is that this team had a relegation battle for nine months. Very turbulent season and it ended with a huge effort to stay in the league, and this is our starting point.

"It's really very important not to blame anybody because sometimes I tell them facts and they say, 'Oh, Glasner is complaining'.

"No, no, no. But then maybe your best midfielder [Elliot Anderson] leaves the club and now we expect we compete for European places because Oliver Glasner is in. Sorry, this is what I can't deliver within six weeks.

"I'm no magician, no messiah, just hard work. That is what we have to do.

"It doesn't make sense talking about seventh two years ago. It's hard, it's tough, but if you ignore the reality then you live in dreamland and this is never the best thing to do."

Leeds boss Daniel Farke told Sky Sports:

"This is what we came for, and this was my main goal.

"You play a cup run to go through. Very happy with the level of the performance, because we had to wait very long for a win here at Nottingham and to do this two times within three days at such a tough ground, this remarkable level of performance was outstanding.

"Saturday was really a tight game, but today I think it's not in doubt that it was a fully deserved win."

Sports.title: All Blacks need late surge to avoid shock defeat to Lions
Sports.content:
New Zealand fought back from an 18-point ‌deficit in the second half to beat the Lions 41-35 and avoid a shock defeat at Ellis Park on Tuesday.

It means that the All Blacks have swept all four provincial teams to remain undefeated on their six-week, eight-match tour of South Africa, on top of beating the Springboks 33-16 in ​the first Test at the weekend.

New Zealand fielded only three players from that Saturday Test victory over South Africa on the same ground and involved five injury replacements summoned on tour - including one who arrived on Monday - as well as giving a debut to prop Saula Ma'u.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights as New Zealand scored five tries to beat South Africa 33-16 at Ellis Park and take a 1-0 lead in the four-Test series of Rugby's Greatest Rivalry

Their defence struggled and missed 19 tackles over the course of the contest that saw them trail 14-0 after seven minutes.

They were still behind at half-time and 35-17 behind in the 47th minute, as the Lions threatened to become the first South African provincial side to beat New Zealand since Orange Free State, now known as the Cheetahs, in 1976.

But like the Stormers, Sharks and Bulls who the All Blacks had already beaten, the Lions are out of season and not match fit.

Having not played since May 30 in the United Rugby Championship quarter-finals, New Zealand eventually came storming back in the last 30 minutes with four successive tries.

Rieko Ioane scored two of them, flanker Ethan Blackadder went over for a second time to earn the All Blacks the lead for the first time in the 62nd minute, while a second too by winger Emoni Narawa in the 79th finally settled the touring side's nerves.

"The Lions came out hissing," Blackadder said. "But we stayed composed and found a way in the end. They were quality tonight."

Blackadder - whose father Todd was on the last traditional tour in 1996 - was one of the New Zealand standouts along with inside center Timoci Tavatavanawai, Narawa, and fly-half Richie Mo'unga, back from Japan and in a black jersey for the first time since the 2023 World Cup final.

All Blacks coach Dave Rennie thought Blackadder was phenomenal. "He's got a massive engine and was everywhere," he said.

Blackadder's Test prospects also improved after Anton Segner was ruled out of the rest of the tour.

Segner was a late withdrawal from the first Test reserves due to an ankle injury that's needed two surgeries. The injury was assessed as acute inflammatory arthritis and he won't be replaced in the squad.

Mo'unga, like New Zealand, got better as the game got older, but he and Beauden Barrett could convert only three of the team's seven tries.

On the other hand, Chris Smith, at home, converted all five of the Lions tries and hit the post with a long penalty.

Sports.title: Wilson scores on full debut as Brentford hit Birmingham for six
Sports.content:
Callum Wilson scored just six minutes into his full debut and captain Nathan Collins converted two headers as Brentford routed Championship side Birmingham 6-1.

The 34-year-old Wilson, who joined on a free transfer from relegated West Ham, seized his first opportunity with a crisp finish which took a deflection off defender Dael Fry, who had a debut to forget.

Brentford's Premier League quality was evident throughout and although Blues equalised through Demarai Gray just before the half-hour they were level for just seven minutes.

Image: Callum Wilson scored six minutes into his full Brentford debut

Lax defending saw Aaron Hickey and Collins score in quick succession to effectively seal the tie before half-time, with Mikkel Damsgaard getting on the end of a counter-attack to add the fourth.

Igor Thiago's smart close-range finish sent fans streaming for the exit, missing Collins' second header.

The Bees, quarter-finalists last season, had not beaten Birmingham in six previous meetings, the last a goalless draw more than five years ago in the Championship before they went on to bigger and better things which their ambitious hosts now hope to emulate.

Birmingham's priority remains promotion so, after opening with two league draws, boss Chris Davies made six changes, including goalkeeper Ryan Allsop, Fry and Argentinian striker Luis Vazquez.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Callum Wilson produced a composed finish to put Brentford ahead just six minutes into his first competitive start for the club.

However, the gulf to a Premier League squad was evident as Keith Andrews retained only three of the team which demolished Tottenham and saw three of his newcomers score and another, Yehor Yarmoliuk, run the midfield before he was forced off with injury.

Davies wants to meet the club's aspirations by playing their way out of the Championship but it proved their undoing before they had even had chance to get a foothold in the game as they fell foul of Brentford's high press at a short goal-kick.

Paik Seung-ho was slow to react to the loose ball and Yarmoliuk played in Wilson to fire home first-time from the edge of the area with the aid of a deflection.

But a miscontrol by Jannik Schuster saw the centre-back booked for bringing down Vazquez and from Paik's short free-kick Gray drilled a deflected shot through a crowd of players.

It was a brief moment of joy in an otherwise chastening night as a failure to deal with Vitaly Janelt's chip and Wilson's strength allowed Hickey to fire home an angled shot.

Collins jumped in front of Fry to nod in a simple header from Jaidon Anthony's cross but a ruthless Brentford went for the kill and, after bringing on the likes of Igor Thiago, Kevin Schade and Mamadou Sangare, scored three more after the break.

The managers...

Birmingham's Chris Davies:

"My message to supporters tonight is 'sorry'. It's not very pleasant and I can understand how frustrating it is for them.

"It was a very tough evening for us, a painful evening, and incredibly disappointing to lose a game 6-1 at home.

"There were many situations where we were just not good enough to compete and I take ultimate responsibility for it - and the players will have to do it in their own minds.

"We were beaten by a team a long way ahead of us in every aspect. Was 6-1 a fair reflection? Probably."

Brentford's Keith Andrews:

"I didn't really blink an eyelid making so many changes.

"There is a huge narrative around cup games with coaches making changes but with the squad we have, there are fine margins between who plays and doesn't play.

"We needed to compete really hard to play the game we wanted. I thought overall we produced a really good performance."

Sports.title: Celtic throw away four-goal aggregate lead to crash out of Champions League against Lask
Sports.content:
Celtic threw away a four-goal lead in Austria as they missed out on the Champions League for the second year running. The Scottish champions looked to be cruising into the league stage when Callum McGregor put them 4-0 up on aggregate against Lask with a 21st-minute deflected strike.

However, they went on to endure one of their all-time European lows with a 5-1 defeat in Linz delivering a £20m-plus blow.

The Hoops had other chances in the first half but the Austrians gave themselves a lifeline when Moses Usor pounced on a loose pass from Benjamin Nygren to level on the night in the 32nd minute.

The tie began to spiral out of Celtic’s control early in the second half as Robert Ljubicic and Samuel Adeniran netted from outside the box. Martin O’Neill’s side looked like they would cling on but Florian Flecker nodded home from close range in stoppage-time to spark an additional 30 minutes.

Celtic had disappeared as an attacking force at half-time and Adeniran delivered the knockout blow that sends them into the Europa League.

The Hoops exited on penalties at the playoff stage last season after failing to sign a proven striker before drawing a blank against Kairat Almaty. Fans will this year question the decision to sell Arne Engels just ahead of the first leg after they lost control in midfield in Austria.

The quality of Celtic’s finishing had been the difference in Glasgow but Lask created chances throughout and the second leg started in similar fashion.

Celtic looked to extend their lead. Mika Baur stabbed an early chance just wide and Kasper Høgh forced a couple of first-half saves from decent opportunities. McGregor opened the scoring in between those chances when he drilled a first-time shot in off a defender after Yang Hyun-jun had played a one-two with Kieran Tierney.

The home side had exerted some pressure just before McGregor’s goal and they levelled following careless play from Nygren. The Austrian champions pulled a goal back three minutes after the restart when Usor outmuscled Auston Trusty and worked the ball inside for Ljubicic to drive home from 20 yards.

View image in fullscreen Dismayed Celtic players react to their capitulation against Lask. Photograph: Severin Aichbauer/SPP/Shutterstock

Celtic endured some nervy moments before they conceded again in the 58th minute when Adeniran curled a wonderful first-time strike into the top corner from 25 yards.
