Because the Ministry has identified the Minister’s vehicle as a specific government vehicle from a stated fleet, it argues the allegation against him requires more than institutional proximity or hierarchy — it requires a demonstrated link showing the particular vehicle was unlawfully acquired, that the Minister knew of an unlawful source, that he solicited an improper benefit, or that he entered into an arrangement with alleged cartel actors. The Ministry says none of those links have been shown.

Nor, the Ministry argues, is it improper on its face for the Justice Ministry to request a vehicle from the LNP. The Ministry says it lacked a budgetary allotment at the relevant time for a new ministerial vehicle, and that ordinary administrative communication between the Ministry and the police force it supervises is not, by itself, evidence of wrongdoing — supervision, it argues, does not eliminate the need for institutional coordination.

The Ministry’s Broader Charge: A “Fishing Expedition”

The Ministry characterized Kollie’s overall pattern as casting an unusually wide net — vehicles, police officers, past dismissals, institutional relationships, alleged conversations, housing projects, historical allegations and the wider drug crisis — and then presenting the accumulation of suspicion as though volume itself amounted to proof against the Minister. The number of allegations, the Ministry argues, does not cure the absence of proof connecting a specific person to a specific unlawful act; ten unproven insinuations, in its framing, do not become one proven fact simply because they are repeated together. The Ministry draws a distinction between saying “this matter should be investigated” and declaring “this official is compromised” or demanding resignation as though guilt were already established — the first, it says, is a call for inquiry; the second is a public verdict issued without the evidentiary chain to support it.

The Ministry went further, framing Kollie’s campaign as a potential distraction from the underlying investigation rather than a contribution to it. Because the fight against drug trafficking depends on investigators following financial trails, communications and verifiable relationships, the Ministry argued that a national conversation pulled toward defending or debating unproven allegations can divert attention from the evidentiary work needed to identify and prosecute traffickers. The Ministry stopped short of accusing Kollie of intentionally helping the network under investigation, but argued that irresponsible, unsubstantiated allegations can have that practical effect regardless of intent — and suggested, in unusually pointed language for an official government response, that the matter could rise to the level of criminal interference with an active investigation, a characterization Kollie has not publicly responded to and which this newspaper has not independently assessed.

What the Ministry Is Asking For

The Ministry’s closing position is that the burden now rests on Kollie to move from accusation to substantiation. If the underlying claim is that the vehicle came from drug money, the Ministry argues the evidence must connect the money, the purchase, the vehicle and the Minister specifically — not merely gesture at proximity between the Ministry and a broader scandal. If Kollie disputes the Ministry’s stated procurement trail, the Ministry says the proper response is documentary evidence identifying the specific discrepancy, not repetition of the original claim. “We call on the Ministry of Justice to remain focused on the lawful dismantling of criminal drug networks,” the Ministry said of its own mandate, adding that those who make grave public allegations should be held to the same evidentiary standard they demand of public officials.

What This Doesn’t Resolve

This is not the first time a vehicle has become a flashpoint inside Liberia’s drug investigation. LDEA Officer-in-Charge Fitzgerald Biago recused himself earlier this year over a separate, unresolved allegation involving vehicles accepted from a figure tied to the case. That precedent is part of why a vehicle allegation involving the country’s chief law enforcement officer has drawn this much attention so quickly — Liberians have already watched one senior official’s position become entangled with exactly this kind of claim once this year. The Ministry’s rebuttal is detailed and specific about the Minister’s own vehicle. It does not, however, address the broader question raised by Kollie’s original allegations concerning Coleman and the three “cash-gifted cars” — a claim the Ministry treats as a separate matter rather than one it is defending. Tuesday’s closed-door Senate session, called specifically because of the vehicle questions, remains undisclosed. Until its substance becomes public, or until either side produces the documentary evidence each is demanding of the other, this remains what the Ministry itself says it should not become: a contest of accusations rather than a settled account of the facts.

World.title: Liberia: Gongloe Urges Government to Match Humanitarian Generosity With Capacity as Liberia Receives U.S. Deportees
World.content:
Monrovia — Renowned Liberian human rights and constitutional lawyer Cllr. Tiawan Saye Gongloe has called on the Liberian government to carefully balance its longstanding tradition of humanitarianism with the country’s limited capacity as it begins receiving third-country nationals deported from the United States.

Gongloe’s comments come as Liberia has agreed to receive up to 1,200 foreign nationals transferred from the United States over a one-year period. The first group of 20 deportees arrived in Liberia last week, triggering public debate over the government’s decision and its potential implications for the country.

In a commentary on the policy, Gongloe said Liberia has a “long and honorable tradition” of welcoming people fleeing difficult circumstances in their home countries.

He recalled that during the Biafran Civil War in Nigeria in the 1960s, Liberia received thousands of Nigerians. He also pointed to Liberia’s role in providing refuge to Sudanese during conflicts in Sudan and welcoming Africans fleeing colonialism and liberation struggles across the continent.

“Liberia was also a home for Africans during the struggle for independence across the continent and during the liberation struggles in Southern Africa,” Gongloe said.

He recalled seeing students from countries including Angola, South Africa, Namibia, Zimbabwe and Uganda at the University of Liberia, Cuttington University and various high schools.

According to Gongloe, Liberia’s history of hospitality extends beyond Africa and is deeply connected to the country’s founding as a refuge for formerly enslaved Africans and free-born Black people of African descent seeking freedom and security.

He also noted that Liberians themselves have benefited from the generosity of other nations.

“Since 1980, military rule, political persecution and civil conflict forced many Liberians to seek safety abroad,” he said, citing the United States, Canada, Europe, Australia and African countries that opened their doors to Liberians during periods of crisis.

“We therefore cannot reasonably become a country that rejects people simply because they are facing difficult circumstances elsewhere,” Gongloe argued.

However, he stressed that Liberia’s humanitarian tradition must be weighed against its present-day socioeconomic realities.

“The concern is not whether Liberia should remain welcoming. It should be whether Liberia has the capacity,” he said.

Gongloe said Liberia today faces serious challenges, including unemployment, food insecurity, inadequate healthcare and education, poor housing, limited electricity and insufficient access to clean water.

He said those challenges raise legitimate questions about whether the country can responsibly accommodate a large number of additional people without placing further pressure on already strained public services.

The human rights lawyer said the issue deserves even greater consideration because many of the individuals being transferred to Liberia are coming from a socioeconomic environment significantly better than what they are likely to encounter upon arrival.

“The question, therefore, is not whether Liberia should close its doors,” Gongloe said. “It is whether we can responsibly provide decent living conditions, healthcare, housing, security and opportunities for those we receive without worsening the hardship already faced by ordinary Liberians.”

Gongloe ultimately urged the government to preserve Liberia’s reputation as a welcoming nation while ensuring that humanitarian commitments are supported by adequate resources and planning.

“Liberia should remain a welcoming country. But humanitarian generosity must be matched by humanitarian capacity,” he concluded.

World.title: Liberia: How a Gbarnga Tailor Built a School That Trains Hundreds and Offers a Model for Small Businesses in Rural Areas
World.content:
ACD Vocational Training Institute’s main building in Gbarnga, Bong County, houses its vocational training, school uniform production and literacy programs, with a business center operating on the ground floor. Credit: Nukanah Kollie/New Narratives

Summary:

ACD Vocational Training Institute in Gbarnga has trained hundreds of young people, especially women, over 25 years after starting with one borrowed sewing machine, creating pathways to employment and self-reliance without government or donor funding.

Despite its success, ACD faces challenges including high training costs, limited equipment and unpaid student fees, mirroring broader struggles in Liberia’s vocational training and small business sectors.

Experts say ACD’s self-sustaining model offers a blueprint for workforce development throughout the country, showing how local ownership and market partnerships can succeed without donor dependency.

By Nukanah Kollie with New Narratives

GBARNGA, Bong County —A bright blue two-story building stands in central Gbarnga, overlooking Broad Street. Red railings surround the balcony, where freshly sewn school uniforms hang beneath a sign reading, “ACD Vocational Training, School Uniform Production, Literacy Program.”

Inside, shelves hold colorful fabrics as sewing machines hum across the center. Founder Joseph M. Kamara, 66, sits on a wooden bench behind a black sewing machine, a measuring tape around his neck, turning cloth into uniforms while leading the self-financed vocational campus he has built over 25 years.

“I think the best thing to do for our people is impact knowledge in them,” said Kamara as he inspected a uniform completed by one of his employees. “When we talk about empowerment, I think the best empowerment is what gives them skills.”

Kamara has grown Accelerated Career Development Incorporated, known as ACD, which from a single borrowed sewing machine in 2001 into a two-campus institution that produces school uniforms sold across the region and creates opportunities for hundreds of women and young people.

Today, the school trains students in professional tailoring, driving, satellite installation, catering, hairdressing and weaving. It has grown at a time when experts say practical skills training is increasingly important in Liberia. The 2022 Liberia Population and Housing Census found that more than half of rural Liberians have no formal education, while rural literacy stands at 44 percent.

Nationally, Liberia’s vocational training sector has grown through international partnerships. A mid-term evaluation of the €25 million ($29 million) Youth Rising Project which ran from 2018 – 2024 rated the program as “satisfactory” but flagged heavy reliance on outside funding and gaps in graduate support.

Liberia’s private sector is dominated by small businesses. The World Bank’s 2024 Liberia National Establishment Census counted more than 40,000 businesses nationwide, 86 percent of them micro-enterprises. Development experts say their growth is a key factor in job creation and economic stimulation. But the World Bank has found that entrepreneurs continue to face limited access to finance, high interest rates and unreliable electricity.

Abraham Tumbey, a staff member at the UN Development Program, said vocational training is critical to addressing Liberia’s youth and female unemployment in a post-conflict economy where formal education cannot scale fast enough to absorb the labor force.

Joseph M.Kamara, founder of ACD Vocational Training Institute, works at a sewing machine in the school’s uniform store in Gbarnga, Bong County. Credit: Nukanah Kollie/New Narratives.

A School Built Almost Entirely By Women, For Women

Roughly 90 percent of ACD’s students are women, many of them single mothers. Kamara said the imbalance is intentional. The last Demographic and Health Survey in 2020 found that women head about one in three Liberian households, carrying the burden of supporting their families alone. Of the 107 students who have completed ACD’s full three-year tailoring program since 2001, about 96 percent have been women.

“Many of the men, they born by women, they leave the children with them, they go by their business, and the women struggle,” Kamara said.

For many women, the training was less about learning a trade than reclaiming independence. Patience Kollie, 40, a mother of three, completed ACD’s tailoring course before becoming an instructor in 2019 after the father of her children left the family.

“I want to tell all women out there who may be facing hard times,” she said. “Whether ACD can help you or people can help you, if you are serious, you can even pay your school fees yourself.”Martha Paye, 26, a mother of two and eight months pregnant, became an instructor in 2022 after her partner abandoned the family.

Former graduate and instructor Martha Paye, eight months pregnant, works alongside her colleagues at ACD’s new space known as “Annex Two”. Credit: Nukanah Kollie/ New Narratives.

“I decided to come to ACD to learn something, at least to help myself, because there was no support,” she said. “If I say I won’t go to school, we shall not have anybody to send me to school, and it will be suffering for myself.”

Korpo Boakai, another graduate turned instructor, said the training transformed her life.

“I able to support my home,” she said. “I’m trying to do something good for my children, and I change my life. I able to support my three children.”

Beyond tailoring: uniforms, employment and a growing footprint

The institution has relied on commercial bank loans seven times over the years to sustain and expand operations rather than turning to donor funding. He said the key to his success has been being careful with money.

“When you are doing business, you don’t play with the business money. We have always been very careful with it, not to tamper with it. We also go around looking for contracts, and the people we are training are our manpower.”

Kamara said professional tailoring is the course ACD can guarantee leads to work because graduates are absorbed into the school’s own production operations, including a uniform business that has grown into a storefront on Broad Street.

Tumbey said connecting graduates directly to production contracts turns capability into capital.

“Training alone does not put food on the table, market access does,” he said.

The scale is significant. Kamara said ACD partnered with the American Institutes for Research on a contract to produce 17,500 sets of school uniforms distributed across Bong, Lofa, Margibi and Grand Bassa counties. The school has also trained students in Bong, Margibi, Montserrado and parts of Lofa County.

It manufactures graduation gowns annually for Cuttington University. Workers, paid every two weeks based on output, earned a combined US$4,320 producing gowns and hats for Cuttington in June 2025 alone.

Aaron G.V. Juahkollie, Executive Director of the Foundation for International Dignity, said ACD has achieved what many vocational institutions struggle to do: survive without unreliable and unpredictable donor funding.

“The sustainability of any organization is what matters,” he said. “With the fact that they are sustaining themselves up to now, I think they are to be emulated, and government needs to look at them too, especially for the skills they are providing to women in the community.”

He pointed to ACD’s uniforms, tax compliance and 25 years of operation as proof of its credibility.

Persistent struggles faced by all small businesses

Without support from government or donors building the business has been challenging.

“Every day we beg, we go online, we look for people to help this program,” Kamara said.

He listed recurring challenges: high material costs, difficulty paying instructors and students struggling to complete tuition. Students unable to pay can work off fees once advanced enough to contribute to production.

Students echoed those concerns, describing a lack of personal sewing machines and difficulty accessing water.

“We don’t have, money and water around here,” Paye said. Like everyone here. She is hoping some benefactor will step up. “If they can help us with a water pump… that can help us to carry our school far, we’ll be happy.”

Tumbey has recommended that government make available low-interest micro-loans for small businesses like ACD, along with government investment in rural infrastructure – roads, electricity, water access – and tax incentives for businesses that hire and train young people.

One of the newly constructed buildings at ACD vocational training institute’s Annex Two in Gbarnga, Bong County. Credit: Nukanah Kollie

A school uniform for the future

Kamara said ACD’s ambition is to expand uniform production into a full factory capable of supplying government schools nationwide.

“Our first target is government schools,” he said. “We want to target government schools so that any government school in the republic… everything about school uniform, we’re going to produce.”

Tumbey called ACD an example other Liberian entrepreneurs could replicate, proving a movement does not require a massive grant; it can begin with a single borrowed machine.

ACD’s growth continues largely through word of mouth and Kamara’s outreach on local radio, where he encourages young people, particularly women, to enroll.

“If you don’t have any skill in your head, you have no hope,” he said. “But if you get skill in your head as you’re moving, you have hope that you will get something to do.”

Twenty-five years after beginning with one borrowed sewing machine, Kamara’s experiment has become far more than a tailoring school. It is a business, a training center and a source of opportunity for women and young people who might otherwise struggle to find a livelihood.

“You live by what you learn,” Kamara said.

This story is a collaboration with New Narratives as part of the “Investigating Liberia” Reporting Project. Funding was provided by the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency. The donor had no say in the story’s content.

World.title: Weah Consoles Guinea After Conakry Landfill Landslide Kills 30
World.content:
Paynesville — Former Liberian President George Manneh Weah has extended condolences to Guinea’s President Mamady Doumbouya and the people of Guinea following a devastating landslide at a major landfill in the capital, Conakry, that killed at least 30 people and critically injured six others.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

The disaster occurred early Sunday, August 24, when heavy rains triggered a landslide at the Dar es Salaam landfill, a massive open-air waste dump in Conakry. The collapse buried nearby makeshift structures and destroyed several homes.

In a statement issued Tuesday, August 25, the Office of Former President Weah said he conveyed his “profound condolences” to President Doumbouya, the Guinean government and, particularly, families affected by the tragedy.

Weah also wished those injured a speedy recovery, saying he shared in the grief of the Guinean people during what he described as a difficult national moment.

“It is my fervent prayer and hope that you, your Government and the people of the Republic of Guinea, including, but not limited to the bereaved and affected families, in your usual resilience, will take solace in God The Almighty, as you go through this challenging national period of your existence,” Weah said in his message.

Disaster Strikes Before Landfill Closure

The landslide reportedly occurred shortly after 2 a.m. GMT on Sunday following heavy rainfall. Authorities said the rains washed over the enormous heap of refuse at Dar es Salaam, causing the unstable waste pile to collapse onto nearby dwellings.

Authorities launched a search-and-rescue operation to locate possible survivors. Six people were reported seriously injured, while several homes were destroyed.

The landfill had reportedly been designated for closure on Sunday, according to Lt. Col. Baldé Mamadou Bailo, a sanitation official with Guinea’s military engineering battalion.

The disaster has drawn renewed attention to the dangers posed by informal settlements around large waste dumps, particularly during Guinea’s rainy season.

Weah Praises Guinean Resilience

In his condolence message, Weah expressed confidence that President Doumbouya, his government and the Guinean people would overcome the tragedy with renewed strength and hope.

He said Guinea’s resilience would help the country navigate the aftermath of the disaster and urged the affected families to find comfort in their faith.

The former Liberian leader’s message comes as rescue workers and authorities continue efforts to respond to the deadly landslide and assess the full extent of the destruction in Conakry.

Weah concluded by assuring President Doumbouya and the Guinean people of his solidarity as they mourn those who lost their lives.

World.title: PUL Revives Blyden Forum as Top Experts Tackle Liberia’s Drug Trafficking Crisis
World.content:
Monrovia – The Press Union of Liberia is set to relaunch its flagship intellectual platform, the Edward Wilmot Blyden Intellectual Discourse, with a high-level panel discussion focused on Liberia’s escalating drug trafficking crisis and the urgent need to strengthen institutions, accountability and the rule of law.

The forum, scheduled for Wednesday, August 26, comes as Liberia confronts the fallout from major cocaine seizures and growing public concern over the country’s capacity to investigate and prosecute complex drug trafficking cases.

The inaugural edition of the relaunched Blyden Forum will be held under the theme: “Confronting Drug Trafficking: Strengthening Institutions, Advancing Accountability, and Safeguarding the Rule of Law.”

Five prominent voices from government, the legal profession, civil society and the media will lead the discussion.

The panel includes Justice Minister and Attorney General Cllr. N. Oswald Tweh; Gbarpolu County Senator and Chairman of the Senate Committee on Audits and Public Accounts, Amara M. Konneh; President of the Liberia National Bar Association, Cllr. F. Juah Lawson; Executive Director of the Center for Transparency and Accountability in Liberia (CENTAL), Anderson Miamen; and Infinity Broadcasting Corporation (Power FM & TV) Chief Executive Officer Aaron Kollie.

The discussion is expected to examine Liberia’s institutional response to drug trafficking, the effectiveness of ongoing investigations and prosecutions, accountability within law enforcement and justice institutions, and safeguards necessary to protect due process and the rule of law.

The forum also comes amid intense national debate over Liberia’s handling of the multimillion-dollar cocaine investigations, including questions about accountability, transparency and the independence of institutions responsible for enforcing the law.

According to the PUL in a release issued by its President Julius Kanubah, the forum is intended to provide a platform for informed and factual discussion of issues of national importance while bringing together policymakers, civil society actors, academics, journalists and media practitioners.

Named after Edward Wilmot Blyden, the pioneering Liberian journalist, intellectual and statesman, the forum is designed to generate expert perspectives, deepen public understanding and contribute to national policymaking through constructive dialogue.

The PUL said the platform will focus broadly on democratic governance, transparency, accountability and the rule of law—principles it considers essential to Liberia’s long-term stability and development.

The program begins at 11:00 a.m. at the PUL headquarters on Warner Avenue, 9th Street, Sinkor, Monrovia. Guests have been requested to be seated by 10:45 a.m.

World.title: Liberia: AFL Wants 20% Women in Uniform, Takes Recruitment Drive to Sinoe
World.content:
GREENVILLE, Sinoe County — The Armed Forces of Liberia wants women in one of every five uniformed posts, a target that would require nearly tripling their share of the force, and it took that recruitment drive to Sinoe County.

Women make up about 7.5 percent of the AFL, and the government’s goal is 20 percent, according to Junior Aloysius Morris, senior policy analyst at the Ministry of National Defense, who is traveling with the outreach team.

The five-member team includes two enlisted women, Sgt. [Patricia Lincoln] and Sgt. Newton L. Newton, who are talking to women in the county about enlistment requirements, career paths and the work soldiers do. Also on the team are Morris; Boyee S. Mussah, the AFL public relations officer; and Menicond B. Yarkpazna, junior policy analyst at the Ministry of National Defense.

The team is pointing women toward professional training, promotion into leadership and selection for United Nations peacekeeping deployments, which carry allowances and overseas service that few other public-sector jobs in Liberia offer.

The gap the campaign is trying to close is wide and has narrowed slowly. Women hold 11.5 percent of officer positions and 7.1 percent of enlisted positions, according to the project documentation. The Gender and Security Sector National Taskforce put women at 3 percent of the AFL in 2017, then the lowest share of any Liberian security institution, meaning the force has added roughly four and a half percentage points in about nine years.

The Sinoe outreach falls under a project the Ministry of National Defense and the AFL launched with UN Women on Feb. 9, 2026, titled “Strengthening Armed Forces of Liberia’s women active participation in peace and security through deployment to peacekeeping missions,” financed by the Elsie Initiative Fund. Beyond recruitment, the project funds pre-deployment preparation for female and male soldiers, including basic computer training, and public campaigns intended to counter the view of soldiering as men’s work.

The effort rests on an assessment the AFL ran in September 2022 using the Geneva Centre for Security Sector Governance’s Measuring Opportunities for Women in Peace Operations methodology, which examined what inside the institution keeps women from being deployed. The project is also framed against U.N. Security Council Resolution 1325, which calls for more women in the institutions that prevent and settle conflict and in U.N. field operations.

The campaign is designed to reach all 15 counties, grouped into four regions, in phases determined by recruitment potential, population, the presence of secondary schools and universities, and how easily the team can move. Alongside community meetings, the campaign is to run through schools, universities, county authorities, religious leaders and women’s organizations.

Neither the ministry nor the AFL has said what the enlistment numbers from the campaign have been so far, or by what year it expects to reach 20 percent.

World.title: Reform Front Liberia Moves Civic Reform From Ideas to Action
World.content:
Founder and Executive Director: Doug Zack Miller

Paynesville – The Reform Front Liberia, Inc. (TRFLI) is taking its civic reform message beyond discussion and into practical action through a growing platform focused on civic education, public engagement, reading, community development and positive journalism.

Built on the belief that sustainable national progress begins with informed, responsible and engaged citizens, TRFLI is a nonprofit, nonpartisan civic organization committed to education, empowerment, accountability, civic responsibility and constructive national dialogue.

Educate. Empower. Engage. Reform.

During August and September 2026, TRFLI’s mission is taking shape through three flagship programs: TRFL Radio Prime, the Reading & Comprehension Initiative, and The Reformpreneur Magazine.

Together, the initiatives provide platforms through which Liberians can listen, learn, read, think, discuss and participate in efforts to build stronger communities and a stronger Liberia.

From Vision to Action

TRFLI believes reform cannot exist merely as a slogan. It must ultimately be reflected in the way citizens think, communicate, work, lead, learn and participate in their communities.

The organization is therefore developing practical civic platforms that reach Liberians through radio, community education and publishing.

TRFL Radio Prime Launched August 1

TRFL Radio Prime, the organization’s first major public program, officially launched on August 1, 2026.

The weekly program airs every Saturday from 4:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. on Blaze Radio 90.7 FM, providing a platform for civic education, public discussion and conversations about the responsibilities citizens share in Liberia’s development.

Radio Prime promotes informed citizenship, personal responsibility, accountability and constructive dialogue. Rather than viewing national development solely through the actions of government, TRFLI also asks: What responsibility does the citizen have in building the Liberia we want?

The program is sponsored by Uncle Z Spice International, Inc. (UZSII).

Reading & Comprehension Initiative Takes Education Into the Community

Three weeks after launching Radio Prime, TRFLI took another part of its mission directly into the community.

On August 22, 2026, the organization officially launched its Reading & Comprehension Initiative at Kids and Us Preparatory Elementary School in Jackson Hill, Rehab Community, Paynesville.

The initiative is designed to help young adults and adults strengthen practical reading and comprehension skills while building confidence in communication and critical thinking.

Participants engage with reading materials and exercises intended not simply to determine whether they can pronounce words, but whether they can understand, explain, question and apply what they have read.

TRFLI considers reading and comprehension essential to civic reform, arguing that access to information alone is not enough. Citizens must also be able to understand information, evaluate it critically and make informed decisions.

TRFLI in action: Participants engage in reading and comprehension exercises during the official launch of the initiative on August 22, 2026, at Kids and Us Preparatory Elementary School in Jackson Hill, Rehab Community, Paynesville.

“A citizen who can read, understand and think is a citizen who can build, lead and transform.”

The Reformpreneur Magazine Set for September Launch

TRFLI’s third flagship platform, The Reformpreneur Magazine, is scheduled to launch in September 2026.

The digital publication will expand the organization’s educational mission through articles, research, interviews, commentary and positive stories centered on Liberia and its people.

The magazine will cover issues including reform, entrepreneurship, education, agriculture and food security, leadership, civic responsibility, business, community development and the stories of Liberians working to create positive change.

TRFLI also expects the publication to contribute to a stronger culture of reading while connecting Liberians at home with the diaspora and friends of Liberia.

Three Programs, One Civic Mission

The three initiatives are designed to complement one another.

TRFL Radio Prime gives citizens a platform to listen, learn and engage.

The Reading & Comprehension Initiative provides an opportunity to read, understand, question and develop critical-thinking skills.

The Reformpreneur Magazine will provide a platform to read, learn, document ideas and share positive Liberian stories.

The organization describes the rollout as:

August 1: A voice for civic education.

A voice for civic education. August 22: Education in the community.

Education in the community. September: A platform for ideas, research and positive stories.

Why the Reform Front Liberia Was Established

TRFLI says Liberia’s future will depend not only on its political leadership but also on the quality of its citizens, institutions, businesses, educators, professionals, communities and civic organizations.

The organization was established around the conviction that national development requires responsibility at every level of society.

“Government has responsibilities. Institutions have responsibilities. Businesses have responsibilities. Community leaders have responsibilities. And citizens have responsibilities,” the organization says.

TRFLI seeks to encourage a culture in which Liberians become better informed, accept greater personal and civic responsibility, demand accountability appropriately, value education and reading, participate constructively in their communities and contribute solutions rather than merely identifying problems.

Nonpartisan, Civic and Educational

The Reform Front Liberia, Inc. emphasizes that it is not a political party or political campaign organization.

Its mission is civic and focuses on citizens, education, responsibility, accountability, entrepreneurship, community development and Liberia’s long-term progress.

The organization believes Liberians with different political views, backgrounds and experiences can find common ground around education, responsible citizenship, stronger institutions and national development.

Message From the Founder and Executive Director: Doug Zack Miller

Miller says Liberia’s transformation will require more than the efforts of any single individual, organization or government.

“Liberia’s transformation will not come from one person, one organization or one government. It will require citizens who are informed, responsible, educated and willing to participate in building their communities and their country.”

According to Miller, TRFLI was established because reform must move beyond conversation.

“We must educate, organize, build programs and demonstrate through action what responsible citizenship can accomplish.”

He said the organization’s three flagship programs are intended to provide different avenues for civic engagement.

“Radio Prime gives us a voice. Our Reading & Comprehension Initiative takes education directly into the community. The Reformpreneur Magazine will give us another platform to document ideas, entrepreneurship and positive Liberian stories.”

“We are starting deliberately and building step by step,” Miller added. “Our objective is not simply to talk about a better Liberia. We want to participate constructively in building one.”

What Comes Next

TRFLI says it intends to continue developing its programs carefully and sustainably, with an immediate focus on strengthening the three flagship initiatives already underway or scheduled for launch.

Radio Prime will continue its weekly civic education broadcasts, while the Reading & Comprehension Initiative will continue its community-based educational activities.

The first edition of The Reformpreneur Magazine is scheduled for September 2026.

As its organizational capacity grows, TRFLI says it will explore additional educational and community-impact programs consistent with its civic mission, with emphasis on sustainable initiatives with clear and achievable objectives.

An Invitation to Liberia and the Diaspora

The Reform Front Liberia is inviting citizens, educators, professionals, businesses, community organizations, young people, volunteers, Liberians in the diaspora and friends of Liberia to participate in its civic efforts.

Opportunities include volunteering, contributing professional expertise, partnering with programs, sponsoring initiatives and supporting the organization’s educational and community-impact activities.

TRFLI particularly welcomes businesses and institutions that view investment in education, informed citizenship and community development as an investment in Liberia’s future.

World.title: Zesco face Malawi’s Strikers in COSAFA semis
World.content:
Zambian champions Zesco Ndola Girls will face Malawi’s Silver Stars in the semifinals of the ongoing CAF Women’s Champions League | COSAFA Qualifier Botswana 2026.

Zesco and Strikers will clash in the first semifinal on Thursday afternoon.

Strikers booked a date against Zesco after defeating Nsingizini Hotspurs 5-1 on Tuesday evening to make it two wins from three in Group B.

Carolyne Mathyola netted a hat-trick, while there were further strikes from Grace Kakangula and Gladys Banda.

The match between Zesco and Strikers is expected to be another battle between old foes Zambia and Malawi on the COSAFA platform.

Zesco were beaten finalists last year and have more experience, but Strikers have shown enough in this tournament to suggest they can be a match for anyone.

The Ndola-based Zambian champions booked their semi-final spot in style, securing top spot in Group A with a 2-0 victory over hosts Gaborone United at the Gaborone United Stadium on Monday evening.

Zesco finished Group A with maximum 9 points from 3 games: following victories over Lesotho Defence Force (1-0) and Zimbabwe’s Herentals Queens (5-2).

Zesco coach Florence Mwila says her side is ready for the semi-finals.

“We are prepared. This is a tournament so you meet any opponent and you must be prepared,” she told journalists in Gaborone.

Meanwhile, Sundowns confirmed top spot in Group B with a 4-1 win over Costa do Sol in their final pool encounter at the Gaborone United Stadium on Tuesday.

It was another comfortable outing for The Brazilians as goals from Asanda Hadebe, Wendy Shongwe, Ronnel Donnelly and Melinda Kgadiete sealed victory.

Lucia Moçambique scored directly from a corner for Costa do Sol to take her tally in the tournament to four goals and move into the outright lead in the Golden Boot race.

Sundowns collected a full haul of nine points from their three group games, though they conceded for the first time in the tournament.

World.title: Let love lead: Zambia’s digital conscience after the ballot
World.content:
For generations, Zambia has worn the identity of a peaceful nation, a country where people of different tribes, faiths and political loyalties have lived side by side, recognising one another first as fellow citizens. It is worth asking, honestly, whether that identity is beginning to slip.

It has become disturbingly common to see a person’s death met not with condolence but with mockery, insult or a political score being settled in real time on social media. Behind every death sits a family in mourning. Death is not a contest, and it is certainly not licence to humiliate the departed or gloat over their pain.

Before posting anything online, a simple test still applies: is it true, is it necessary, is it kind? Words now move faster than judgment. A careless post can circle the country within minutes; a cruel meme can land in front of a grieving child and remain there indefinitely.

Freedom of expression carries a corresponding duty. The right to hold an opinion does not confer the right to strip a grieving family of dignity, or to desecrate the memory of the dead. Zambia’s stated values of human dignity, unity and non-discrimination cannot live only in the Constitution or in ceremonial speeches. They must show up in how citizens actually speak to one another, especially when political feeling is running hottest.

The greater danger is not today’s cruelty but its normalisation. Children are watching, absorbing the words their elders choose and the behaviour their communities reward online. No nation builds lasting peace while quietly teaching its youngest citizens that laughter is an acceptable response to another person’s death, simply because that person voted differently.

The Zambia worth protecting is one where political opponents can still greet each other, where neighbours mourn together regardless of ballot choices, and where death is answered with dignity rather than derision. Before sharing an unkind word about someone’s passing, one question is usually enough to give pause: what if this were my own father, my mother, my sister, my child?

Before political affiliation, Zambians are Zambians. Before tribe, they are human beings. It is time to disagree with dignity, contest ideas rather than insults, and mourn with compassion instead of celebrating with hatred. Politics must never be allowed to strip that humanity away.

By Osmond Kalaba

Source: Zambia Daily Mail (“Call for Zambia to embrace love, humanity”)

World.title: Petition Or No Petition, Zambia’s Courts Hold The Real Verdict
World.content:
Zambia’s transition of power now rests on an unresolved legal question with a fixed deadline attached: does the Constitutional Court have a valid petition in front of it, and can it rule before Hakainde Hichilema is sworn in on September 1. The Constitution gives the court 14 days from a properly filed petition to decide. Nobody, not the Judiciary, not State House, not the lawyers involved, agrees on whether that clock has even started.

The stakes go beyond procedure. A government bond auction closed this week with demand exceeding its K6.3 billion target by 37 percent, a sign investors are pricing in political continuity after the election. That confidence assumes the transition holds. An unresolved petition, or a Constitutional Court ruling that reopens the result, would test it directly.

The Judiciary’s official account is simple. Chief administrator Nalishebo Imataa told Secretary to Cabinet Patrick Kangwa that no petition had reached the Constitutional Court Registry by 18:00 hours on August 24, the seventh and final day allowed under Article 103 of the Constitution. Kangwa announced the September 1 swearing-in on that basis. Lawyer Linda Kasonde disputes the premise entirely. She says she attempted to file electronically through the Registry before the deadline and the submission bounced, so she forwarded the documents instead to Chief Justice Mumba Malila’s private email address. Malila has confirmed receiving them, called the method “highly irregular,” and referred them to the Constitutional Court regardless of the irregularity, meaning the question of whether the filing counts sits with the court itself rather than settled by administrative rejection.

Neither side has produced a timestamped record resolving the dispute. The Judiciary has not released logs showing the Registry submission failed or when. Kasonde has not published proof of the attempted filing time. That gap is the actual story: not who is lying, but that nobody has yet shown their work.

What sharpens the doubt is what was happening at the courts during the window Kasonde says she was trying to use. The Law Association of Zambia has confirmed court premises in Lusaka and Ndola were sealed off with tape marked “Crime Scene,” with no public explanation released at the time. LAZ president Lloyd Kaluba says the association still has no formal word on the legal basis for the closure, its scope or its duration, and has demanded both reopening and clarification.

State House rejects any link to the petition. Chief communications specialist Clayson Hamasaka says the August 24 measures covered the Ministry of Justice, the National Prosecution Authority and the Attorney General’s Chambers as well as the Judiciary, calling them intelligence-led precautions rather than action against a single litigant. His position is that the filing window opened on August 18, when the Electoral Commission declared the result, and that courts operated normally on the working days before the closure, with no petition lodged in that stretch. He has challenged anyone claiming a prepared petition was blocked to produce evidence of when and how they tried to lodge it. The Judicial Workers Union offers a third, unrelated explanation, with president Peter Mwale saying the closure followed the arrest of a Judiciary security officer over a detected threat and had nothing to do with any petition.

Constitutional lawyers are split on what happens if the Court finds the filing came late. Mehluli Batakathi says the seven-day window is absolute and no avenue remains once it closes. Tresford Chali argues the Court can extend the deadline where circumstances beyond a petitioner’s control, court closures among them, justify it, and that the Constitution should not be read so rigidly that the facts on the ground are ignored. Which interpretation prevails will likely determine whether the Court even reaches the merits of the case.

A second, separate legal challenge adds further pressure regardless of how the filing dispute resolves. Activist Brebner Changala and Kasonde have petitioned the Constitutional Court citing Christian Churches Monitoring Group data placing Hichilema’s vote share at 56 percent against the Electoral Commission’s declared 60.5 percent, and alleging vote figures were altered between polling stations and constituency tally centres.

The petitioners also cite the killing of former Lunte Member of Parliament Mutotwe Kafwaya and the deployment of the Zambia Defence Force to polling stations as evidence the election environment fell short of constitutional standards. Kafwaya’s death has kept NRPUP’s presidential candidate, Brian Mundubile, and running mate Makebi Zulu, out of public view; both say they remain in a secure location over safety concerns, a decision that has split their own party. NRPUP’s registered president, Ezra Tembo, has broken with his party’s candidates to congratulate Hichilema and accept the result.

The Drug Enforcement Commission’s parallel case has not slowed the legal standoff but has added to the week’s uncertainty. The agency says 79 people of nine nationalities, arrested at Evana Estates in New Kasama, ran a digital laboratory targeting government systems linked to the Electoral Commission, with computers, hard drives and foreign currency seized. Spokesperson Allan Tamba says all suspects will be processed under normal constitutional protections.

What happens next has a clock on it. If the Constitutional Court accepts either petition as validly filed, Article 103(2) gives it 14 days to rule, a window that would run past the scheduled September 1 inauguration. Whether the ceremony proceeds as planned, is delayed, or goes ahead under legal challenge is now the single fact markets, diplomats and Zambians themselves are waiting on the Court, not the politicians, to settle.

World.title: When Words Become Weapons
World.content:
The Book of James offers an old warning for a modern crisis: the tongue is small, but it can set a forest ablaze. After a contested election, Zambia is discovering just how quickly loose words can outrun public patience.

Abigail Kabandula, a scholar who has spent more than a decade studying conflict in Somalia and South Sudan, watched Zambia’s 2026 election unfold with mounting unease, not chiefly because of the political contest itself, but because of how casually some quarters flirted with violent language, against a backdrop of reported firearms and machetes seized from individuals allegedly preparing for confrontation.

Zambia has been fortunate. It has absorbed political tension, disputed results and sporadic violence without ever tipping into the full-scale civil wars that have scarred its neighbours. That record breeds a dangerous illusion that war happens elsewhere, to other people. Kabandula’s own experience argues otherwise. At the University of Zambia she befriended a Burundian who had walked, largely on foot, across the continent to escape ethnic slaughter in 1993, unsure if any of his family had survived and unable to go home. Years later, at Meheba Refugee Settlement, she found Hutu and Tutsi refugees still housed apart more than a decade after Rwanda’s genocide the mistrust too deep, even then, for them to live side by side. War, she learned, does not end when the shooting stops. Buildings can be rebuilt. Trust between neighbours is far harder to restore.

That is the lesson James’s counsel offers today: truth must still be spoken, but it must be disciplined and evidenced, never weaponised. A supporter declaring readiness “to die and to kill” is no less combustible than an opponent accusing the state of wanting to “kill people with military weapons” before any claim has faced a courtroom. Both freeze public opinion into camps before the facts have had their say.

Government has alleged armed insurrection and militia activity; opposition figures have called the security response fabricated and political. Contradictory public explanations on both sides including a violent statement first dismissed as artificial intelligence before later being acknowledged as genuine have only corroded trust at the moment the country needs it most.

History is not subtle about where this road leads. Rwanda’s genocide did not begin with machetes; it began with language that stripped neighbours of their humanity long before killing followed. The former Yugoslavia told its communities that coexistence was weakness until checkpoints and killing fields replaced daily life. Kenya’s 2007 election crisis showed how quickly disputed results, ethnic suspicion and inflammatory broadcasting can combine to cost more than a thousand lives.

Maturity now requires government to separate criticism from treason and dissent from conspiracy unless proof says otherwise and it requires opposition figures to separate resistance from recklessness. Courts exist to determine guilt; accusation is not conviction, and evidence must always travel further than a slogan. No grievance, however real, is worth the country in which it is aired. Zambians who can disagree politically while still sharing a meal, marrying across tribal lines and sending their children to the same schools have built something rare and it survives only as long as the tongue that built it does not turn against it.

By Dr Lawrence Mwelwa and Abigail Kabandula

Source: The Mast (“A nation can bleed from the tongue before the sword,” Weekly Reflections) and Zambia Daily Mail (“Flirting with war: A cautionary tale”)

World.title: Mazembe trample Nkana in test match
World.content:
In a closed-door pre-season friendly, Nkana FC on Tuesday welcomed continental heavyweights TP Mazembe of DR Congo as they suffered a 3-1 defeat at home in Wusakile.

Yet for Coach Elijah Tana and the 13-time Zambian champions, the scoreline at Nkana Stadium told only half the story.

According to Tana, the friendly match was not about winning. This was about measuring.

Mazembe are no ordinary opponents. Five-time CAF Champions League winners.

The standard-bearers of Central African football. For a Nkana side rebuilding ahead of the 2026 MTN Super League Transition Season, this was exactly the kind of test Tana asked for.

“We wanted high-level opposition,” a member of the technical bench told this magazine after the game. “You learn more in 90 minutes against Mazembe than in three games against local sides.”

Kalampa came out with purpose. The frontline pressed high, and early on Lazarous Kambole beat the offside trap and forced Mazembe’s defence into a scramble inside the box. For 43 minutes, Nkana looked the more energetic side.

In the 44th minute, just before halftime, Dante Joël Molindo Mbala found space and broke the deadlock. 1-0 to Mazembe at the break.

If the first goal was a warning, the next two were a masterclass.

4Barely a minute after restart, Bingi Belo struck to make it 2-0 before Gideon Mwanza added a third with a composed finish. 3-0.

With 21 minutes left, Kalampa got a lifeline when Charles Zulu stepped up and converted from the penalty spot.

With Nkana pushing, Kambole, tireless as ever, almost pulled a second in the 78th minute but was denied by a superb save from Mazembe keeper Aliou Faty.

Meanwhile, Nkana’s defeat comes as Zambian football prepares for a unique 2026 Transition Season – a bridge campaign designed to realign the league calendar.

World.title: The petition is bigger than Mundubile and Makebi
World.content:
Zambia’s present political crisis runs deeper than a dispute over who won the presidency. At its core lies a harder question: who controls the country’s institutions, and whether the major decisions shaping the nation’s future are still being made with the informed consent of its people.

A disputed election, a proposed United States–Zambia health financing agreement, unresolved IMF negotiations, quiet talk of scrapping presidential term limits, and sudden pressure on Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu to abandon their election petition are not unconnected stories. They are threads of the same anxiety: whether Zambia’s institutions still serve the public, or have been quietly reorganised to protect presidential power instead.

At the centre of it sits a proposed US health financing deal worth roughly US$1.5 billion over five years, covering HIV, tuberculosis, malaria and maternal health. Zambia’s own Ministry of Foreign Affairs publicly objected in May to terms it considered inconsistent with citizens’ privacy rights, and to American demands for preferential access to Zambia’s critical minerals. Reports that the agreement was signed before polling day but kept from public view would, if true, mark a serious accountability failure, irrespective of whether the deal itself proves beneficial. Voters were entitled to know what their government had committed on their behalf before they cast a ballot, not after.

A parallel concern hangs over Zambia’s next IMF programme, under negotiation since the last Extended Credit Facility concluded in January. The previous programme delivered improving headline numbers alongside fuel, electricity and transport costs that many households felt acutely. Whether an elected government should sign fresh IMF commitments on tax, subsidies and public spending without first showing Parliament and voters the likely impact is not an academic question. It is one that will define kitchen-table budgets for years.

A third, quieter warning concerns the constitutional two-term presidential limit. A December 2025 amendment scrapped term limits for mayors and council chairpersons, leaving the presidential limit untouched, but setting a precedent through which the public could gradually be conditioned to accept the same argument at the top. Zambia has faced this fight before and won it, when churches, civil society, opposition parties and ordinary citizens turned back Frederick Chiluba’s third-term bid. Term limits are not a punishment reserved for unpopular leaders; they are a safeguard against the concentration of power in the hands of popular ones too.

Against that backdrop, calls from figures such as Chris Zumani Zimba urging Mundubile to drop his petition in the name of reconciliation deserve closer examination than they have received. A properly conducted election petition is itself a peaceful instrument of reconciliation. It moves grievance from the street into a courtroom, where evidence rather than rhetoric decides the outcome. Reconciliation that demands one side suppress its own evidence is not reconciliation at all; it is surrender dressed as peace.

Nor can NRPUP’s registered president, Ezra Tembo, constitutionally veto a petition he did not file. Article 103(1) of the Constitution grants “a person” the right to petition the Constitutional Court within seven days of a presidential declaration. It requires no sponsoring party’s consent. Mundubile and Zulu’s standing rests on their own participation as candidates, not on Tembo’s continuing blessing.

What ultimately hangs in the balance is whether Zambia’s institutions still defend democracy, or merely defend the presidency; whether foreign interests can be shielded from public disclosure; and whether temporary political authority can be quietly converted into something more permanent. It is better to petition and lose than never to petition at all. Failure after a fair hearing leaves behind a legal record and a lesson for the next reform. Silence leaves only precedent, proof to the next government that intimidation, applied firmly enough, can place an election beyond question.

By Kanyanta Chanda Kapwepwe

Source: The Mast (“The petition is bigger than Mundubile and Makebi”)

World.title: Zambia must choose dialogue over division
World.content:
Zambia has just come through a bruising election, and the burden of what happens next falls squarely on its leaders. Left unattended, electoral grievance hardens into national fracture. That responsibility begins with President Hakainde Hichilema and opposition leader Brian Mundubile, whom Malawi-based clergyman Pastor Dingiswayo Banda has urged to set the country above their rivalry and reconcile in the name of national unity.

A call for reconciliation is not a call to bury legitimate disagreement — quite the opposite. Democracy depends on it. Opposition parties exist to question government and hold it to account; government, in turn, is obliged to protect the rights of those who oppose it. What cannot be tolerated is a political contest curdling into a war between citizens.

Pastor Banda has named the danger precisely: rising division, mistrust, arrests and loss of life risk putting the nation’s hard-won stability on trial. A country cannot advance while its politicians spend more energy fighting each other than solving the problems of the people who elected them.

Leadership at moments like this is not measured only by who won. It is measured by who is willing to heal. Extending a hand to Mundubile, running mate Makebi Zulu and other opposition figures would cost President Hichilema nothing and demonstrate everything — the confidence of a leader secure enough in his mandate to sit across the table from his rivals. That obligation runs both ways: opposition leaders must match any olive branch with restraint, rejecting inflammatory rhetoric in favour of lawful, constitutional channels.

This is precisely where the Church holds ground no politician can occupy. Jimmy Ng’ambi, national executive director of House of Clergy Zambia, has urged pastors to use the pulpit to condemn divisive language and remind citizens that governments change while the nation endures. The Church’s credibility rests on its perceived impartiality — a trust that allows it to cool tempers that politics too often inflames. Anglican bishops have gone further still, declaring the pulpit “too sacred” for partisan politics.

Due process for those detained or facing prosecution is not a courtesy extended to government’s friends; it is a constitutional guarantee owed to everyone, and the rule of law proves its worth precisely when it shields the unpopular. Zambia does not need another cycle of confrontation. It needs leadership — political and spiritual — capable of recognising that unity is not weakness, but the foundation on which everything else is built.





Source: The Mast (“Our View: Zambia must come first, de-escalate tension”) and Zambia Daily Mail (“Church key in promoting unity, peace”)

World.title: Counterfeit money case adjourned
World.content:
The Kabwe Magistrates’ Court has adjourned a case in which four Kabwe businessmen are accused of being in possession of forged bank notes after one of the accused failed to appear in court due to a road traffic accident.

Resident Magistrate Lishaniso Wamundila adjourned the matter to September 10, 2026 after defence lawyer Paul Chiteta informed the court that his client, Sydney Mutale Chanda, was unwell.

Mr Chiteta told the court that Chanda had been involved in a road traffic accident and was receiving treatment in hospital, making him unable to appear before the court.

The four accused persons are Andwell Mwanabowa, Sydney Mutale Chanda, Innocent Musonda and Geoffrey Musonda.

They are jointly charged with possession of forged bank notes, contrary to Section 358 of the Penal Code, Chapter 87 of the Laws of Zambia.

Particulars of the offence are that on December 28, 2025, in Kabwe District, the four accused persons, jointly and whilst acting together, knowingly and without lawful authority possessed 14 K500 forged bank notes and 12 K200 forged bank notes.

The matter came up before the court for commencement of trial, but proceedings could not continue after the court was informed that one of the accused was unwell.

Magistrate Wamundila has since adjourned the matter to September 10, 2026, to allow Chanda to recover and be discharged from hospital.

The four accused persons are on police bond and are represented by Mr Chiteta of Chiteta and Company, while the State is represented by Joseph Zimba of the National Prosecution Authority.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - August 26, 2026
World.content:
Ramaphosa Vows Arrests Over Anti-Migrant Violence

President Cyril Ramaphosa has pledged that perpetrators of violence against foreign nationals will be arrested and prosecuted once police have gathered sufficient evidence. He rejected claims that the government tolerates xenophobia. Ramaphosa also denied that South Africa had been isolated by other African leaders over the recent violence. He said the country remained a respected pan-African actor. He said the government had engaged African leaders on migration and that regional cooperation was needed to address the underlying causes of migration, including insecurity and poor governance.

Nigeria Launches Manhunt After Mass Abductions



Nigerian President Bola Tinubu has ordered a manhunt for armed kidnappers who attacked four villages in Niger State. The attackers killed more than 40 people and abducted an unverified number of residents. Local officials said that as many as 500 people may have been taken. A video released by the kidnappers appeared to show some of the captives alive in a forest. Survivors have fled to neighbouring states and Benin. Others are receiving treatment for injuries. The attacks, which also involved improvised explosive devices, come amid growing insecurity in the region and concerns over the spread of jihadist groups along Nigeria's north-western border areas.

Anger Mounts After Deadly Guinea Landfill Collapse

Two days after a deadly landfill collapse in Guinea, rescuers are using giant excavators to search for victims. Anger is growing among residents who said that they had repeatedly warned authorities about the landfill's dangerous condition and urged its closure. At least 31 people have died, and more than 20 were injured after a landfill collapsed in Conakry's Dar es Salam neighbourhood following heavy rain. Hundreds of displaced residents are sheltering at a school, and dozens of households remain at risk. The site has been linked to previous deadly collapses and severe pollution. The government plans to replace it with a new landfill, which has been underway since 2022.

ICC Clears Libya Case for First Trial

The International Criminal Court has confirmed 17 charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity against former Libyan security official Khaled Mohamed Ali El Hishri. This paves the way for the first Libya-related case to reach trial since the ICC opened its investigation 15 years ago. El Hishri is accused of torture, rape, murder, enslavement and other abuses against Libyan and migrant detainees at Tripoli's Mitiga prison. Survivors and rights groups said that the case could expose the wider system of migrant detention and exploitation in Libya, including alleged links to European migration-control policies. They called for further investigations into the responsibility of European officials.

Close 

Interpol Arrests 58 in Global Cybercrime Operation

Interpol said 58 people linked to organised West African cybercrime networks have been arrested in a global operation targeting romance and investment scams across 22 countries and six continents. Operation Jackal IV, conducted between November 2025 and June 2026 and identified 263 suspects. It uncovered fraud involving cryptocurrency, email compromise, money laundering and sextortion, including the targeting of minors. In South Africa, police arrested 39 people, raided seven sites, and seized $2.67 million. They also blocked 257 bank accounts linked to a syndicate. Interpol said the operation highlights the growing global reach of networks such as Black Axe and the importance of international cooperation in disrupting their finances. Black Axe is a shadowy criminal network with trafficking, prostitution and killing operations around the world.

World.title: South Africa: Mogotsi Escape Plot Report Due in Court - South African News Briefs - August 26, 2026
World.content:
Mogotsi Escape Plot Report Due in Court

Self-proclaimed political fixer Brown Mogotsi’s alleged escape plot is set to return to court on 1 September, reports EWN. The case was postponed after the State could not produce a report from Correctional Services to prove his alleged attempt to break free. Mogotsi allegedly planned to disguise himself in a Correctional Services uniform and walk out of the Johannesburg Magistrates Court cells. He was removed from a police van before being taken to court and placed in leg irons, with security also tightened. Mogotsi has been in custody since May after failing to secure bail over allegations that he provided false addresses.

Gauteng Health Probes Bribery Allegations



The Gauteng Department of Health is investigating allegations that officials may be accepting bribes from patients in exchange for appointments, access to medical files and the collection of medication outside normal procedures, reports SABC News. Department spokesperson Steve Mabona condemned bribery, corruption and preferential treatment in public healthcare. He said that the allegations are serious enough to warrant an investigation into whether officials are soliciting or accepting payments from patients.

Biko Family Seeks Testimony From Apartheid Spy

The reopened inquest into the 1977 death of anti-apartheid activist Steve Biko could examine the role of former apartheid spy Craig Williamson, reports EWN. Biko’s family is seeking to have him subpoenaed. The family says Williamson’s previous evidence that Biko was under surveillance could help answer questions about what security forces knew before his death. Biko’s widow, Nontsikelelo, is also expected to testify about the surveillance operation. The family has requested more time to prepare her and review evidence from the original inquest and Truth and Reconciliation Commission. The court is expected to rule on the postponement request.
