World.title: Romanian prosecutors expand criminal investigation in Nordis case
World.content:
Romania’s Directorate for the Investigation of Organized Crime and Terrorism (DIICOT) announced on Tuesday, August 25, that it has expanded the criminal investigation in the case of real estate developer Nordis.

Nordis, a premium developer, allegedly collected money from buyers, embezzled company funds, and misled customers during the signing of pre-contracts and sales agreements, according to investigators. Moreover, the company illegally obtained refunds or compensation from the state budget. In total, the group leaders are believed to have collected EUR 195 million from 2019 to 2024.

According to prosecutors, 50 new criminal complaints filed by more than 100 new victims have been added to the case file, leading to an expansion of the investigation. The additional damages were estimated at over RON 42 million, EUR 14 million, and USD 17,000.

“The measure targets the administrators of a group of companies, defendants in the case, as well as four commercial companies, all under criminal investigation, for committing the offense of fraud with particularly serious consequences,” according to a DIICOT press release.

Moreover, prosecutors ordered the expansion of the criminal investigation for a distinct offense of fraud with particularly serious consequences, following a complaint filed by a commercial company. In this case, damages were estimated at RON 7 million.

The investigated offenses concern the establishment of an organized criminal group, embezzlement with particularly serious consequences, money laundering, tax evasion, fraud with particularly serious consequences, and the bad-faith determination by the taxpayer of taxes, fees or contributions, resulting in the unlawful obtaining of refunds, reimbursements or offsets from the consolidated general budget, all in continued form.

In total, the Nordis case caused damages that exceed EUR 75 million, with 850 victims on record. The first expansion of the investigation took place in October 2025, when 300 victims came forward.

The case impacted much of the presidential campaign at the end of 2024 and the beginning of 2025 due to the political connections of the accused managers of Nordis, particularly their ties with the Social Democratic Party, or PSD.

World.title: Romania’s centrist parties fail to break Wage Law deadlock
World.content:
Romania’s centrist parties failed to reach an agreement on the new Wage Law for the budgetary sector after nearly two hours of talks convened by president Nicușor Dan on August 25, leaving the legislation at risk of missing its August 31 deadline under the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR), Digi24 reported.

The meeting brought together the leaders of the National Liberal Party (PNL), Social Democratic Party (PSD), Save Romania Union (USR) and Democratic Alliance of Hungarians in Romania (UDMR), but ended without consensus. Political sources cited by local media said the discussions could resume, although the chances of adopting the law within the PNRR deadline are now considered very low.

Romania risks losing about EUR 770 million in Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) funding if the milestone is not completed. The Wage Law is intended to establish a new framework for remuneration in the budgetary sector, including more predictable wage coefficients and rules for bonuses.

Interim prime minister Ilie Bolojan said the reform should not be assessed only in terms of the RRF funds at stake, arguing that the absence of a predictable wage system creates broader risks for Romania’s public finances and labour market.

“The wage law is more important than the EUR 770 million we could be disbursed under the RRF. It's a project that's about trust in Romania, because it's a commitment made by Romanian governments for years, which they could have put into practice, but they didn't,” Bolojan told Digi24.

He added that the government had been required to address the issue over the past three months and that a clear wage framework was important for budget planning because personnel expenditure represents a significant component of public spending.

Bolojan also warned that the lack of a stable framework could allow wage policies to become subject to electoral considerations, particularly given the experience of 2023 and 2024.

“Considering what happened in 2023 and 2024, pre-election and election years, when governments got things out of control by playing only according to electoral calculations and not according to budgetary balances, we risk finding ourselves slipping again and all the efforts made during this period being nullified by such a thing,” he said.

The Wage Law is one of the most politically sensitive outstanding PNRR reforms, with trade unions and political parties disputing proposed wage levels, bonus limits and the overall impact on the public payroll.

(Photo source: Presidency.ro)

World.title: Romanian government’s deputy secretary general Cristina Trăilă probed for complicity in influence peddling
World.content:
Cristina Trăilă (Liberal Party, PNL), deputy secretary general of the interim government of Romania headed by Ilie Bolojan, is being prosecuted in the case of businessman Fănel Bogos from Vaslui, accused by anti-corruption prosecutors of "using networks of influence" to change the management of the Vaslui sanitary inspectorate DSVSA, according to a press release of the National Anticorruption Directorate (DNA).

Last year on September 23, Bogos met with PM Bolojan in the government’s headquarters to discuss his case, prompting a political scandal despite the prime minister later denying any involvement and saying that “there were no follow-ups” after the meeting.

In an interview given to Digi24 on the same day, PM Bolojan said that a decision on Traila’s position in his cabinet will be taken after assessing the situation.

"I saw the Prosecutor's Office's statement today. I called Mrs Trăilă afterwards. I asked her to come tomorrow morning so we can have a discussion, so I can understand what the charges are against her, and we will make a decision tomorrow. After the discussion I will have with her,” PM Bolojan said.

Trăilă is being investigated for "complicity in the use of influence or authority for the purpose of obtaining undue benefits," the DNA announced.

Trăilă, who is a suspect, was questioned on August 25 at the Iași DNA. No preventive measures were ordered against her.

The DNA sent a press release stating that, at the beginning of November 2025, Trăilă, "as Deputy Secretary General of the Romanian government, allegedly supported the actions of the defendant Barbu Mihai to exercise influence over the president of the ANSVSA, in order to replace the director of the Vaslui DSVSA with a person approved by the defendant BF."

According to prosecutors, the intended purpose was to obtain undue benefits for Fanel Bogos and the company owned by him, "consisting, among other things, of approving a compensation file worth approximately EUR 3 million, as well as of reducing or ceasing sanitary and veterinary controls at the company's farms."

Mediafax wrote in November 2025, citing DNA documents, that Fanel Bogos "handed over the sum of EUR 1.5 million to the person who brokered the meeting with Ilie Bolojan."

"The prime minister emphasises that he has no knowledge of whether anyone has claimed/received any benefit of any kind for the promise of an audience with him," government spokesperson Ioana Dogioiu said at that time.

World.title: Bucharest-based Waldevar builds 95 MWp hybrid solar park for China’s Sany
World.content:
Waldevar Holding is building two co-located energy projects for China’s Sany Group in southern Romania at Dobrești, Dolj County, with a capacity of 95 MWp of solar energy, 220 MWh of battery storage, and the high-voltage infrastructure necessary for grid connection.

The symbolic inauguration of the project took place on Friday, August 14, when a Sany delegation from China, together with its partners, joined Waldevar representatives on the construction site in Dobrești, according to a Waldevar press release quoted by Economica.net.

The Dobrești project combines large-scale solar power generation with 220 MWh of battery storage and dedicated high-voltage infrastructure, including a 110/20 kV transformer station and a 110 kV underground line.

The project will contribute to Romania's energy security by increasing the share of electricity produced locally from renewable sources. According to project estimates, the photovoltaic plant will generate approximately 135 GWh of clean energy annually.

Waldevar is a European renewable energy group, headquartered in Bucharest, Romania, providing integrated turnkey solutions in the fields of energy production, transmission and distribution. With over 3.5 GW of projects delivered and under construction, over 2,000 specialists and a fleet of over 400 specialized equipment, the company offers end-to-end capabilities.

World.title: Romania’s Senate approves green hydrogen law tied to EUR 1 bln RRF milestone
World.content:
Romania’s Senate has approved legislation updating the framework for integrating renewable and low-carbon hydrogen into the transport and industrial sectors, a measure linked to a National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR) milestone worth more than EUR 1 billion, according to Economedia.ro.

The bill was adopted on August 24 as the first Chamber notified and now needs approval by the Chamber of Deputies before entering into force. It amends Law 237/2023 and Government Emergency Ordinance 163/2022 to establish rules for the production, use and monitoring of renewable hydrogen and align Romania’s framework with national and European Union requirements.

The legislation had previously received negative reports from the Senate’s Economic and Energy committees, but amendments were subsequently agreed and approved unanimously within the committees, according to Social Democratic Party (PSD) Senator Radu Oprea.

“We had it in debate in the last session, it had a negative report from the Economic Committee and the Energy Committee, and in the meantime we managed to find some amendments that we proposed together with the chairmen of the two committees and which were voted unanimously,” Oprea said.

He said the amended version balanced the obligations imposed on fuel suppliers and described the measure as a PNRR milestone worth more than EUR 1 billion when considered together with Romania’s hydrogen strategy.

The legislation would require fuel suppliers, starting in 2030, to ensure that at least 1% of the fuel supplied comes from renewable sources of non-biological origin, including green hydrogen.

The Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR) opposed the bill, arguing that the new obligation could increase petrol and diesel prices. Senator Corneliu Negru said Romania already faces high fuel prices and lacks sufficient domestic production to supply the market at affordable levels.

“The introduction of this new obligation will cause an increase in the price of gasoline and diesel fuel, that is, conventional fuel, all in the name of the so-called green transition,” Negru said.

Meanwhile, OMV Petrom has begun developing a 55 MW green hydrogen production facility at its Petrobrazi refinery, comprising projects of 20 MW and 35 MW.

World.title: Plea Deals Reveal Logistics of Smuggling Macedonian Marijuana into Serbia
World.content:
Shortly after midnight on January 15 this year, a truck crossed from North Macedonia into Serbia. Several hours later, having crossed the length of the country, it caught fire near Serbia’s second city of Novi Sad.

According to paperwork, the truck was carrying textiles for export to Britain. In reality, it was stuffed with tonnes of marijuana; the smugglers set it on fire to cover their tracks.

Two weeks later, police seized five tonnes of marijuana in the village of Konjuh, near the central Serbian town of Krusevac.

According to plea bargains reached last week between prosecutors in North Macedonia and two of the smugglers, the January shipment was just one of five carried out between mid-2025 and early 2026.

More people are under investigation. Sources close to the probe say prosecutors in North Macedonia are also looking into the finances of three companies tied to Skopje-based Alfapharm Group, which allegedly served as a front for the drugs production.

The case is the latest to raise questions about North Macedonia’s legal medicinal marijuana industry, legalised in 2016, and whether it is fuelling the smuggling. In recent years, 14 firms have lost their permits to grow medicinal marijuana for failing to comply with the law, the Health Ministry said.

World.title: Riots, Teargas and ‘Gruesome Photos’ Behind Serbian Photographer’s Success
World.content:
An Orthodox priest talks to a young man during street protests in Belgrade. A police cordon faces the crowd in Serbia’s capital, holding plastic shields. A wounded demonstrator lies prone as riot police run past him.

These images date back to March 2011, when protesters packed the streets after the arrest of Bosnian Serb military chief Ratko Mladic. They were the first photos that Andrej Cukic sent to EPA Images (European Pressphoto Agency). Now he is set to lead the organization, as editor-in-chief.

“I was in the right place at the right time,” he tells BIRN. “I had some gruesome photos. Somebody thought that they were very good, and they ran them, and the photos were kind of published everywhere.”

The photos led to Cukic gaining regular work from Belgrade for EPA Images, an international news photo agency based in Frankfurt. BIRN has a contract with EPA and regularly uses its images.

World.title: Greek Neo-Nazi Casts Himself as Political Martyr Ahead of Prison Release
World.content:
On the Greek capital’s bustling Omonia Square, a group of young men held Greek flags and chanted: “Ilias, stay strong on the road to freedom” and “Remember Ilias, we are with you”.

It was July 20 and Ilias Kasidiaris - on day release from prison - was inaugurating the offices of a new party he had announced the previous month.

Convicted in 2020 of directing a criminal organisation, Kasidiaris has no legal grounds to lead a political party, but media reports this month suggest a relative of his has submitted a request to do so before the Supreme Court.

Addressing his supporters, Kasidiaris called on them to gather outside Domokos prison come mid-September, when he is due to be released.

Together, he said, they would “send a message of resistance to all those who are selling out Greece”, and vowed to run in the next parliamentary election, expected in the spring of next year.

World.title: Bulgaria Violated Rights of Roma Families by Demolishing Settlement, Court Rules
World.content:
Bulgaria breached the human rights of dozens of Roma families in Sofia by demolishing their homes without giving them a chance to contest the decision, the European Court of Human Rights ruled on Tuesday.

The government must pay 10,000 euro in damages to each party to the case and reform its demolition procedures.

The demolition took place in Sofia’s Orlandovtsi neighbourhood in August 2023, despite residents insisting that the authorities had not consulted them over the plans. Some of the families said they had lived in their homes since the 1950s.

The authorities insisted that they had carried out a formal process for issuing demolition orders. This was denied by the residents, who said the authorities deliberately concealed their intentions, gave evasive answers to repeated requests for information and refused to engage directly with the community.

The court ruled that Bulgaria had violated Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects family life and homes. It found that residents had no effective procedure to challenge the plans for demolition based on their personal circumstances, including length of residence, vulnerability and the availability of alternative housing.

The court also ruled, however, that the residents held no property rights in the demolished houses that would be recognized under Bulgarian law.

The ruling is not yet final and Bulgaria has three months to request that the case be referred for further review. The residents may make a similar application.

The flattening of Roma settlements in Bulgaria has become a repeated problem and a source of tension between the ethnic minority and local authorities. Demolitions also took place in the Orlandovtsi neighbourhood in 2017.

The ECHR has now heard four cases involving Roma settlement demolitions since 2012. In 2025, BIRN covered two similar cases: in April 2025, despite an ECHR ruling warning the municipality not to “proceed with the demolition of the homes of the applicants until further notice”, authorities still flattened houses in the enclave which had been there for decades.

A similar operation followed in the town of Stara Zagora in August the same year.

World.title: Serbia Again Requests “Humanitarian” Release of Ratko Mladic
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp

Serbia’s Justice Minister Nenad Vujic has once again called for the release of the convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic. On Tuesday, he asked the UN war crimes court in The Hague to consider a new request by the family of the former Bosnian Serb military leader.

Vujic made the plea in a letter to Graciela Gatti Santana, the president of the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals, IRMCT. It follows last week’s decision by the IRMCT to reject a request by Mladic’s defence for conditional early release and transfer to Serbia on health grounds.

Vujic noted a report by the medical officer at the detention unit in The Hague stating that Mladic had entered the final phase of his life, after a rapid decline in his health. The minister argued that, under these circumstances, Mladic should be allowed to spend his final days in Serbia. The government has offered to transfer him to Belgrade’s Military Medical Academy and accept restrictions and monitoring imposed by the court.

In last week’s decision rejecting an early release, the IRMCT ruled that Mladic was receiving comprehensive medical care and assistance, as well as an exceptional visitation regime allowing meaningful contact with his family. It said that his condition alone did not justify humanitarian early release, given the gravity of his genocide conviction and life sentence. The court stressed that it would continue to protect Mladic’s fundamental rights and dignity.

This is not the first time that Mladic’s defence has sought his release on humanitarian grounds. During his time in custody in the Netherlands, Mladic has had several serious medical problems and has suffered two strokes and a heart attack.

In June 2025, Mladic’s lawyers made an urgent request to the IRMCT for his release after he was transferred to palliative care, saying he had only has months to live. His defence again sought his immediate release in May this year after a serious medical episode, arguing that he was approaching the end of his life.

Mladic has been in custody in The Hague since his arrest in 2011. He is serving a life sentence for committing genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes during the 1992-95 war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The court confirmed his conviction and sentence after an appeal in 2021.

World.title: European Court Orders Turkey to Release Osman Kavala Immediately, Again
World.content:
The European Court of Human Rights, ECHR, on Tuesday ruled for a second time that Turkey should release the jailed philanthropist and human rights activist Osman Kavala. Judges found that his detention and conviction violated multiple provisions of the European Convention on Human Rights.

“The respondent State was required to secure the applicant’s release at the earliest possible date,” the Court said, adding that Turkey must eliminate the consequences of the measures taken against him. It said Kavala’s criminal conviction should be regarded as “null and void” under the Convention’s provisions.

Kavala is a prominent civil society figure and former board member of the Open Society Foundations in Turkey. He has been in custody since October 2017, facing charges in connection with the 2013 Gezi Park protests and the failed coup attempt of July 2016.

An Istanbul court sentenced Kavala to “aggravated life imprisonment” – without the possibility of release – in April 2022. He was convicted of attempting to overthrow the government through his support for the Gezi Park protests. The months of demonstrations constituted the largest popular uprising against the authoritarian leadership of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

Two appeal courts upheld Kavala’s conviction in December 2022 and September 2023.

In its latest ruling, the ECHR found violations of several provisions of the European Convention on Human Rights, including freedom of expression and assembly, the right to a fair trial and the right to liberty and security. It also found that Kavala’s aggravated life sentence without the possibility of release violated Article 3, which explicitly prohibits “torture [and] inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment”.

Judges concluded that a desire to silence Kavala was behind the criminal proceedings, his conviction and his continued detention. The Turkish authorities aimed to punish him for his role in the Gezi Park demonstrations and for expressing his opinions as a human rights defender.

The judgment follows years of pressure over Turkey’s failure to implement previous ECHR rulings concerning Kavala. The Council of Europe’s Committee of Ministers eventually launched infringement proceedings against Turkey in 2022. That process could ultimately lead to sanctions, including the suspension of voting rights or even membership.

The Court also ordered Turkey to pay Kavala 70,000 euros in non-pecuniary damages and 43,342.57 euros in costs and expenses.

World.title: Kosovo Starts Countdown on KLA Leaders War Crimes Verdict
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp



Countdown monitor installed at Pristina city center photographed on August 24, 2026. Photo: BIRN/ Islam Berisha

The clock is ticking in Ferizaj/Urosevac. Kosovo’s third-largest city now has installed a countdown timer on Monday, which will reach zero on the day that former president Hashim Thaci is due to learn his fate. The capital, Pristina, has a similar installation, with other cities due to follow suit.

Along with three other former senior leaders of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA), Thaci is accused of committing crimes against humanity – including murder, torture and illegal detention – during the Kosovo conflict in the late 1990s. Prosecutors at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague are calling for a 45-year prison sentence.

But as far as Ferizaj/Urosevac’s mayor Agim Aliu is concerned, Thaci and his co-defendants – Kadri Veseli, Jakup Krasniqi and Rexhep Selimi – are heroes of Kosovo’s independence struggle. And he believes the newly-installed timer in the city’s main square is counting down the days to what should be a massive celebration.

“Ferizaj and the entire Kosovo [will] experience September 16 as a new date of freedom,” he says, adding that he expects a “historic verdict” reflecting “the sacrifice” the four defendants made for Kosovo’s freedom.

On Monday, Ferizaj/Urosevac became the second municipality to receive a countdown clock, courtesy of the initiative “Freedom Has a Name” (Liria Ka Emer). It plans to install similar timers in other municipalities around Kosovo.

One of the initiative’s leaders is Eliza Hoxha, an MP representing Thaci’s former party, the PDK (Democratic Party of Kosovo), which is currently in opposition. She says she believes in the four defendants’ innocence.

“Kosovo is waiting, we are all waiting. We will count down hours, minutes, seconds until September 16. Kosovo waits for Thaci, Veseli, Krasniqi and Selimi to once again stamp our right to be free and independent.”

The charges facing the four men are serious. Prosecutors accuse them of individual and command responsibility for crimes committed against prisoners held at KLA detention facilities in Kosovo and in neighbouring Albania. Those include more than one hundred murders.

The charges cover the period during and just after the Kosovo War in 1998 and 1999. All four defendants have pleaded not guilty.

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers (KSC) was created specifically to try former members of the KLA. As prime minister in 2014, Hashim Thaci signed an agreement with the European Union to establish the court.

It is based in The Hague and staffed by international judges and prosecutors due to doubts about the Kosovo justice system’s ability to try former KLA fighters. Veterans are widely viewed as heroes in Kosovo and the potential for witness intimidation was a serious concern.

During the trial, the prosecution argued that the defendants’ senior roles in the KLA meant they were responsible for subordinates who committed crimes. The defence insisted that the KLA did not have a proper army command structure, so the defendants did not have real authority over lower-ranking fighters.

Thaci resigned as Kosovo’s president in November 2020 to face the charges. Since then, he and his three co-defendants have been in detention in The Hague, with the trial starting in April 2023. KLA veterans and their supporters have staged protests in Pristina, Tirana, Skopje, Strasbourg and The Hague, accusing the KSC of bias.

Prosecutors brought further charges against Thaci In 2024. He and four others, including former Justice Minister Hajredin Kuci, are accused of obstruction of justice and witness tampering. Prosecutors say Thaci and his co-accused attempted to direct witness testimony in his war crimes trial.

The second case went to trial in February this year, just days after proceedings in Thaci’s first trial concluded. All the accused have pleaded not guilty.

World.title: Planned Amazon Warehouse in Czechia Faces Local Resistance, Again
World.content:
August deadline

Now being developed by investors Accolade and Garbe, the land of the Borsov Economic Development Zone I was purchased in 1998, with initial zoning plans banking on the construction of a large shopping centre.

This never materialised, and in 2020 developers received zoning approval for the construction of four smaller, separate industrial halls – two of which already have building permits – for a total built area of over 148,000 square metres. Now, the modalities have changed again.

Accolade and Garbe redesigned the entire project into a single, larger building (77,000 square metres in size, about 500 metres long and 15 metres high) specifically for a single tenant – Amazon – on an expected 20-year-lease agreement. About 2,500 people could be employed there, working on a two-shift rotation running almost non-stop from 06:30 to 04:30.

According to Borsov nad Vltavou’s mayor, Romana Rycova, the municipality was only informed about the change at the end of April. And in a video posted on August 13, Mayor Rycova stated that the municipal council must now approve the new variant by the end of August or the investors will redesign the project so they can bypass the municipality’s approval – despite an earlier promise made to residents to “wait as long as you need”.

Representatives for the investors tell BIRN that their earlier communication might have been misconstrued. “When we said that there would be no time pressure, we meant that we would not push municipal council members towards a particular decision or influence how they vote,” says Tomas Mile, project manager at Accolade.

“It did not mean that the project itself had no commercial timetable,” he says, adding that the municipality had been informed since late 2025 about the changes. Rather than a sudden change, Mile describes the new single-building option as “the gradual development of a new option in response to a specific requirement from a prospective tenant”.

Furthermore, he says that while “we understand the concerns raised by residents”, he makes the case that developers have shown goodwill and transparency over the past several months to explain the differences and varying impacts to local residents.

Amazon did not respond to BIRN’s requests for comment.

However, Horakova says she has attended all the public meetings held over the past several months and describes the communication there from developers as “misleading at best”.

Considering the new parameters of the project, she also believes that fresh independent studies should be conducted to upgrade now-outdated environmental impact studies and properly evaluate the impact of such a massive distribution centre on traffic, air-quality, noise pollution and local landscape preservation – just a few of the main concerns expressed by both residents and city officials over the past several months.

“We’ve found no evidence that these studies have been updated for the new design, including in the investor’s own newest technical documentation,” Horakova explains.

Echoing the thoughts of other locals, Horakova accuses the developers of “not being a trustworthy party”. Case in point, Veronika Zacha – who became Garbe’s senior manager for business development for Czechia after moving from Panattoni in 2022 – promised during an August town hall meeting: “We don’t want to pressure the municipality, we also understand that you need to familiarise yourself with all the information, so you have time.”

Yet shortly afterwards, city councillors received an SMS clarifying that developers expect a decision by the end of the month – or else they will move ahead with the four-hall format, according to information from iRozhlas.cz and other local outlets.

World.title: Billionaires Gather on 200 Million Euro Yacht Near Mljet
World.content:
August the 26th, 2026 – Multiple billionaires have come together on a 200 million euro yacht near the southern Croatian island of Mljet. Jeff Bezos, and Jan Koum are among them.

Poslovni reports that this impressive vessel can accommodate 16 guests along with 32 crew members, and the yacht’s price is nearly 200 million euros. Mljet is set to be hosting a meeting of two of the world’s biggest technology billionaires, Jan Koum and Jeff Bezos, over the next few days. They met on Koum’s yacht worth nearly 200 million dollars.

Jan Koum, co-founder of WhatsApp whose wealth is estimated at 17 billion dollars, anchored his superyacht Moonrise near Mljet, and the same day Jeff Bezos, owner of Amazon, arrived in the company of American media mogul Barry Diller. Koum arrived on the Moonrise by helicopter on Monday, and Bezos visited him in the late afternoon hours. The three billionaires, Koum, Bezos and Diller, thus found themselves on the same vessel in the middle of the Adriatic Sea.

Koum is no stranger to the Croatian coast; he has holidayed in our beautiful country before. His superyacht Moonrise was photographed between the islands of Lopud and Šipan back in 2021 and 2024, and it was recorded that on one occasion he arrived for a summer holiday in Croatia with as many as three vessels: in addition to Moonrise he was accompanied by the 74-metre yacht Mogambo and the 55-metre Power Play, which served him as a helipad. The Amazon owner regularly summers on the Mediterranean on his superyacht Koru, where he cruised the Adriatic in the summers of 2023 and 2025, with recorded stays on Hvar, Mljet, Korčula, and a visit to the Šibenik archipelago.

The yacht Moonrise isn’t just an ordinary vessel. It’s a 100-metre superyacht from the Dutch shipyard Feadship, built in 2020. The sophisticated exterior design is by De Voogt, while the interior is the work of French designer Rémi Tessier. The vessel can accommodate 16 guests along with 32 crew members, and the yacht’s price is nearly 200 million euros.

World.title: Pula Receives 12 Electric Buses Worth 6.8 Million Euros
World.content:
August the 26th, 2026 – Pula has received 12 electric buses worth a total of 6.8 million euros with an aim of increasing passenger comfort and being more environmentally friendly.

Pulapromet has put another six new electric buses into service, thereby completing the project of acquiring a total of 12 electric vehicles for Pula’s public transport. Index reports that the project was fully financed with funds from the National Recovery and Resilience Plan, and the total value of the purchased buses amounts to 6,763,900 euros. For the project, Pulapromet had been allocated 6,994,998 euros, but after the public procurement procedure the total value was somewhat lower.

Specifically speaking, Pulapromet acquired six MAN and six Iveco electric buses. Director Tomislav Josipović said that this is an important step in modernising the vehicle fleet and raising the quality of public transport.

“By putting these new six electric buses into service today, we are completing the project through which Pulapromet has received a total of 12 new electric vehicles,” said Josipović, adding that almost 6.8 million euros of investment has been directed into the development of public transport without any financial burden on Pulapromet. The new buses should reduce emissions of harmful gases and noise while increasing energy efficiency and passenger comfort.

an increase in public transport use in pula

Pula Mayor Peđa Grbin said that the project does not stop at the acquisition of buses. He announced the installation of solar panels on the canopy at the depot (Remiza), for which the City is waiting for the opening of appropriate co-financing tenders. “The goal is for these electric buses to run on electricity that will be produced here, in Pula, from the most ecological possible source, which is solar energy,” said Grbin. He added that since the beginning of the year the use of public city transport has increased by almost 10 percent. According to him, this has also been contributed to by the City of Pula’s decisions on free transport for pupils, students and pensioners.

Istria County Prefect Boris Miletić thanked the City of Pula, Pulapromet, the surrounding municipalities and the Ministry of Maritime Affairs, Transport and Infrastructure for implementing the project. He emphasised that electric buses, especially if powered by energy from solar sources, can contribute to reducing the impact of traffic on the environment. Miletić also said that Pulapromet first secured the infrastructure and charging stations, and then acquired the vehicles. He assessed that higher-quality public transport could further increase the number of passengers.

World.title: Istria Showcased in Front of Millions of German Viewers
World.content:
August the 26th, 2026 – Gorgeous Istria has been showcased in front of millions of German viewers, shining the spotlight on Croatia’s largest peninsula.

Morski reports that one of the most successful German travel programmes, “Wunderschön”, devoted a full 90 minutes of airtime to Istria, presenting the diversity of the peninsula to a million-strong audience in the German-speaking world – from Kamenjak, Pula and the Brijuni Islands, via Učka, Buzet and Pazin, to Poreč and Rovinj.

The project was realised in cooperation between the Tourist Board of Istria County and its long-standing PR partner ART Redaktionsteam from Salzburg. Viewers are guided through Istria by well-known German television presenter Stephanie Müller-Spirra, under the direction of award-winning journalist and author Stephan Heise. Alongside numerous local protagonists, the programme also features Marko Purišić – Baby Lasagna, Rade Šerbedžija and extreme alpinist Ines Papert. Istria is presented to the audience through a blend of natural and cultural attractions, active holidays, local stories and top-class food and local wine.

The first broadcast of the report reaches around two million viewers, while through further screenings in Germany, Austria and Switzerland the total viewership is expected to exceed five million, making the project one of the most significant television promotions of Istria on its most important outbound market.

World.title: Belišće – The Croatian Town Around Which an Industrial Empire Grew
World.content:
August the 26th, 2026 – Belišće isn’t a name you’ll likely have ever heard if you’re not from Croatia, but this Croatian town had an industrial empire grow out of it.

It’s also unusual because of the fact that it is one of the few Croatian towns whose beginning can be fixed almost like a date of birth. Putni kofer turns the hands of the clock back to the year 1884, and we find ourselves in a place with a pasture-and-arable clearing called Belistje. It sits just beside the banks of the Drava, and the reason a large sawmill that the Gutmann family builds there. Soon after, a railway, workers’ houses, a school, a post office, an electricity network and a water supply all arrive. In just a few decades, the industrial plant thus created an entire settlement around itself, and from it grew today’s town.

the family company that built an entire town

In 1884, two companies belonging to the Gutmann family from Velika Kanjiža bought from the Valpovo landowner the right to a ten-year use of a huge expanse of oak forests. They erected the sawmill on the Belistje clearing, after which the settlement later took its name. The Croatian Biographical Lexicon notes that the Gutmanns further expanded their business by purchasing forests from the Prandau family of Valpovo and that at the beginning of the 20th century they controlled massive swathes of of forest and land. From the very start Belišće was therefore tied to one of the most valuable resources of the area, Slavonian oak.

the biggest and most modern sawmill in europe

According to data from Belišće, the sawmill was one of the most modern of its time and probably the largest in Europe for cutting oak timber. Large-scale production also needed a good transport link, so already in 1884 the first kilometres of the forest-industrial railway were laid. Over time the network grew to 335 kilometres and developed into the Slavonia-Podravina Railway with public transport, a station, a locomotive shed and a workshop in Belišće. The Croatian Biographical Lexicon emphasises that this railway also carried passengers and thus compensated for the lack of state railways in this part of Slavonia.

Alongside the sawmill and the railway an industrial colony grew. Official sources state that the first residential houses were soon built and a fire brigade founded; in 1886 a school classroom and a post office were opened, and in 1890 a primary school was constructed. By 1892 the place already had an electricity network and a water supply with sewerage, which was still rare in the surrounding villages at that time. Development was also visible in the architecture. Next to the workers’ houses arose a house for the owners and offices, the officials’ social centre Casino, and in 1905 the Gutmann Palace, known in Belišće as Palej. Up to the First World War the workers’ settlement continued to expand, and some of its parts remained known by the names Five Stars, Green Houses, Mitrovica and Pekmez Street.

workers arrived from across the world

Industry drew workers from the Valpovo and Miholjac areas and from Lika, while specialists arrived from other parts of Austria-Hungary. Among them were many Germans, Hungarians and Czechs. With the newcomers cultural life also developed. The Rosenberg family arrived in 1888, and their son Sigmund spent part of his childhood precisely in Belišće. Later, in the United States under the name Sigmund Romberg, he became a well-known composer of operettas and musicals and dedicated the Belišće March to the place of his childhood.

By the time 1918 rolled around, the company moved its headquarters from Budapest to Belišće, and in 1927 the place became an independent municipality. After 1945 followed the period of the Kombinat, and a new major industrial phase began in 1960 with the opening of factories for semi-cellulose, paper and packaging. The old production lines and the narrow-gauge railways gradually closed down, but their traces still determine the appearance of the town today. The Gutmann Palace has been restored as an interpretation centre of industrial heritage; nearby is a gate from the first sawmill, installed in 1889; the complex of workers’ houses is protected as a monument ensemble; and a train with a locomotive from 1913 has also been preserved. Belišće has thus turned its industrial past, from which it literally arose, into the most recognisable part of its own heritage.

World.title: August 25th 1991 – The Battle of Vukovar Begins
World.content:
August the 25th, 2026 – On August the 25th, 1991, the battle of Vukovar began, marking the start of one of the most devastating chapters of the Croatian War of Independence.

The most harrowing episode of the Homeland War began on this day in the eastern Croatian city of Vukovar when members of the JNA from the barracks in Vukovar joined Serbian paramilitary units. After doing so, they jointly launched an attack on both Borovo and Vukovar. Index writes that the siege lasted 87 days and transformed Vukovar into a symbol of Croatian resistance and heroism during the Homeland War.

the initial conflicts begin

Slobodan Milošević – NATO

After Croatia declared independence on the 25th of June 1991, local conflicts in eastern Slavonia had already begun. For centuries Vukovar had been a city where Croats, Serbs and Hungarians lived in peace, but the situation changed at the end of the 1980s with the rise of nationalism and the policies of Slobodan Milošević, who wanted to consolidate power in Belgrade.

On the 25th of August, the JNA left the barracks with six tanks that blocked the road towards Bogdanovci. The very next day a new attack on Borovo began that lasted the entire day. The firing briefly stopped, and already during the following night another offensive started. By the 30th of August, the clashes continued one after another, after which a short ceasefire occurred during which weapons were delivered to the Croats in Vukovar from Slavonski Brod, Vinkovci and Zagreb. At that time Mile Dedaković arrived in Vukovar and organised the army and defensive positions in the city.

the serbs wanted to go all the way to zagreb

The JNA commander in Vukovar was Života Panić, who wanted to capture Vukovar as quickly as possible in order to prevent further mobilisation of the Croatian army. The original JNA plan was to take Vukovar and Osijek, then occupy all of Slavonia so that the road towards Varaždin and Zagreb would be open. However, problems already appeared when fewer than two thousand Croatian soldiers withstood numerous JNA attacks in Vukovar.

The plan was not helped by the fact that only 13% of those fit for military service responded to the call-up. After news arrived of the large number of casualties in Vukovar, many soldiers deserted, and by the end of 1991 there were six thousand open court proceedings against deserters. The failure of mobilisation meant the cancellation of the grandiose conquest of the whole of continental Croatia, culminating with Zagreb.

the fall of vukovar and horrific crimes against humanity

Vukovar endured a three-month siege in which seven thousand projectiles fell daily. On the 18th of November the city fell, although only 10–15% of the buildings actually remained. The rest were entirely destroyed. The army entered the city and the expulsion of the non-Serb population and horrific war crimes and crimes against humanity began. Neighbours accused other neighbours of being a defender, informed on where families were located, and just a few days later more than 250 civilians were brutally killed at Ovčara in one single night.

The sight of the murder of hundreds of innocent civilians – Perun

The total number of victims is measured in the thousands of people, and there are probably other undiscovered mass graves containing those who disappeared during the war. The Serbian government under Aleksandar Vučić refuses to cooperate so that the remaining mysteries from the war can finally be resolved.

The city was returned to Croatia only in 1998 through peaceful reintegration, and the 18th of November is marked in Croatia as the Day of Remembrance of the Victims of the Homeland War. Vukovar has still not recovered from the war: today it has just over 25,000 inhabitants, while in the years before the war it was home to 45,000 people. As the largest Croatian port on the Danube, Vukovar was a busy centre of trade and transport.

Today. it is only a shadow of what it once was, and Croatian authorities from the 1990s until today have not invested enough in it. It was the fifth-largest city in the former Socialist Republic of Croatia, then larger even than Zadar, while today it is not ranked among the ten largest Croatian cities.

World.title: Croatia is Full of Tourists, But “Coolcations” Are Increasingly Popular
World.content:
August the 25th, 2026 – Croatia remains full of tourists, but with horrifically hot temperatures now the norm, “coolcations” pose a serious threat to hotter countries as they become increasingly popular.

The director of the Croatian National Tourist Board, Kristjan Staničić, said that there are still more than a million tourists per day in Croatia and that August is so far at the level of last year’s results. Index reports that when speaking on HRT’s Dnevnik, Staničić said that Croatia is still at the peak of the tourist season, but he did not want to forecast what August would be like until the end. “For now I can say that August is at the level of last year’s figures,” he said.

“coolcations” are becoming more and more popular as people tire of overwhelming heat

Staničić also commented on a new tourist trend, the so-called “coolcation”, or the growing interest in cooler destinations in northern Europe. As he explained, because of ever higher summer temperatures and repeated heatwave cycles, many people are looking for places where July and August are more pleasant than on the Mediterranean and in southern Europe. He believes this trend will continue in the coming years and that the tourism sector must be prepared for it. He recalled that climate change has been affecting travellers’ decisions for a longer time, but considers that Croatia, thanks to its diverse offer, can respond to such changes as well.

As an example he mentioned Gorski kotar and Lika, where lower temperatures, quality accommodation, good gastronomy and contents linked to nature and active holidays can be found even during the summer.

inspectors clamp down on illegal rentals and s

Staničić also commented on the intensified work of the tourist inspection this season. Because of illegal operation, eight campsites, 23 holiday homes, 56 apartments, one smaller hotel and one hostel have been closed. He thanked the staff of the State Inspectorate and everyone involved in combating the black market. “Unfortunately, this is a phenomenon that is present and to which a response is needed,” he said. He added that cooperation of all institutions, tourist boards and competent services in the field is important, especially when there is knowledge of unregistered guests or facilities that provide services without being registered for it.

croatian tourism requires proper order

Staničić also spoke about the amendments to the Hospitality Activity Act, against which the Association “Save Small Family Renters” has submitted an objection to the European Commission. They object, among other things, to re-categorisation every decade, the need for co-owners’ consent in multi-apartment buildings, and the conditions for obtaining host status. Staničić expects the law primarily to help in combating the black market.

As one of the most important novelties he singled out the introduction of a registration number that every accommodation service provider will have to have if they want to advertise on global platforms. According to him, such a system should enable more effective control of both accommodation facilities and the online platforms on which they are advertised.

“Everyone has the right to turn to the European Commission,” Staničić said, adding that Croatia has taken over the European acquis which includes the introduction of a registration number. He assessed that this measure should be one of the key tools for combating the black market and “introducing order into Croatian tourism”.

World.title: Croatian Railway Ambitions Tie in With European Defence Efforts
World.content:
August the 25th, 2026 – Croatian railway ambitions are closely linked with European defence efforts, as the country’s “decade of the railway” is still not really being felt on the ground by most.

Any reason for the renewal and development of the railway system in Croatia is very useful, including the security and defence one. But its civilian role remains primary. Index/Deutsche Welle/Igor Lasic reports that following two serious railway traffic incidents at the beginning of this month in Croatia, this mode of passenger and freight transport is once again a topic for the Croatian public.

Moreover, the general public has been reminded of the fact that Croatia is apparently currently in the middle of its “decade of the railway”. This is a state project for the development of this long-neglected mode of transport, with an investment of six billion euros for new tracks and vehicles. Yet despite years of reconstruction, the results are still not really visible on the ground, even though some concrete works have long been planned. The announced “railway renaissance” will therefore clearly still have to wait, and the recent traffic accidents have uncomfortably highlighted this uncertainty.

On top of everything, a new element has been included in the reasoning for the renewal of the Croatian railway sector, and that’s the wider European defence system. Europe is rapidly arming itself, and Croatia has also bought, among other things, more than 40 German Leopard 2 tanks. These, however, because of their exceptional weight, require equally exceptional railway transport capacities. All of this ultimately enters into the final calculation of the development project of the public company Croatian Railways. On the other hand, its relative urgency and the need for centralisation of the system somewhat remove the possibility of imminent privatisation of the sector, which until recently was quite realistic.

so long, privatisation

“Only through the security sphere and social cohesion around the issue of defence have we come to the conclusion that the railway must be managed by the state if we want an efficient system,” Ante Klečina, a railway expert and lecturer at the Department of Sustainable Mobility and Logistics of the University Sjever (North) in Koprivnica and Varaždin, told DW. He referred to the experience of some more developed European countries, such as Great Britain, whose experiments with railway privatisation ended rather ignominiously. Services became of poor quality and too expensive, the system failed in various aspects, and over time it was abandoned.

“First and foremost should be their functionality for civilian needs and, in fact, the organisation of civilisation,” Klečina continues, “which is relevant at every moment if we do not put that priority out of our minds. Whoever swears by the advantages of market mechanisms forgets that they are not developmentally suitable for large public systems, those that enable basic requirements.” In his opinion, the same applies to other elementary systems, e.g. healthcare, education and the judiciary, etc. The private sector, says Klečina, can be a supplement in certain segments, but the backbone must remain public.

“The reason is the necessity of central planning of such systems, as well as their primarily non-profit task, but also the need for enormous investments for which private individuals usually have neither the capacity nor the interest. Having seen this in practice, Europe has recently abandoned the idea of privatising railways, and the defence topic came afterwards as an additional reason,” considers Ante Klečina, formerly president of the Railway Alliance in the Republic of Croatia. He further notes that this mode of transport has no equal with regard to a series of key factors: above all overall cost-effectiveness, economic multiplier effects and environmental suitability.

central planning will always be needed

Socioeconomist Toni Prug, for his part, believes that behind the question of Croatian railways lies the general problem of political and scientific rejection of planning and public production as a relic of the past. That past concerns the period of socialism and Yugoslavia, and everything connected with it remained at the very least stigmatised after the war in Croatia. “In reality, however, all successful states are huge public production systems,” says Prug, “in which planning decides on the largest budgets within economies, on interventions whose importance for the population surpasses the importance of decisions that market actors make.”

This assistant professor at the Faculty of Humanities and Social Sciences of the University of Rijeka highlights the rule in business that when a market actor makes a mistake, i.e. when things go badly, competition replaces him. “And railways, like all other production systems of a public character that are physically fixed and have monopoly status, need to be carefully planned. Mistakes are much harder to correct. They are also managed differently, different parameters are optimised, a focus on profit does not help. It often cannot even be the goal; the goals are determined by the plan.” At the same time the question arises of whether the Republic of Croatia has the professional staff for designing and implementing this.

“private goals have prevailed over practicality”

“Our profession and managerial staff are educated through faculty and professional curricula that say almost nothing about why and how to produce systems and services of a public character, and why they are superior for certain needs,” Prug is convinced, adding that this knowledge still exists in some Croatian public systems, while in others it has collapsed and been left to spontaneity. In his assessment, the City of Zagreb represents a recent example in Croatia that planning can return and capacities be rebuilt. And on higher-quality, data- and analysis-based foundations, which does not concern the railway but can be a general model.

Toni Prug, who in his scientific work has dealt quite a bit with the topic of public sector management, finally conveyed to us the impression that Croatian Railways have so far been a kind of victim of the oil and automobile lobby. “Their private and profit goals have prevailed over the practicality, efficiency, safety and ecological superiority of modern railway systems,” he told DW. Such a hierarchy could change soon thanks to military priorities. But the future of the railway and of social development in general will certainly not be bright if its primarily civilian advantages remain somewhere beside the tracks.

World.title: Croatia Among European Record Holders for Firefighter Numbers
World.content:
August the 25th, 2026 – Croatia is among the European record holders when it comes to firefighter numbers as the overall number within Europe has fallen.

Poslovni reports that the total number of firefighters across the EU fell from 390,600 in 2024 to 372,400 in 2025, a drop of 18,200 people in a year that was the worst in EU history in terms of burned area.

Croatia is among the European record holders for firefighter numbers, holding one of the highest shares of professional firefighters in employment in the entire EU. Back in 2025, they accounted for 0.43 percent of total employment, making Croatia second among the 22 EU Member States for which data has been made available. This places Croatia right behind Greece (0.47 percent), according to Euronews. The EU average was 0.18 percent. Portugal follows with 0.33 percent, while the lowest shares are recorded by the Netherlands (0.05), Austria (0.07) and Sweden (0.10 percent).

Across the entire EU there were around 372,400 professional firefighters. Germany had the most, 57,700, followed by France with 47,700 and Italy with 43,500. Next come Poland with 40,000 and Spain with 38,500; the four largest EU economies together account for 187,400 firefighters, or 50.3 percent of the total number. The overall figure in the Union fell from 390,600 in 2024 to 372,400 in 2025, a drop of 18,200 people in a single year that was the worst in EU history for burned areas. The European Trade Union Confederation and EPSU call this drop “reckless cuts” and note that Poland lost 9,000 and France lodt 4,100 firefighters.

Croatia doesn’t rank among the leaders in total numbers, but its share of total employment is among the highest. Eurostat data refers to professional firefighters, including forest firefighters, but not volunteer firefighters. The data also doesn’t show precisely how many professional firefighters are specialised specifically in fighting open-air fires.

The data comes at a time when Europe is facing an ever-growing fire risk. According to the European Forest Fire Information System (EFFIS) by the 13th of August, the figure had risen to 568,415 hectares from 1,647 fires. For comparison, 2025 was the most destructive season ever recorded in the EU, with 1,079,538 hectares burned in 25 of the 27 EU Member States.

For 2026 the EU has secured a fleet of 22 firefighting aircraft and five helicopters, and in the event of major fires member states can request additional firefighters and equipment through the European Civil Protection Mechanism. In addition, a record 777 firefighters from 14 European countries have been pre-positioned in Cyprus, Greece, Italy, France, Spain and Portugal. Croatia contributes two medium amphibious aircraft to the European fleet, and in 2026 the Commission is also opening a new regional firefighting base in Cyprus with capacity for six aircraft.

World.title: Kilvar Kessler: Something has gone awry in the European apparatus
World.content:
Something has gone wrong with the European apparatus when an Estonian entrepreneur lands their first customer in Spain, only to discover that before shipping the goods, they must first navigate Spain's packaging registry, Kilvar Kessler writes.

Uno Loop and Heidy Tamme warned as far back as 1965 that you should not knit the sun into your mittens because then the snowball in your hand may melt. With the new European packaging rules that took effect on August 12, 2026, it is worth asking whether we have woven something into the bureaucracy that is causing the single market itself to melt away.

European single market as the engine of prosperity

The European Union grew out of the practical idea that if European countries removed barriers to trade among themselves and allowed goods to move freely, people would become more prosperous. The single market is not a byproduct of the European project, but one of its foundational ideas.

The European Union today is, of course, something different from the economic community established in 1957. The EU treaties place the internal market, economic growth and environmental protection alongside one another. The environment must therefore be protected in a way that does not simultaneously damage Europe's engine of prosperity: the single market.

This is especially important for Estonia. A French or Polish company can grow quite large without ever leaving its home market. In Estonia, with a market of just over 1 million consumers, the key to growth for our companies lies in Stockholm, Warsaw and Berlin. Small businesses account for more than 99 percent of EU companies. For a small country, cross-border sales are not a luxury but a way to achieve the scale that companies in larger countries can attain in their domestic markets.

When the medicine becomes the disease

This brings us to the paradox of the new Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation, or PPWR. The PPWR was adopted under the internal market provision of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union and its first recital emphasizes preventing barriers to the internal market arising from packaging-related requirements. The goal is sensible: less packaging waste, more recyclable packaging, fewer hazardous substances and more uniform requirements across Europe.

Under the PPWR, a producer must register in every member state where it places packaging or a packaged product on the market. It is also subject to certain extended producer responsibility requirements there. In addition, the PPWR requires a company selling directly to end users in another member state to appoint a local authorized representative.

Imagine a small Estonian online store that finds five customers in Austria, 10 in Spain and a few in Bulgaria. In the digital single market, this should be a success story: an Estonian business has found new customers and European consumers have gained more choice.

In regulatory reality, however, every new member state can mean a new registry, extended producer responsibility system, reporting requirements and local representative. The lower the sales volume, the more absurd the fixed cost per product sold becomes. For a large corporation, this is a job for the compliance department. For an Estonian company with three employees, it may be reason enough to say: We'd better not sell elsewhere in Europe.

Where are clarity and political pressure from Estonia?

Most tellingly, the European Commission itself has already acknowledged the problem. For example, the Commission wants to postpone some of the more onerous bureaucratic obligations for years. It has also acknowledged that the regulation's practical implementation has raised numerous questions because of its novelty and complexity.

A strange vacuum has emerged. The PPWR has applied since August 12, even though the Commission itself has drafted legislation to suspend one of the regulation's more burdensome requirements. The EU legislature, however, has yet to adopt the amendment.

At the same time, neither the Commission nor Estonia has so far publicly taken any visible steps to suspend enforcement of the requirement until the amendment is resolved. Some member states have already begun implementing the regulation. For businesses, the result is confusion: a requirement applies today that may no longer be necessary tomorrow.

Similar situations have been handled more clearly in the financial sector. When a requirement was due to take effect in European securities markets at the beginning of 2022 even as a postponement was being prepared, the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), which brings together Europe's financial market regulators, said directly at the end of 2021 that it could not make existing EU law disappear, but that national regulators would not prioritize enforcing the requirement in the meantime. This gave the market an official signal and some breathing room until lawmakers finished their work. We hope an equally clear interim solution will emerge for the packaging rules.

The criticism from our businesses is directed not so much at reducing packaging waste as at the way this is being done through the PPWR and the accompanying measures. In addition, the Estonian Employers' Confederation has warned, figuratively speaking, that if Estonia builds its own, stricter system alongside the directly applicable EU regulation, there will be at least twice as much bureaucracy.

These warning signs were already visible to politicians and officials while the regulation was being adopted. Three years ago, for example, the Riigikogu European Union Affairs Committee discussed exemptions for small businesses, assessments of the actual environmental impact and the need to avoid unnecessary bureaucracy in connection with the PPWR. Nearly a year ago, Germany's environment minister explicitly called for businesses to be given more time to implement the PPWR. Yet in Estonia, where a functioning cross-border market is even more important because of the country's small domestic market, strong political pressure on the issue has not been evident in public debate recently.

A small member state cannot be Brussels' taskmaster

A small country's role cannot simply be to diligently administer whatever text arrives from Brussels. Estonia must go to extraordinary lengths to ensure that the European single market works for small countries and small businesses.

In the first years of EU membership, Estonia's main task may have been to learn and implement the new rules. Twenty years later, the ambition must be to define Estonia's interests, build coalitions and shape European rules before, rather than after, they are adopted. We must also seek allies among other member states, demand genuinely proportionate treatment for micro and small businesses and refrain from adding extra requirements in Estonia. I would be glad to read about and applaud success stories like these.

Something has gone wrong with the European machinery when an Estonian entrepreneur lands their first customer in Spain, only to discover that before shipping the goods, they must consult Spain's packaging registry and find a local authorized representative. The European single market was created so that borders would cease to have economic significance. The Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation should not rebuild those borders in the form of bureaucracy.

World.title: Criminal probe opened over ecstasy drink-spiking by Estonian Drama Theater employee
World.content:
Oliver Reimann was previously a student at the Estonian Academy of Music and Theater (EMTA) when the allegations took place, and is now employed directing productions at the Estonian Drama Theater (Eesti Draamateater) in central Tallinn.

Eesti Ekspress reported that while he was a student at the theater Reimann allegedly laced two acquaintances' drinks with MDMA, also the main ingredient in ecstasy, without their knowledge or consent.

Prosecutor's Office spokesperson Kauri Sinkevicius told Eesti Ekspress on Tuesday lunchtime that criminal proceedings would be launched against Reimann. "Initially, we are opening proceedings under the section dealing with the unlawful handling of a small quantity of a narcotic substance," Sinkevicius said.

Reimann, 24, has made contributions to various ETV shows, mainly investigative show "Ringvaade."

Earlier on Tuesday, Reimann posted on Facebook, stating: "A few years ago, during my first year at university, there was a period when I was using illegal substances. A crisis of motivation, an overly intense start to student life, heartbreak and widespread drug use in the circles around me made it easier to enter that world. Experimenting quite quickly turned into repeated use, and although I thought I had the situation under control, the reality was different."

"Unfortunately, I also hurt people close to me. In addition to my own, on two occasions I also put a party drug into a friend's drink without us having agreed on that beforehand," Reimann went on, adding that he was not looking for excuses. He said the act was not malicious, though conceded it was entirely wrong.

Reimann also stated in his post he had apologized to both of the people involved and that earlier this year, ahead of joining the drama theater, he had informed its management of what had happened and sought professional help. Reimann said he had also missed out on job opportunities as a result of the incident, and expressed a desire to change after acknowledging his mistakes.

Oliver Reimann Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

Eesti Ekspress reported that when he was a drama student and prior to landing a job at the theater, Reimann spiked the drinks of coursemates Robi Varul and Richard Ester with MDMA without their consent. After the first incident, the school was informed. Koldits spoke to both Reimann and Varul, while Reimann was allowed to continue on condition nothing similar happened again. Varul did not demand his expulsion.

When rumours of a second incident surfaced, Koldits dismissed them until Varul confirmed, during the summer break, that Ester was also affected. Koldits then advised Reimann to seek help and tell the press the truth.

Koldits has rejected claims of a cover‑up, telling Eesti Ekspress the case was discussed with those involved and with Reimann's future employer, the drama theater. The theater's artistic director, Hendrik Toompere Jr., also spoke with Reimann and allowed him to continue, as he had appeared remorseful. The drama school confirmed the matter had been dealt with.

Eesti Ekspress said a few weeks later Toompere learned of the incident involving Ester. He now says his earlier belief that the matter would be resolved was naive, and when no resolution had been reached, Ester said he and Varul would go to the media.

Last week, Toompere informed Reimann that his new production, "Samueli võlupadi," scheduled to premiere on December 5, would not be going ahead and that all further plans involving Reimann had been put on hold. It is unclear whether Reimann will remain on the drama theater's payroll.

Reimann's supervisor: I acted according to my conscience

Head of the EMTA drama school Mart Koldits, who was Reimann's supervisor when he was a student, subsequently gave comment to Vikerraadio, saying he acted according to his conscience in the case and calling for more systematic drug education.

He said incidents dated back to around three years ago. "They (Robi Varul and Oliver Reimann - ed.) had very serious looks on their faces, and I immediately understood that something had happened. As it was a suitable moment and the situation was discreet, Oliver immediately began talking. It was very difficult for him to talk about it. I was very shocked; at first my brain couldn't even process what the context was, what the substance was," Koldits recalled.

Mart Koldits. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

"I questioned them to get as clear a picture as possible. I sent Oliver out of the room, spoke some more with Robi and then with both of them together. They had first gone to their class and held a huge meeting there, where Oliver confessed to everything. They had the courage to come and talk about it themselves," Koldits went on.

There were two incidents. The first was what happened with Robi Varul. I and the school and the faculty learned about it two weeks after it happened. We dealt with it then, and at that point I felt that, taking all the nuances and background into account, it was possible to protect the students and make as humane a decision as possible. After speaking with the victim, Robi, with Oliver Reimann and with the entire class, we ultimately decided that the matter could be resolved in a way that allowed us to give Oliver another chance and let him remain at the school. The situation did resolve itself well, and in the end everyone felt safe and they worked on productions together."

"As for what happened this past summer, it emerged that Oliver had not actually told us everything. It turned out that there had been a similar incident that same summer, a few days earlier. That created a situation where the students, Robi and Richard Ester, came to me themselves and said that they no longer wanted to put up with the speculation and rumors that had already taken on hyperbolic proportions in the theater and around town. They said, 'let's go to the media and tell the story, and then it will be viable to move on from the issue'. That's how the article in Eesti Ekspress came about," Koldits went on.

He said EMTA thought carefully about whether to go to the authorities at the time, and after talking to Varul decided "considering all the circumstances, it did not seem like the right idea. At the time, it seemed that the best solution was the one we chose. We discussed everything within the class. Oliver pulled himself together, and I later saw no signs at school that he was using intoxicating substances," Koldits added.

You have to act as much as possible according to your own conscience and inner moral compass, and I would like to hope that I still have mine," Koldits said.

Reimann was a drama student at EMTA, picture here, and went on to work for the Estonian Drama Theater. Source: Siim Lõvi /ERR

He called it a "humane solution," though added "knowing what later emerged, it's difficult to say."

As to whether drug use is widespread among drama school students, for instance as a consciousness-expanding activity, Koldits said he would "prefer to believe not," adding this was the first such case at the theater and drama school, which he said has an "absolute zero tolerance for the use of such substances.

"You alter your state of consciousness by changing your attitude and your patterns of thought. That requires consistent work, attention to yourself and focus. Chemical substances only lead you down a hole," Koldits went on.

In light of the case, Koldits said the issue may need more discussion within the EMTA school.

Reimann has apologized to the "Ringvaade" production team.

"His actions are, of course, unacceptable, and we have told him so. At the same time, it is important to us that he has understood his mistake and, as could also be read in the article, has taken concrete steps to address his problems," said Karmel Killandi, head of entertainment at ETV. Reimann has no ongoing projects with ETV, including with "Ringvaade."

MDMA (3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine) is a synthetic psychoactive drug that acts as both a stimulant and a mild psychedelic, and is commonly known as ecstasy or molly.

World.title: Government to debate online casino tax break once again
World.content:
The government will revisit the online casino tax reduction introduced earlier this year during state budget and fiscal strategy talks, Prime Minister Kristen Michal said. He noted that if the measure does not bring additional revenue, there is no reason to continue lowering the tax.

A law passed by the Riigikogu last December reduces the gambling tax on online casinos from 6 percent to 4 percent over two years. The goal was to attract more online casinos to register in Estonia and thereby increase tax revenue. Instead, the state budget has seen several million euros in shortfalls.

Michal said the government must therefore consider whether further tax cuts make sense.

"Certainly this debate will happen. The first clear principle I stated is that culture must not lose out. We have already compensated the missing funds caused by this legislative mistake, and we must find the rest as well so that culture does not suffer," he said.

Because the tax cut has been in place only a short time, Michal said it is difficult to assess whether more online casinos are actually registering in Estonia. It is also not yet clear why gambling tax receipts have fallen. The government expects a clearer picture in the coming weeks.

If tax revenue does not increase, continuing the tax reduction would not be justified, Michal added.

ERR reported in June that the tax change — intended to boost state revenue by attracting foreign online casinos — has not brought new operators to Estonia.

The Riigikogu approved the amendment last December, led by Eesti 200 MP Tanel Tein, lowering the online casino tax from 6 to 4 percent over two years.

The change faced significant criticism, including from coalition members. The Ministry of Finance warned that the tax cut would create a budget gap: gambling tax revenue would fall by €6 million in 2026, €8 million in 2027, €10 million in 2028 and €13 million in 2029.

The bill also contained a typo that would have allowed online casinos to operate tax‑free in 2026. The Riigikogu had to pass a corrected version of the law in February.
