Max Reeves was too good for Oliver Firth in the last of the prelim fights.

After a pretty steady start, the heavily tattooed "Mad Max" upped the intensity at the start of the fourth and not long after blood appeared of indeterminate source on the body of Firth.

Firth's left eye was a mess by the end of that fourth round, the corner having to go to work hard on it between rounds.

Firth was still willing, but Reeves shots were carrying more power and the blood began to flow once more after Firth was rapped a couple more times on the head.

A TKO win for Mad Max.

World.title: Video shows antisemitic road rage abuse in Adelaide's CBD
World.content:
The Anti Defamation Commission says a Jewish woman visiting Adelaide was subjected to antisemitic abuse on her first day in the city.

In a video released by the commission, people in a car driving on Hutt St in the city appear to be yelled at by someone in another car.

"Come and face me you f***ing gutless c***. You're a Jew aren't you? You're a f***ing Jew aren't you?" the man can be heard yelling in the video.

The car then speeds away, using the right turn lane to cut in front of traffic heading north.

While only a short clip of the interaction has been made public, Anti Defamation Commission chairman Dvir Abramovich said the abuse came "out of the blue".

"One theory is something enraged him about the car or about traffic," Dr Abramovich said.

"He saw those two individuals and he exploded into rage using that word Jew but there was no context, there was no interaction, there was no engagement between the Jewish passengers in that car and that individual."

The video captured an incident on Hutt Street, in Adelaide's CBD. (Supplied: Anti-Defamation Commission )

Dr Abramovich said the woman lives in Melbourne and was visiting another Jewish person in Adelaide, who was also in the car, to see if the city would be a good place to relocate as she feared what he said was rising antisemitism in Melbourne.

"The irony here is unbelievable. Here you have an Israeli-Jewish woman who wants to relocate from Melbourne," he said.

"She arrives in Adelaide, on her first day she's exposed to Jew hatred of the worst level."

Dr Abramovich said the pair were considering reporting the man to police, and had recorded his number plate.

SA Police said it had so far not received any formal report relating to the footage.

"SAPOL encourage the owner of the footage to contact police by attending at their nearest police station and providing their details and a copy of the footage," a spokesperson said.

"We also encourage those involved to report the matter to police."

World.title: Bus company fined $650k over deadly Greta crash
World.content:
Grieving families and survivors of a bus crash that claimed 10 lives have described the lasting impacts of the tragedy as a judge fined the bus company $650,000 for employing a drug-impaired driver.

Brett Andrew Button, 61, is serving a maximum of 32 years in jail for the Greta bus crash in 2023.

Separately, Linq Buslines and its directors Christopher Fogg and Anthony Royle have pleaded guilty to charges brought by the National Heavy Vehicle Regulator.

They admitted to failing in their duty of care in relation to risks linked to speeding, fatigue and the employment of drug-impaired drivers.

Christopher Fogg pleaded guilty to breaching heavy vehicle law. (ABC Central Coast: Sarah Forster)

In sentencing proceedings in Gosford Local Court, Judge Kirralee Perry today imposed a total of $650,000 in fines on Linq Buslines but said "no amount would take away the pain" for victims' families.

She agreed with prosecutor Georgia Lewer that Linq Buslines recruited a driver who put the community at risk.

"The offender [Linq Buslines] recruited a man [Button] who had been stood down from a previous employer with an opioid dependency and posed a significant risk," Judge Perry said.

The court heard the only check on Button's reference was by text message, with a former boss calling Button a "good bloke".

Linq Buslines has ceased operating. (ABC Newcastle: Romy Stephens)

The text message exchange also described bus drivers as "steering wheel attendants", a term that drew the ire of Judge Perry.

"It is flippant at best and it is wholly inappropriate in terms of being used as a way to provide a reference check for somebody who is going to be put in charge of driving a heavy vehicle," she said.

Mr Fogg and Mr Royle faced maximum fines of $59,000 for offences related to "overspeeding".

Judge Perry said the offending related to seven drivers who sped on 12 occasions.

"The company and directors fell short in ensuring they complied with their duty," she said.

The judge fined Mr Fogg and Mr Royle $12,000 each and said the offending was at the "lower end" of the range.

She declined a request not to record convictions for both men.

Anthony Royle pleaded guilty to breaching heavy vehicle law. (ABC Central Coast: Sarah Forster)

She said Mr Royle was "in shock and overwhelmed with sorrow and so gutted by the incident".

The judge said Mr Fogg had also shown remorse.

"He has had a strong stress response to the crash and subsequently over the past three years he has been preoccupied by the sheer scale of the loss of life," she said.

Judge Perry expressed her sympathies to families affected by the "devastating crash" throughout proceedings.

Linq Buslines is no longer trading after bus contracts were not renewed and accreditation was terminated in March.

Victim tells of 'hideous disfigurement'

Families and survivors of the crash delivered emotional victim impact statements in court today.

Sharyn Junkeer suffered horrific injuries and travelled to Gosford from Melbourne to deliver her statement.

"It looks like a shark has taken a bite out of my thigh and hip, leaving me with a hideous disfigurement," she said.

Ms Junkeer choked back tears describing the impact of the crash when she thought she would die.

Jason and Sharyn Junkeer choked back tears describing the moment their lives changed. (ABC News)

"Every day I have to live with the knowledge that I survived this tragedy while so many others did not," Ms Junkeer said.

Her husband, Jason Junkeer, also gave a statement and paused at times while delivering it.

"It's been three years now and I have not got better," he said.

"I still live with chronic pain, a brain injury, PTSD and depression."

Matt and Leanne Mullen gave victim impact statements. (ABC News)

Parents 'broken' by loss

Matt and Leanne Mullen travelled to Gosford from Singleton to deliver their addresses, with both describing crippling grief.

Their daughter, Rebecca, a young doctor, died that night at Greta, along with nine others.

"The impact on the family is that it has broken me," Mr Mullen said.

" I can still see the bus on its side. I wake up to it often at night. "

He told the court he was glad Mr and Mrs Junkeer, whom he previously did not know, survived the crash.

Mrs Mullen spoke of the daily impact losing a daughter has had on her life.

"That night has changed my daily interactions with my community," she said.

"Life is no longer simple or carefree in the community that I love."

World.title: Anita Perrottet paid $254k for being a ‘sounding board’, corruption inquiry hears
World.content:
Anita Perrottet was paid $254,666 in a three-month period for being a “sounding board” and providing verbal advice to Jeremy Greenwood with no evidence of written work, a corruption inquiry has heard. In evidence before the Independent Commission Against Corruption on Wednesday, Perrottet denied claims put to her that she was in an “impossible position” because she was being asked to lie under oath and cover for her husband Charles, a former Liberal powerbroker who is one of three party apparatchiks under investigation for receiving a $2 million bribe from a disgraced developer Jean Nassif. Anite Perrottet leaves the ICAC on Wednesday. James Brickwood Anita Perrottet has not been named as a person of interest in the ICAC inquiry into illegal political donations, but the commission is investigating whether she played a role in helping receive money from Nassif for her husband. Charles declined to turn up and give evidence to a 2023 parliamentary inquiry into illegal donations and The Hills Shire Council. His brother Jean-Claude stayed in Fiji for the duration of the inquiry while Christian Ellis and Jeremy Greenwood hid so that a summons could not be served on them.



The commission heard Anita Perrottet’s company was paid significant lump sums for strategic work for two of Jeremy Greenwood’s firms, Beckington and JPG Advisory. That advice was mostly verbal and over encrypted messaging apps, or using her husband Charles’ phone to speak with Greenwood. The most significant payments were made in the final quarter of 2022, when Perrottet invoiced Greenwood for a total of $254,666 for her strategic advice. One example she gave to the ICAC was for a vaping industry client some of that oral advice included “minors shouldn’t be able to be buying vapes”, Perrottet said. “So that’s based on a salary of a million dollars, Mrs Perrottet – let’s get serious,” Counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer, SC, said. “You are giving evidence under oath. Do you seriously suggest that the commission should accept that, as truthful evidence, that you were entitled to charge $254,666 for work that you actually did … providing an oral sounding board or advice to Jeremy Greenwood for that quarter?” Perrottet said yes, that was her truthful evidence.



Dwyer also asked Perrottet to explain why her computer metadata showed an invoice from her company Macquarie Consulting was created by her husband in January 2022, and then modified in March 2023 – the same month Charles was avoiding the inquiry. “Mrs Perrottet, can I suggest to you, you have been put in an impossible situation because you are being asked to lie under oath to cover for your husband?” Dwyer said. “I reject that, I’m not lying,” Perrottet said. Dwyer reminded Perrottet she had taken an oath on the Bible to tell the truth to the ICAC and stressed to her it was an offence to lie. Anita Perrottet appears at the ICAC. ICAC



The commission was shown evidence of friendly text messages between Charles Perrottet and Jean Nassif, which included Charles thanking the property developer for hosting him and his children at his home. Greenwood and his business partner Christian Ellis and their partners were also invited to lunch with Nassif, but Anita Perrottet said she wasn’t there. She couldn’t remember if Charles ever talked about meeting Nassif, or if he told her he was taking their children to his home, Perrottet said. In other memory lapses, Perrottet said she could not remember whether she has ever been a party member, nor recall details of her husband’s role in a powerful Liberal Party subcommittee. Perrottet told the commission on Wednesday that she was not currently a member of the Liberal Party but was not sure whether she had been in the past. She said when her brother-in-law Dominic Perrottet became premier of NSW in 2021 she was happy for him, but it had little impact on her family because she was living in Victoria at the time. Dominic Perrottet is not accused of any wrongdoing.



Perrottet also said she could not remember anything about her husband’s role in the Liberal Party’s local government oversight committee, a powerful body that oversees the preselection of candidates for council elections. She said she had heard the words “local government oversight committee” but did not remember anything about it. Dwyer read out evidence from a secret hearing in February 2024 in which Perrottet gave evidence that she knew Charles Perrottet was bringing matters to that committee, and remembered he began his position about 2018 or 2019. “Does that refresh your memory?” Dwyer asked. “No, not really, sorry,” Anita Perrottet said.



In her opening statement, Dwyer said she expected evidence to show Charles Perrottet anticipated receiving significant funds from Nassif, but there was no evidence of him receiving money directly. Instead, Dwyer said she expected evidence would show the funds were paid into an account by the company name of Macquarie Consulting Pty Ltd – with Anita Perrottet as the sole director and shareholder. Related Article Analysis

Operation Rosny One common factor among ICAC witnesses makes their questionable actions even more stupid Dwyer’s opening statement said she anticipated that the commission would “receive submissions to the effect that the payments to Macquarie Consulting were for consulting work legitimately carried out by Anita Perrottet for Beckington and JPG Advisory. “Yet, in the nearly four years that the commission has been investigating the allegations the subject of this inquiry, it has uncovered no evidence of Anita Perrottet carrying out any work for either Beckington or JPG Advisory,” Dwyer said in her opening statement.



“Instead, the commission’s investigation has unearthed evidence of Mr [Christian] Ellis dictating to Charles Perrottet, and not his wife, how he should structure the invoices that were ultimately issued by Macquarie Consulting to Beckington for the 2021/2022 financial year.” Anita Perrottet told the commission she could not remember why she urgently asked to be removed as a shareholder from a company called Beckington National. The company was established during the COVID-19 lockdowns, when Charles Perrottet feared he may be made redundant from his position at BP. Anita Perrottet’s business was listed as a shareholder, as was Ellis’ wife. She does not remember setting up the company, nor sending an urgent email to her accountant asking to be removed as a shareholder. Dwyer pressed her on this. “Can I suggest to you, Mrs Perrottet, that this is your opportunity to be really honest about these accounts … It appears that this had nothing to do with you, and had something to do with people behind the scenes setting it up. Is that the true situation?”



Anita Perrottet: “No.” Dwyer: “But you have no memory of this, is that right?” Perrottet: “I can’t remember it. It’s not to say I didn’t read it but I, I don’t remember it now.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Police investigating death of Sydney teenager after suspected choking act during sex
World.content:
Breaking PoliticsNSWCrime Police investigating death of Sydney teenager after suspected choking act during sex Jack Gramenz Updated August 26, 2026 — 6:46pm ,first published 3:16pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Police are investigating the death of a 16-year-old girl on Sydney’s northern beaches after a suspected choking act during sex. The teenager died in hospital two days after emergency services responded to a concern for welfare at an Elanora Heights on Sunday night. They found the girl unresponsive. Loading She was flown to Royal North Shore Hospital in a critical condition, where she died on Tuesday night. Two sources with knowledge of the case confirmed the teenager is believed to have engaged in a choking act during sex.



Warnings about sexual strangulation have increased amid scrutiny of violent online pornography, which experts say has warped young peoples’ understanding of sex and normalised concerning behaviour. Researchers at the University of Melbourne and University of Queensland reported in 2024 that about 50 per cent of young people had engaged in choking or strangulation during sex, partly because many people mistakenly believe it can be done safely. “It [sexual strangulation] is happening incredibly frequently, people are doing it regularly … and half the people are doing it at least several times,” lead author Professor Heather Douglas said at the time. The 16-year-old died at Royal North Shore Hospital on Tuesday night. Renee Nowytarger “Brain injury accumulates – the more times you are strangled, the greater the impact on the brain. I suspect there are probably a lot of young people with impacts on their brain as a result of this behaviour and that’s incredibly concerning.”



The NSW government’s own submission to a recent parliamentary inquiry said depictions of sexual aggression including strangulation in pornography has been linked to increased intimate partner violence, citing research from 2017 by the federal government’s Australian Institute of Family Studies. Federal independent MP Zali Steggall, from the neighbouring electorate of Warringah, said the teenager’s death underscored the need for a national education campaign to tackle misogyny and teach respectful relationships. “My thoughts are with her family, friends and community at this incredibly difficult time,” she said. “Police are investigating the circumstances of the girl’s death and no charges have been laid. We must allow the legal process to take place. “Regardless of the circumstances of this particular case, the Albanese government itself has confirmed that rates of sexual violence, particularly amongst young people, are rising.



“The Albanese government must urgently roll out a national campaign ensuring young people receive ongoing sexual-health and relationship education.” Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732). World.title: Premiers to demand more federal cash after Albanese’s refusal to change GST deal
World.content:
Premiers will demand Prime Minister Anthony Albanese permanently hand over more federal taxpayers’ money to them as the price for his emphatic support for WA’s sweetheart GST deal, while federal Labor has softened its stance on using green energy to power data centres. Sources inside Sydney’s national cabinet meeting told this masthead the GST was only briefly discussed, after the prime minister recommitted to the special Morrison-government era deal which is on track to cost taxpayers $60 billion but is viewed as key to winning seats in WA. WA Premier Roger Cook, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and NSW Premier Chris Minns. Dominic Lorrimer But the same sources said frustrated premiers, including NSW’s Chris Minns, Victoria’s Ben Carroll, and South Australia’s Peter Malinuaskas, have been told by Canberra that the WA deal will be subject to a proper discussion at a national cabinet meeting in February or March next year. The Productivity Commission’s interim report published earlier this month labelled the deal a mistake that had created perverse fiscal outcomes, almost all of which had benefited Western Australia at the expense of the rest of the federation and federal taxpayers.



It warned the deal could end up costing federal taxpayers $12 billion a year. Related Article GST PM backs GST deal, leaves future taxpayers on the hook for billions But the report, due to be finalised by the end of the year, has sparked a transcontinental war of words with WA Premier Roger Cook attacking the Productivity Commission as a bunch of “east coast clowns” and opponents to the deal as “whingers”. Albanese, who declared in Perth this week that the deal would not change while he was prime minister, waded into the furore by describing the commission’s report as the work of economic rationalists. Following Wednesday’s national cabinet meeting, Albanese ducked a question on whether Minns, Carroll or Malinauskas had raised the issue. Asked about NSW’s complaints about the GST, Albanese talked up his relationship with Minns, who faces an election in March next year.



“This bloke here, the premier of New South Wales: I’ll be working hard to make sure he stays the premier after March next year. And under my government, NSW will always get support,” Albanese said. This masthead understands key premiers plan to press Albanese to make permanent the most expensive feature of the WA deal, which is a “no worse off guarantee”. These payments, worth about $6 billion a year, are made to all states bar WA to ensure no state and territory is financially penalised by the deal. Loading The guarantee has been extended by the Albanese government to the end of 2030. The states and territories not only want it permanent, but hope to have it bolstered so they receive extra federal assistance. Outside the meeting, Treasurer Jim Chalmers chided Cook for his criticism of the Productivity Commission, saying some of the commentary about the institution’s report was “unfortunate”.



“I don’t believe that is appropriate. I think you can disagree with the conclusions of the Productivity Commission without denigrating them,” he said. “I think it is important that even when those conclusions are contested – as they often will be – that we continue to respect the people of the PC and the really important work that they do.” The national cabinet meeting agreed to push forward a new plan to reduce domestic violence, ban 3D-printed guns, and ban foreigners from holding gun licences, a move prompted by the Bondi massacre. A proposed national gun buyback is still opposed by all administrations bar NSW and the ACT, but leaders agreed to greater intelligence sharing on the same day as the antisemitism royal commission wrapped up its final hearings. Albanese also got an agreement on his proposed national AI framework, after accommodating the position of conservative states. The conservative governments of Queensland and NT had baulked at the federal government’s proposal to mandate that data centres must only be powered by green energy. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor backed Queensland’s position.



Wednesday’s agreement gave ground to Queensland, which has a fleet of state-owned coal plants in competition with wind and solar farms. The NT is backing the development of a gas field in the Beetaloo Basin, which it says could fuel an industrial boom. Albanese acknowledged the different situations facing Queensland and the NT given the public ownership of power generation, transmission and distribution. Queensland Premier David Crisafulli said his state had a “really big point of difference”. “We own distribution, transmission, generation, and that enables us to control that energy mix,” he said. “We believe that we can control our data sovereignty, protect the rights of local communities, and enable that energy mix to bring those data centres on.”



The meeting’s official communiqué did not mention renewable energy. Instead, it talked up the “generational opportunity” offered by AI and noted environmental issues surrounding large data centres would be addressed by federal legislation early next year. World.title: Trump’s abuse of once-great nation is an American tragedy
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

What an insult to the memory of all those involved in both D-Day in 1944 and the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989 that the yes-men in Washington should invoke these events, likening them to their own utterly inept, unnecessary and wasteful – both in lives lost and economies ruined – bungle in Iran (“The White House says this is the Iran endgame. We’ve heard that before”, August 25). The self-aggrandisement of this administration is breathtaking and knows no limit. What a tragedy for a once-great nation to be used by such a fool as nothing more than his personal plaything. History will not be kind. Patrick McGrath, Potts Point US president Donald Trump has made 3624 stock trades in his second term so far. Bloomberg The Truth and Accountability Project, a US political action committee and advocacy organisation, has published figures that truly focus the mind on current US corruption and the foolishness of Australia trusting it as a reliable ally (Letters, August 26). The committee has listed the stock trades by the past six presidents while in office during a 33-year period. Bill Clinton, George W Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden made zero stock trades while in office. Donald Trump, in his first term, had 54 trades and during this term of 16 months so far has had, wait for it, 3624. The PAC adds the following: “This is the most corrupt administration to ever hold power anywhere in the history of the world”, which may be an exaggeration. But maybe not. At the very least it’s an ethics disaster and an abuse of the office. Alison Stewart, Riverview When will the Americans wake up to the fact that Trump’s MAGA has morphed into MTRA (Make Trump Richer Again)? John O’Connell, Old Toongabbie Correspondent Vincent Zankin suggests a slogan for Jon Ossoff’s presidential campaign: MAMA (Make America Moral Again). I am all in favour but, Vincent, when exactly was America ever moral? I have read a lot of American history but I just can’t pinpoint it. Paul Sowter, Westleigh How droll it is that senior US officials are constantly referring to the Iranian regime as “evil”. The Trump (mal)administration could, with equal justification, be similarly described. Very few US regimes over the years could be described as benevolent, but the current one outstrips them all.

Ian Usman Lewis, Armidale



Stand with Canada Just like our correspondent from Campsie (Letters, August 26), I too am awaiting the announcement from our prime minister about the American president’s outrageous verbal attacks and tariff war on our commonwealth partner Canada. Isn’t it about time Anthony Albanese took to the microphone and denounced these attacks, and while he’s at it, he could follow PM Mark Carney and Doug Ford of Ontario and tell Trump where he can put his tariffs? I won’t hold my breath, but in the meantime I will refuse to buy any products from America and thank goodness I can still get my Canadian maple syrup. Llieda Wild, Eastwood Goodbye, Dolly Most of the tributes I have seen mention Dolly Parton’s singing, songwriting and acting talents, which many of us love (“Country music legend Dolly Parton dies aged 80”, August 25). Very few of them acknowledge the arguably greater contribution she made as a philanthropist. Mostly through her Dollywood Foundation, she funded the Buddy Program to encourage kids to stay at school, raised money for HIV and AIDS-related charities, donated to the development of a COVID vaccine, and provided various other forms of community support. My personal favourite as a retired librarian is her contribution through her literacy program, Imagination Library, which has brought books to hundreds of thousands of children who possibly would not have had access to them, from birth to school age, in many countries including Australia. So vale to Dolly Parton, who shared her wealth around and always considered those less fortunate than herself. Mary Anne Kennan, Burwood Country star Dolly Parton was also a generous philanthropist. AP Photo/Jonathan Short Dolly Parton and Donald Trump were both born in 1946. On her death, the messages from the people who knew her frequently used the adjectives “talented”, “generous”, “humble”, “funny” and “genuine”. None of these words could aptly be applied to Trump. When he dies, the flags will fly at half-mast, just as they will for Dolly this week. But whereas the death of Dolly has brought immense sadness, Trump’s death will bring a sense of relief that he can do no more damage. Mike Reddy, Vincentia Dolly onstage at a gusty KGV oval in Glenorchy, Tasmania: “If this wind keeps blowin’ I might be the first singer strangled to death by her own wig.” Bill Casey, The Gap (Qld)



To credit of few Ross Gittins may not be an economist, but his critique of carbon credit and offset systems is on the money (“Why Labor’s carbon credit scheme’s an economist-conceived sham”, August 26). Real climate action requires slashing pollution from coal, oil and gas, ending land clearing and restoring carbon‑rich ecosystems – all at the same time. Offsetting burnt coal and gas by protecting a tree is at best problematic and at worst a dangerous crutch undermining progress. Many carbon offsets are dodgy. When will the Albanese and state governments strengthen integrity rules so carbon accounting reflects reality rather than wishful thinking? Sarah Brennan, Hawthorn (Vic) Ross Gittins’ opinion piece on the Albanese’s government environmental offset mechanism concludes: “The truth is that the economists’ lovely offset scheme is a sham that Labor is using to make us think it cares about climate change when it doesn’t”. Making matters worse, NSW Premier Chris Minns is now retreating from his promise on the NSW government’s long-promised Great Koala National Park. Just as Nero fiddled while Rome burned, so too do our Labor politicians, state and federal, fiddle their con-jobs while Northern Europe burns. Who to believe, Ross Gittins or Albanese and Minns? I’ll trust Ross every time over the others. Michael Davis, Balmain East Worthy young men As an AFL household (no, not Swans fans) all I’ve heard for the past week and a half is the trouble with the Swans. If the AFL is serious about player behaviour, why do they have a “Mad Monday”, the title of which implies that anything goes (“AFL players red-faced over Mad Monday”, August 26)? I don’t think the problem is men per se. I have been married to one for 45 years. The problem is individuals and individuals in company. The other week we watched a heartfelt farewell speech from Adelaide Crows player Tex Walker as he prepared to hang up his boots. And at the awards night on Tuesday, a young man whose name I do not know spoke sincerely, succinctly and from the bottom of his heart about the need to be aware of mental health, having lost his brother to suicide earlier in the year. There are some terrific men out there. Genevieve Milton Dulwich Hill It seems pretty low-brow for a photographer to be stalking a private party of a team of AFL players who came 17th on the ladder this year. We’re really not interested at all at what they “got up to” at their party. Leave them alone. James Butchart, Lilyfield These AFL stories reminds this bloke of Lord Chesterfield’s line: “Young men are apt to think themselves wise enough; just as drunken men are apt to think themselves sober enough.” Howard Hutchins, Wantirna (Vic)



Photo: Cathy Wilcox Truth stripped bare While Jenna Price makes a fair point about the need for many men to grow up when it comes to attitudes towards women, the suggestion that women would always opt for something like room service and a long shower to celebrate an achievement and would never consider something as debased as hiring a couple of strippers can’t go unchallenged (“Women have changed. Why are men struggling to keep up?” August 25.) A quick Google search reveals several establishments around Australia that seem to be doing quite well offering, for hens nights and similar celebratory occasions, anything from male strippers to naked male waiters and male lap dancers. One even offers a “suck and blow card race”. While I can’t possibly imagine what that involves, presumably it’s something a little more adventurous than curling up under the doona with a camomile tea and a Mills & Boon novel. Ross Duncan, Potts Point Place for shame In response to a schoolboy’s question “How do you control a wife?” youth educator Daniel Principe is reported as not shaming the boy but rather using his remark as “an opening to unpack where the student had learnt the premise” (“This Sydney private school asked students to help solve the consent crisis”, August 26). It’s all very well to try to “understand” where these attitudes derive from (no great mystery actually), but let us not remove shame from the equation. Misogyny is evil and should be viewed and treated as deeply shameful. Whether it be a prime minister who engages in sexist banter while willingly participating in some vapid podcast, or overpaid and over-exposed footballers indulging in dehumanising debauchery, or a classroom provocateur mindlessly spewing the latest vile catchphrase he’s absorbed from the so-called manosphere, these behaviours should always be called out and the perpetrators shamed. It’s the increasing shamelessness of our society (and tolerance or apathy) that contributes to the normalisation of disgraceful attitudes and behaviours. Kathleen Riley, Burradoo We are one but many Perhaps Pauline Hanson and One Nation need to think more deeply about identity (“The figure One Nation supporters back more than anyone but Hanson”, August 25). Identity is shaped by the characteristics, beliefs, values, experiences and attributes that define who we are, how we see ourselves and how we are recognised by others. Australia’s identity has never been a single, uniform pathway. It has been shaped by many cultures, backgrounds, experiences and perspectives coming together to create the country we are today. One Nation appears intent on reducing that complexity to a single, narrow definition of what it means to be Australian. But that is not the Australia I believe we are, nor the Australia I believe we want to become. Our identity is not diminished by diversity – it is enriched by it. Stephen Wilson, Kangaroo Valley



While based in London in the 1990s I frequently used to spend a week at a time working on-site with collaborators in Milan. I was particularly struck when walking around the city that there were no “foreign” faces – everyone was “Italian-looking”, with no one visibly from other cultures or continents. There were few, if any, Chinese restaurants at the time. It made me feel slightly uncomfortable, having grown up in cosmopolitan, multicultural Sydney. Perhaps Pauline Hanson would appreciate this form on monoculture . I thought of this the other day while travelling home on Sydney’s Metro and looking at who else was on the train. I’d like to invite Hanson to join me on that trip one day. This is the face of modern Australia. Dale Bailey, St Leonards Friendly fire won’t save democracy

Kylie Moore-Gilbert asks why authoritarianism is more popular today, and answers that it’s because of influencers’ propaganda which is akin to that practiced by the Nazis (“The influencers convincing a generation to tear down democracy from within”, August 26). Odd, then, that she focuses on a left-wing Twitch streamer, Hasan Piker, and attacks the Democratic Socialists of America for commemorating Fidel Castro – but doesn’t mention, say, Elon Musk. Another reason authoritarianism is more popular today is that so many influencers insist that left and right become identical at the extremes – and then use that dubious claim to draw parallels between democratic socialism and actual existing right-wing tyrannies. This makes it impossible for the democratic left and democratic centre to band together, and pushes people on the left and the right towards the extremes. By contrast, the best way to save democracy is to build coalitions among democrats. Moore-Gilbert could promote coalitions by reaching out to people who agree with her on the evils of authoritarianism, even if they disagree about the meaning of the Cuban revolution. But instead, she likens them to Hitler – which is a misuse of her own influence, and also breaks the Herald’s letters page tip to “keep it civil”. Justin Evans, Petersham Flawed logic Correspondent Ken Enderby makes the point that we have a continuing dependence on gas for certain industrial processes and so should curtail the use of gas in the home (Letters, August 25). The logic is seriously flawed. Gas-fired generation is and will be an essential part of our baseload (and peaking) generation of electricity. So if domestic use of gas is curtailed, or banned, that gas which would have otherwise been delivered directly and efficiently into domestic situations will now be diverted to gas-fired power stations, where it will be converted into electrical energy at, at best, 60 per cent efficiency. That electricity will then suffer transmission losses in getting to homes, with the result that we will use something approaching one-and-a-half times as much of the scarce gas to get the same amount of energy into those homes. And that is saving our industries? I don’t think so. David King, Crows Nest Only human I shudder at the thought of driverless taxis (“Aussie capitals ‘will be driverless within a decade’, says robotaxi pioneer”, August 26)? Human taxi drivers can and often do tell you how to fix politics, love, sex and sport. They’re raconteurs, historians, poets, comedians, philosophers and, if you believe that their cousin owns the best restaurant in town, epicures as well. Lastly, they’re the person who cleans the cab before taking the next fare. Driverless taxis? No, thanks. Peter Butler, Wyongah

World.title: Anita Perrottet paid $254k for being a ‘sounding board’, corruption inquiry hears
World.content:
Anita Perrottet was paid $254,666 in a three-month period for being a “sounding board” and providing verbal advice to Jeremy Greenwood with no evidence of written work, a corruption inquiry has heard. In evidence before the Independent Commission Against Corruption on Wednesday, Perrottet denied claims put to her that she was in an “impossible position” because she was being asked to lie under oath and cover for her husband Charles, a former Liberal powerbroker who is one of three party apparatchiks under investigation for receiving a $2 million bribe from a disgraced developer Jean Nassif. Anite Perrottet leaves the ICAC on Wednesday. James Brickwood Anita Perrottet has not been named as a person of interest in the ICAC inquiry into illegal political donations, but the commission is investigating whether she played a role in helping receive money from Nassif for her husband. Charles declined to turn up and give evidence to a 2023 parliamentary inquiry into illegal donations and The Hills Shire Council. His brother Jean-Claude stayed in Fiji for the duration of the inquiry while Christian Ellis and Jeremy Greenwood hid so that a summons could not be served on them.



The commission heard Anita Perrottet’s company was paid significant lump sums for strategic work for two of Jeremy Greenwood’s firms, Beckington and JPG Advisory. That advice was mostly verbal and over encrypted messaging apps, or using her husband Charles’ phone to speak with Greenwood. The most significant payments were made in the final quarter of 2022, when Perrottet invoiced Greenwood for a total of $254,666 for her strategic advice. One example she gave to the ICAC was for a vaping industry client some of that oral advice included “minors shouldn’t be able to be buying vapes”, Perrottet said. “So that’s based on a salary of a million dollars, Mrs Perrottet – let’s get serious,” Counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer, SC, said. “You are giving evidence under oath. Do you seriously suggest that the commission should accept that, as truthful evidence, that you were entitled to charge $254,666 for work that you actually did … providing an oral sounding board or advice to Jeremy Greenwood for that quarter?” Perrottet said yes, that was her truthful evidence.



Dwyer also asked Perrottet to explain why her computer metadata showed an invoice from her company Macquarie Consulting was created by her husband in January 2022, and then modified in March 2023 – the same month Charles was avoiding the inquiry. “Mrs Perrottet, can I suggest to you, you have been put in an impossible situation because you are being asked to lie under oath to cover for your husband?” Dwyer said. “I reject that, I’m not lying,” Perrottet said. Dwyer reminded Perrottet she had taken an oath on the Bible to tell the truth to the ICAC and stressed to her it was an offence to lie. Anita Perrottet appears at the ICAC. ICAC



The commission was shown evidence of friendly text messages between Charles Perrottet and Jean Nassif, which included Charles thanking the property developer for hosting him and his children at his home. Greenwood and his business partner Christian Ellis and their partners were also invited to lunch with Nassif, but Anita Perrottet said she wasn’t there. She couldn’t remember if Charles ever talked about meeting Nassif, or if he told her he was taking their children to his home, Perrottet said. In other memory lapses, Perrottet said she could not remember whether she has ever been a party member, nor recall details of her husband’s role in a powerful Liberal Party subcommittee. Perrottet told the commission on Wednesday that she was not currently a member of the Liberal Party but was not sure whether she had been in the past. She said when her brother-in-law Dominic Perrottet became premier of NSW in 2021 she was happy for him, but it had little impact on her family because she was living in Victoria at the time. Dominic Perrottet is not accused of any wrongdoing.



Perrottet also said she could not remember anything about her husband’s role in the Liberal Party’s local government oversight committee, a powerful body that oversees the preselection of candidates for council elections. She said she had heard the words “local government oversight committee” but did not remember anything about it. Dwyer read out evidence from a secret hearing in February 2024 in which Perrottet gave evidence that she knew Charles Perrottet was bringing matters to that committee, and remembered he began his position about 2018 or 2019. “Does that refresh your memory?” Dwyer asked. “No, not really, sorry,” Anita Perrottet said.



In her opening statement, Dwyer said she expected evidence to show Charles Perrottet anticipated receiving significant funds from Nassif, but there was no evidence of him receiving money directly. Instead, Dwyer said she expected evidence would show the funds were paid into an account by the company name of Macquarie Consulting Pty Ltd – with Anita Perrottet as the sole director and shareholder. Related Article Analysis

Operation Rosny One common factor among ICAC witnesses makes their questionable actions even more stupid Dwyer’s opening statement said she anticipated that the commission would “receive submissions to the effect that the payments to Macquarie Consulting were for consulting work legitimately carried out by Anita Perrottet for Beckington and JPG Advisory. “Yet, in the nearly four years that the commission has been investigating the allegations the subject of this inquiry, it has uncovered no evidence of Anita Perrottet carrying out any work for either Beckington or JPG Advisory,” Dwyer said in her opening statement.



“Instead, the commission’s investigation has unearthed evidence of Mr [Christian] Ellis dictating to Charles Perrottet, and not his wife, how he should structure the invoices that were ultimately issued by Macquarie Consulting to Beckington for the 2021/2022 financial year.” Anita Perrottet told the commission she could not remember why she urgently asked to be removed as a shareholder from a company called Beckington National. The company was established during the COVID-19 lockdowns, when Charles Perrottet feared he may be made redundant from his position at BP. Anita Perrottet’s business was listed as a shareholder, as was Ellis’ wife. She does not remember setting up the company, nor sending an urgent email to her accountant asking to be removed as a shareholder. Dwyer pressed her on this. “Can I suggest to you, Mrs Perrottet, that this is your opportunity to be really honest about these accounts … It appears that this had nothing to do with you, and had something to do with people behind the scenes setting it up. Is that the true situation?”



Anita Perrottet: “No.” Dwyer: “But you have no memory of this, is that right?” Perrottet: “I can’t remember it. It’s not to say I didn’t read it but I, I don’t remember it now.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Police investigating death of Sydney teenager after suspected choking act during sex
World.content:
Breaking PoliticsNSWCrime Police investigating death of Sydney teenager after suspected choking act during sex Jack Gramenz Updated August 26, 2026 — 6:46pm ,first published 3:16pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Police are investigating the death of a 16-year-old girl on Sydney’s northern beaches after a suspected choking act during sex. The teenager died in hospital two days after emergency services responded to a concern for welfare at an Elanora Heights on Sunday night. They found the girl unresponsive. Loading She was flown to Royal North Shore Hospital in a critical condition, where she died on Tuesday night. Two sources with knowledge of the case confirmed the teenager is believed to have engaged in a choking act during sex.



Warnings about sexual strangulation have increased amid scrutiny of violent online pornography, which experts say has warped young peoples’ understanding of sex and normalised concerning behaviour. Researchers at the University of Melbourne and University of Queensland reported in 2024 that about 50 per cent of young people had engaged in choking or strangulation during sex, partly because many people mistakenly believe it can be done safely. “It [sexual strangulation] is happening incredibly frequently, people are doing it regularly … and half the people are doing it at least several times,” lead author Professor Heather Douglas said at the time. The 16-year-old died at Royal North Shore Hospital on Tuesday night. Renee Nowytarger “Brain injury accumulates – the more times you are strangled, the greater the impact on the brain. I suspect there are probably a lot of young people with impacts on their brain as a result of this behaviour and that’s incredibly concerning.”



The NSW government’s own submission to a recent parliamentary inquiry said depictions of sexual aggression including strangulation in pornography has been linked to increased intimate partner violence, citing research from 2017 by the federal government’s Australian Institute of Family Studies. Federal independent MP Zali Steggall, from the neighbouring electorate of Warringah, said the teenager’s death underscored the need for a national education campaign to tackle misogyny and teach respectful relationships. “My thoughts are with her family, friends and community at this incredibly difficult time,” she said. “Police are investigating the circumstances of the girl’s death and no charges have been laid. We must allow the legal process to take place. “Regardless of the circumstances of this particular case, the Albanese government itself has confirmed that rates of sexual violence, particularly amongst young people, are rising.



“The Albanese government must urgently roll out a national campaign ensuring young people receive ongoing sexual-health and relationship education.” Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732). World.title: Premiers to demand more federal cash after Albanese’s refusal to change GST deal
World.content:
Premiers will demand Prime Minister Anthony Albanese permanently hand over more federal taxpayers’ money to them as the price for his emphatic support for WA’s sweetheart GST deal, while federal Labor has softened its stance on using green energy to power data centres. Sources inside Sydney’s national cabinet meeting told this masthead the GST was only briefly discussed, after the prime minister recommitted to the special Morrison-government era deal which is on track to cost taxpayers $60 billion but is viewed as key to winning seats in WA. WA Premier Roger Cook, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and NSW Premier Chris Minns. Dominic Lorrimer But the same sources said frustrated premiers, including NSW’s Chris Minns, Victoria’s Ben Carroll, and South Australia’s Peter Malinuaskas, have been told by Canberra that the WA deal will be subject to a proper discussion at a national cabinet meeting in February or March next year. The Productivity Commission’s interim report published earlier this month labelled the deal a mistake that had created perverse fiscal outcomes, almost all of which had benefited Western Australia at the expense of the rest of the federation and federal taxpayers.



It warned the deal could end up costing federal taxpayers $12 billion a year. Related Article GST PM backs GST deal, leaves future taxpayers on the hook for billions But the report, due to be finalised by the end of the year, has sparked a transcontinental war of words with WA Premier Roger Cook attacking the Productivity Commission as a bunch of “east coast clowns” and opponents to the deal as “whingers”. Albanese, who declared in Perth this week that the deal would not change while he was prime minister, waded into the furore by describing the commission’s report as the work of economic rationalists. Following Wednesday’s national cabinet meeting, Albanese ducked a question on whether Minns, Carroll or Malinauskas had raised the issue. Asked about NSW’s complaints about the GST, Albanese talked up his relationship with Minns, who faces an election in March next year.



“This bloke here, the premier of New South Wales: I’ll be working hard to make sure he stays the premier after March next year. And under my government, NSW will always get support,” Albanese said. This masthead understands key premiers plan to press Albanese to make permanent the most expensive feature of the WA deal, which is a “no worse off guarantee”. These payments, worth about $6 billion a year, are made to all states bar WA to ensure no state and territory is financially penalised by the deal. Loading The guarantee has been extended by the Albanese government to the end of 2030. The states and territories not only want it permanent, but hope to have it bolstered so they receive extra federal assistance. Outside the meeting, Treasurer Jim Chalmers chided Cook for his criticism of the Productivity Commission, saying some of the commentary about the institution’s report was “unfortunate”.



“I don’t believe that is appropriate. I think you can disagree with the conclusions of the Productivity Commission without denigrating them,” he said. “I think it is important that even when those conclusions are contested – as they often will be – that we continue to respect the people of the PC and the really important work that they do.” The national cabinet meeting agreed to push forward a new plan to reduce domestic violence, ban 3D-printed guns, and ban foreigners from holding gun licences, a move prompted by the Bondi massacre. A proposed national gun buyback is still opposed by all administrations bar NSW and the ACT, but leaders agreed to greater intelligence sharing on the same day as the antisemitism royal commission wrapped up its final hearings. Albanese also got an agreement on his proposed national AI framework, after accommodating the position of conservative states. The conservative governments of Queensland and NT had baulked at the federal government’s proposal to mandate that data centres must only be powered by green energy. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor backed Queensland’s position.



Wednesday’s agreement gave ground to Queensland, which has a fleet of state-owned coal plants in competition with wind and solar farms. The NT is backing the development of a gas field in the Beetaloo Basin, which it says could fuel an industrial boom. Albanese acknowledged the different situations facing Queensland and the NT given the public ownership of power generation, transmission and distribution. Queensland Premier David Crisafulli said his state had a “really big point of difference”. “We own distribution, transmission, generation, and that enables us to control that energy mix,” he said. “We believe that we can control our data sovereignty, protect the rights of local communities, and enable that energy mix to bring those data centres on.”



The meeting’s official communiqué did not mention renewable energy. Instead, it talked up the “generational opportunity” offered by AI and noted environmental issues surrounding large data centres would be addressed by federal legislation early next year. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.
