World.title: Queensland premier secures data centre power victory over PM
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland government Queensland premier secures data centre power victory over PM James Hall August 26, 2026 — 6:20pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Premier David Crisafulli has emerged victorious from national cabinet, securing an exemption to enable Queensland to power data centres with coal and gas, following a heated weeks-long scrap with the federal government. Heading into the meeting with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and other state and territory leaders, Queensland and the Northern Territory refused to fall into line on federal Labor’s demands to force AI data centres to be exclusively fuelled by new renewable energy sources. Queensland, led by an LNP government that has pushed back its forced closure of coal-powered generators, said limiting the source of power would risk sending investment in data centres offshore. David Crisafulli puts Queensland’s case to the prime minister and other state and territory leaders. Dominic Lorrimer Crisafulli argued during national cabinet that Queensland’s power network was unique in that the state owned its power generators.



“We’ve got a really big point of difference [to other states], and that is we own distribution, transmission and generation, and that enables us to control that energy mix,” the premier told reporters after the meeting. “We believe that we can control our data sovereignty, protect the rights of local communities, and enable that energy mix to bring those data centres on.” Energy Minister Chris Bowen had previously said the government would use federal powers to force Queensland to fall into line. Alex Ellinghausen Albanese conceded national cabinet relented to Queensland and the NT, where the publicly owned generators would enable data centres to be powered with fossil fuels “if there is surplus”. The conciliatory post-meeting comments were in stark contrast to the heated back-and-forth over the past few weeks, with federal Energy Minister Chris Bowen using his National Press Club speech to stare down Queensland and the NT.



He said the Albanese government would use federal powers to force the two jurisdictions to fall into line and fully offset their centres’ electricity use with investments in renewable energy. Related Article Data centres ‘We will use all the powers available’: Bowen lays down law to states on data centres “While I always prefer to work with my state and territory colleagues, the Commonwealth will not be standing by and letting a race to the bottom of states falling over themselves to attract data centres at the cost to household bills, reliability or emissions,” Bowen said during the address this month. “We will use all the powers available to the Commonwealth, including Commonwealth legislation, to ensure that Australian households and Australian energy reliability is put first – even if some states have different ideas.” But Crisafulli dismissed Bowen’s threats, saying as recently as Monday that his position “smacks of ideology”.



“I’ve seen some comments from Minister Bowen. I do disagree with them,” he said. Related Article Energy Queensland to burn coal for decades as LNP tears up Labor energy target “I don’t believe they’re based on any form of logic, to say they have to be one form of energy or another. “That, to me, is ideology. We’re about economics and being practical. And the truth is, if you get that energy mix right, you can actually complement and bring on opportunities like gas peakers. “We believe that renewable energy is part of that mix. So too is some of our coal-fired power stations.”



Albanese told reporters on Wednesday he understood “different states have different issues”, and the concession will now lead to federal laws being passed in coming months. “There is agreement across the board that we need to ensure that the social licence [to build data centres] has occurred,” he said. “The Commonwealth will legislate, and we have the power to do so, and I’m very confident we will move forward with every single jurisdiction making a difference. We want to make sure that in attracting investment, we don’t have eight different systems operating around the country.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: National and Labour spar over how to help struggling NZers get ahead.
World.content:
National's Nicola Willis and Labour's Barbara Edmonds have sparred over their approaches to help struggling New Zealanders get ahead.

The finance spokespeople were speaking at the Politik election summit on Wednesday.

Politik editor Richard Harman had asked Willis and Edmonds to lay out their economic vision, and what they saw as the context for the election campaign.

The pair agreed the economy was not where they wanted it to be, and their challenge was to create the economic conditions to help "mum and dad" ahead.

Edmonds spoke about her own electorate of Mana, where she said people could no longer afford the "slap up meal" of mince on toast, with prices rising excessively.

Willis said it was irresponsible of Edmonds to say she was focused on the price of mince, "unless you have a policy to address the price of mince, and I haven't heard that from the Labour Party".

National's approach to help people get ahead was to control inflation, she said.

Edmonds said that did not cut it.

"When you know what it's like to only have $8 in your hand and you are sweating when you take your car to get a warrant of fitness ... It is really difficult to speak to people and say, 'well, we're going to work on the economy here, and eventually that'll help trickle down'."

Edmonds said Labour was focused on making other things cheaper for people, pointing to its policies to cap public transport fares and offer three free GP visits.

She also referenced the former Labour government's pay equity scheme, "which was to help our lowest paid women who look after our babies, look after our grandparents in the retirement homes, who are the plunket nurses, who are the midwives."

The National-led government tightened the scheme considerably, making it harder for people in female-dominated workforces to apply to be paid on par with men doing similar jobs.

The debate descended over that, with Willis and Edmonds speaking over each other to get their points across.

"The fact now that they cannot apply for a pay equity claim to help lift their wages, that's terrible," said Edmonds.

Willis said that was not true, and women could still apply.

"Good luck finding the $11 billion (to pay for the scheme)," she said.

"We don't think it's the government's job to fund pay settlement for private sector businesses ... your position is that the taxpayer in Porirua who can't afford mince on toast should be paying more tax so that Ryman Healthcare can get a pay equity subsidy."

Edmonds responded: "Those Ryman Healthcare workers, if the market was working, why are they on the minimum wage?"

They also had a tit-for-tat over Labour's campaign policy to slim down the government's Investment Boost, which allows businesses to deduct 20 percent of the cost of a new asset, over depreciation.

Labour would target it to small businesses only.

Willis said Edmonds had supported Investment Boost, and suggested the Labour finance spokesperson had lost an argument with leader Chris Hipkins over the policy.

Edmonds said there was no debate between her and Hipkins about repurposing Investment Boost.

"Yes, it's a good policy, but my policy is better, so that's where we've left it," she said.

But Willis said it had been a "frustrating debate" and a "phony war" with Labour which she said had continued attacking the government but not offered up its own fixes.

However Willis said that war ended on Sunday when Labour "finally" announced its fiscal strategy to increase spending to 33 percent, which she calculated would see every New Zealander pay $100 more in taxes each week.

World.title: ACT MP Mark Cameron concedes he's 'stuffed' due to health issues in his valedictory speech
World.content:
An ACT MP who is leaving Parliament due to ill health said he's conceded he's "stuffed", and urged MPs to continue fighting for farmers.

Mark Cameron and former Health Minister Dr Shane Reti delivered their valedictory speeches at Parliament on Wednesday.

Cameron was leaving Parliament after six years, saying kidney failure, acute heart failure, and his son's death to suicide had taken their toll.

"We all have our s..., as we say in rural New Zealand, and I have certainly had my fill," he said.

Cameron recalled deciding he was going to "carry the world on his shoulders" despite his poor health.

"I remember fairly recently sitting in the chamber, house duty, nauseous, kidneys at 8 percent - most of you wouldn't have known this - bugger all left," he said.

"I conceded that I was stuffed."

But Parliament and farmers had given him a purpose, he said.

"I needed to carry on, so I did dialysis in my flat, and I went back to bloody work."

That was despite knowing his time as an MP would be cut short eventually, he said.

"We agreed farmers needed to be kept out of the ETS, methane limits reduced, private freshwater assets managed better and in the hands of owners, and stupid winter grazing rules fixed," Cameron said.

"At 8 percent kidney function, I could be a passenger in this reality, or a proponent for better outcomes and change. So here I am."

Cameron urged MPs to believe in rural people.

"They're worth fighting for, they are the economic spine of this country.

"And remember this, it is always hard to argue that fact when your mouth is full of their food."

He thanked his party leader David Seymour - a "bloody legend" - and its deputy Nicole McKee, "an awesome sister, the one I wished I'd always had".

Reti's speech followed after.

Dr Shane Reti. (File photo) RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

He was the MP for Whangārei - the first Māori to win the seat - and had been in Parliament since 2014.

Reti served as National's deputy leader under Judith Collins, and was health minister this term, before being demoted in January last year - replaced by Simeon Brown - when health became an increasingly problematic area for the government.

Reti detailed his highlights throughout the years, and most recently as Health Minister, which included the medical school at Waikato hospital, "the biggest funding increase ever in cancer drugs", and extending the breast cancer screening age group from 70 to 74.

But he had unfinished business, too, he said.

"To the fizzy drinks industry, I was coming for you, and you knew it."

Reti said he had been working on a policy to stop the industry adding more sugar to their drinks in New Zealand, versus Australia which had 40 to 50 percent less sugar.

"I say to the fizzy drink industry: Please explain why you have been deliberately sugaring up New Zealanders, and then reformulate to at least the baseline in Australia."

Reti said serving the people of Whangārei had been a privilege, and thanked his colleagues and family.

World.title: Landlord not aware of any issues with pool's gate before child's death
World.content:
The landlord of an Auckland property where toddler drowned says he was not aware of any issues with a pool's gate prior to the child's death.

River Albert-Wihone had only recently turned one when he was found in the backyard pool at his family's Avondale home. He was taken to Starship Children's Hospital where he died in his mother's arms 12 days later.

The property's landlord Vinesh Natali gave evidence to Coroner Alison Mills at Auckland District Court on Wednesday.

The court was told Natali mostly lived overseas while property management company Crockers looked after the home for the majority of the family's tenancy. However, a different agent took over in the months leading up to River's death.

Natali was questioned by a lawyer assisting the coroner, and also by counsel representing River's grandmother Christine Robinson, who was the main tenant of the home used by multiple generations of the family.

Wednesday's hearing focused on the events of January 2022, when Natali - through Crockers - arranged for fences to be built around the pool in order to comply with new regulations.

Natali said that during conversations with Robinson around the time the pool fence was put up in January 2022, he was not made aware of her concerns about the gate.

"She said poor workmanship and so on. I don't think it was specific to the gate opening or closing, or which direction it was opening or closing," Natali said.

He said he told Robinson that Crockers managed the project and any workmanship concerns should be left with the contractors who carried out the work.

The conversation ended there, he said.

Natali said that after construction was completed the fence passed Auckland Council compliance checks in February 2022.

Earlier, the inquest heard that the pool had failed compliance inspections over a period of four years prior to the family moving there in 2020.

A man from a fencing company who examined the pool fence gave evidence that the tragedy could have been avoided if the gate had been installed with better quality hinges and latches.

Natali was questioned by lawyer Danielle Kelly about whether he'd had any input into the products selected for the job.

"Do you have any comment about concern to keep the cost down? Were you concerned to keep the cost as low as possible?" Kelly asked.

"No, I think as long as the costs were reasonable," Natali replied.

"I don't think I set a clear budget for it either, it was what the cost came in, it looked reasonable."

Lawyer Lucy Wright, acting for River's grandmother, asked Natali about a message he had sent to her client about the construction of the pool fence, in which he had said: "Whatever is cheaper."

"Whichever is cheaper doesn't mean it's cheap cheap," Natali said.

"It's a cost benefit as well, it doesn't mean because it's supposed to be cheap, you go and do the cheapest element. We would obviously look at what would be the most cost effective option that was going to be put in," he explained.

Asked about the pool's history of non-compliance, Natali said Crockers started managing his property in 2015, and that they would tell him if any repairs over $200 were required.

River's grandmother Christine Robinson earlier told the inquest she had raised concerns about the pool fence in January 2022, including an intermittent fault with the gate.

Robinson said she had raised this with the builder, with Crockers and with Natali, but she felt that her concerns fell on deaf ears.

Natali was asked if he knew about landlords' obligation to ensure the safety of the swimming pools even if after they've passed compliance checks.

"I would've relied on Crockers to continue to check it in every visit or whatever that they did at the time," he replied.

Natali was asked if, with the benefit of hindsight, he thought he had an obligation to test the pool gate during an inspection he did in October 2023, a month before River's death.

"Possibly," Natali replied.

After Wednesday's hearing, Natali released a statement to RNZ:

World.title: Flu vaccine to be free for all under fives
World.content:
The flu vaccine will be free to all under fives from next year.

Doctors had been calling for the vaccine to be fully funded, with this year's influenza strain causing a big spike in infections.

Children under five had by far the biggest rates of hospitalisation, particularly Māori and Pasifika tamariki.

Pharmac chief pharmaceuticals advisor Adrienne Martin said the change meant next winter about 260,000 more children would be eligible from aged six months until their fifth birthday.

"This will help protect young children and their whānau against influenza and will reduce the impact of seasonal flu on our communities, and the wider health system," she said.

Currently flu vaccines were only free for under fives if they had been hospitalised with respiratory illnesses or had other diseases like diabetes, asthma or a heart condition.

The change would not be in time for this year's flu season.

Martin said that was because it would take time to get the supplies.

"Ordering and manufacturing flu vaccine happens many months before the start of the flu season," she said.

"Vaccines take a long time to make and ship to New Zealand, so manufacturers can't always make more product during the flu season if demand is higher than forecast."

Martin said two new influenza vaccines were being funded for the first time, a cell-based vaccine and an adjuvanted vaccine, and will provide increased protection compared with the currently funded egg-based influenza vaccines.

"We are also widening access to a pneumococcal vaccine to help prevent people who have already had a serious infection from getting it again.

"This will give the 700 people who will be eligible for this vaccine each year much needed reassurance and protection."

The Ministry of Health's Dr Andrew Old, said the influenza vaccine changes will help strengthen the country's defences against flu next season.

"I would also encourage those who haven't had a flu vaccine this season to consider getting vaccinated. Flu cases are on the rise and this year's vaccine still offers the best available protection against current strains for people, their friends and families this winter."

The influenza vaccine changes come into effect from the start of next year's influenza season on 1 April 2027. Changes to meningococcal, pneumococcal and all other vaccines take effect from 1 July.

National Hauora Coalition clinical director Dr Nina Bevin told Checkpoint changes to flu vaccinations were needed a year ago, before this year's flu season started.

Under fives to be eligible for free flu vaccines next year Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

Bevin said the 59 practices across the coalition's network were all under the pump.

"I was talking to one GP working in South Auckland, and she said Monday was their biggest day in history. She said they were slammed with 146 walk-ins and 89 people waiting for phone triage, and that's on top of their normal booked patients."

Bevin said they are "reaching the limits" of clinical safety.

GP colleagues had written a letter on behalf of the Royal New Zealand College of General Practitioners asking Health New Zealand to immediately fund access to flu vaccines, especially for tamariki under five, she said.

World.title: NZ First candidate steps down after earlier shopping himself around to other parties
World.content:
A NZ First candidate has stepped down just a month after being announced as a candidate, after confirming he had earlier shopped himself around to other parties.

George Ngatai was announced as New Zealand First's Papakura candidate in July, but has said "after careful consideration" he had decided to step down.

He admitted that he had communicated with other parties, but no meetings took place.

"Earlier this year there was a period of considerable uncertainty about whether I would have the opportunity to stand as a candidate," his statement said.

"It was personally disappointing and, during that period, I considered what other options might exist."

Screenshots of undated messages posted by the account Shubz Live on Thursday morning purportedly show "Uncle George Ngatai" referring to the party as "Winston Peters first and then Shane first," and another discussing whether to run for ACT.

"ACT have 2 MPs not returning. They have 11 MPs and expect to get 10 in this year. We need to be in the top 10. If I get the nod then I will start and support. Then my role is to prep you to replace me after a term."

"See if David will consider list for a strong Maori who is more pakeha than pakeha in thinking," another message said.

Other messages show Ngatai being introduced to ACT leader David Seymour and Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong.

Screenshots of undated messages posted by the account Shubz Live. Screenshot

Screenshots of undated messages posted by the account Shubz Live. Screenshot

Seymour told reporters on Wednesday he remembered getting a message, but did not think it went anywhere.

"If you want to stand for the ACT Party, it's almost like trying to get into the SAS these days, and I don't think he would have made it," he said.

"We test our candidates on what they believe, and it sounds like this guy just believed anything as long as it got him into Parliament."

Ngatai's statement said "a member of his team" Martel Wikeepa had made contact with people outside New Zealand First, and while some private communications occurred about "possible alternatives," it never developed into a meeting or commitment by Ngatai to another political party.

Wikeepa runs the Shubz Live account.

On Wednesday, Radio Aotearoa - a station owned by Ngatai and his wife Raewyn Bhana - announced an "indefinite stand-down" of Shubz's show.

New Zealand First deputy leader Shane Jones referred questions on what he described as "the woes of George Ngatai" to the party.

"It's a tad above the Matua's paygrade. But it sounds as if he bought the same parachute as Mr Stu Nash."

RNZ has contacted New Zealand First for a response.

World.title: 'Modern day slavery': Gloriavale leavers file $40m lost wages and entitlements claim against Overseeing Shepherd
World.content:
A group of 61 Gloriavale leavers has filed Employment Relations Authority claims against the Christian community's Overseeing Shepherd for lost wages, entitlements, compensation and damages totalling almost $40 million for work they say amounted to modern day slavery.

In applications lodged on Wednesday, the former Gloriavale members said the Overseeing Shepherd failed to provide them with minimum basic employment entitlements including wages, holiday pay, compulsory KiwiSaver contributions, parental leave and written individual employment agreements.

They want compensation for breach of the statutory duty of good faith and breach of contract and have sought leave to raise personal grievances out of time because of a lack of knowledge about their employment rights and the failure of the Labour Inspectorate.

Lawyers Brian Henry (L) and Stephen Patterson (R), who represent former members of the Gloriavale Christian Community. LOUIS DUNHAM / RNZ

"For applicants work conditions amounted to modern day slavery, including forced child labour, forced labour and servitude in breach of the Employment Relations Act and New Zealand's international human rights treaty obligations," the documents said.

"For most of their working life in Gloriavale the applicants were trapped.

"The applicants did not enjoy a good faith employment relationship but were in a sustained exploitative employment environment."

The legal action followed two landmark Employment Court rulings in 2022 and 2023 that found three men and six women were Gloriavale employees, rather than volunteers, working in factories, on farms or on the community's domestic teams.

Former Gloriavale member Ruby Trust at a press conference on Wednesday.

The court found the women were required to work from a young age, work was effectively assigned from birth and they had no real choice about working on the teams in Gloriavale's commercial-sized kitchen and laundry.

They were required to obey male leaders in a patriarchal community with a strict hierarchy and worked "extremely hard" under "punishing conditions", leaving "deep scars", the court said.

In the men's case, the court found that they were employees from the age of six until they left Gloriavale, ready access to child labour was a significant factor in the success of the community's business model and none of them had a choice as to if and where they worked.

They were subjected to rigorous, sometimes violent supervision in their work and were hit if they were not working hard or fast enough, with some children denied food and publicly shamed.

The nine former members previously lodged claims for lost wages and compensation totalling $5.2 million.

Documents filed with the authority on behalf of the other 61 leavers said they lived in the same controlled, authoritarian environment that did not permit dissenting voices and compelled obedience through fear, including the requirement to work from an early age.

As children they were required to leave school to work and worked hard over excessively long hours without statutory rest and meal breaks, the applications said.

Gloriavale leaver Anna Courage. RNZ/LouisDunham

They worked in an environment that was dangerous for many, where serious accidents happened, were subjected to an emotional and psychological discipline regime and depended on the community for accommodation, food and other necessities of life.

The documents said the former members were taught from an early age that if they did not work they did not eat and disobedience could result in a feared Shepherds and Servants disciplinary meeting.

At the age of 16 they were required to join Gloriavale's Christian Partners and were told where, when and for whom they would work.

"They received money into their bank account (which they had no control over) for labour services provided, from which it would immediately be taken out and put into the Gloriavale sharing account," the documents said.

The applications said the former members were Gloriavale employees who worked under coercion, did not receive remuneration, annual leave entitlements, rest breaks, compulsory employer KiwiSaver contributions or an employment agreement and worked on public holidays.

They have asked the Employment Relations Authority to order payment for lost wages, with deductions for board and food, holiday pay, KiwiSaver contributions, compensation for failing to provide rest and meal breaks, parental leave, a written individual employment agreement, breach of the statutory duty of good faith, breach of contract and hurt and humiliation under personal grievance claims.

The leavers were also seeking exemplary damages because of the "flagrancy" of the conduct and interest on wage arrears.

Barrister Brian Henry said the leavers were Gloriavale employees and were entitled to wages.

"They were denied wages, denied holidays, worked horrific hours and this is the consequence of someone who creates a business model based on child labour. Eventually it catches up with them," he said.

"There is millions and millions of dollars worth of free labour that this organisation has enjoyed and that was illegal."

'Treated like a slave'

Leaver Ruby Trust said she was treated like a slave.

"They say we had a choice but what choice do you get from being born in there with no knowledge of whether or no we were allowed to say yes? We were always taught from a young age that if we didn't work, we would go to hell, we were sinning, we were going against God.

"It was drilled into us from a very young age. What other than slavery is that? They didn't actually give us a choice."

Barrister Stephen Patterson said he calculated that 41 per cent of the men involved in the claims had a debilitating, life-long injuries, including hands crushed in machines, amputated fingers and scalded arms and legs, while many women suffered back problems.

"That's a ratio that should not be occurring in New Zealand in a workplace," he said.

Gloriavale has been contacted for comment.

In May the Employment Court ruled that the clock started ticking on the statutory six-year time limit for wage arrears claims when the nine men and women found to have been Gloriavale employees left the community and experienced the outside world and employment law norms.

While the former members were outside the 90-day timeframe for raising a personal grievance, chief judge Christina Inglis noted they were entitled to apply for leave to do so out of time, with their age and Gloriavale's "uniquely prohibitive circumstances" of potential relevance.

In separate court proceedings, the nine leavers were also seeking damages and declarations of slavery and servitude following an August ruling that the Labour Inspectorate made legal errors in two employment investigations in 2017 and 2021.

Inglis found the Labour Inspectorate misunderstood its jurisdiction and failed to consider children.

"The context of this case involves forced child labour, workplace abuse and servitude," she said.

The inspectorate's 2017 "desktop inquiry" noted that if Gloriavale members were considered employees "there would inevitably be many serious breaches of employment law".

In 2023 Gloriavale members told the Employment Court the community could not afford to pay everyone wages and employment relationships would destroy their Christian way of life.

World.title: Te Pāti Māori unveils 'Kiwi tax plan' with new 5 percent 'stamp duty'
World.content:
Te Pāti Māori has unveiled its "Kiwi tax plan" for the November election, which retains some policies from last election, tweaks some others, and launches an entirely new one.

The party leaders said they wanted give New Zealanders "room to breathe" by putting money back in their pockets, and they would "tax workers less."

The party's announcement on Wednesday afternoon laid out the nine key tax changes the party wanted to see, with just one it had not previously campaigned on: a new 5 percent "stamp duty".

Documentation provided by the party suggested this would apply to "residential sales, excluding first home buyers for homes under $1 million".

Nothing to do with postage, a "stamp" or "transfer" duty is a tax on property, land and sometimes other transactions like vehicle sales, military commissions, or marriage licenses depending on the jurisdiction.

Such a tax resembles a capital gains tax, but stamp duties are typically charged to the buyer rather than the seller.

They are used in countries including the United Kingdom, United States, the European Union, India, Singapore, Indonesia, the Philippines, Ireland, Sweden, Denmark and some Australian states.

Speaking to reporters, co-leader Debbie Ngarewa-Packer said Te Pāti Māori was announcing a plan to transform the "broken tax system".

"Because people across Aotearoa are struggling more now than ever before, 3 million people in Aotearoa are living off less than $60,000 a year, and it's a statistic that politicians and certainly this government is responsible for."

Co-leader Rawiri Waititi said Labour's Capital Gains Tax didn't go far enough when it came to transforming the tax system.

He wouldn't discuss coalition agreements but said Te Pāti Māori's bottom line was ensuring "we can have those discussions around a transformative tax policy and changing those settings."

Asked for his message to Labour leader Chris Hipkins - who outlined the only tax he would introduce was Labour's targeted capital gains tax - Waititi said "I will see you on the eighth," referencing the day after the election.

National's campaign chairperson Simeon Brown immediately responded to the announcement, saying it confirmed "every single part of Chris Hipkins' coalition wants to increase your taxes."

"This is the biggest tax grab in New Zealand's history that we are seeing right now."

Spot the differences

Three of the policies in the party's offering were revisions on ideas presented at the last election.

The promise to remove GST from fresh food is now a "targeted tax credit" for those earning under $60,000 a year, with the party saying the payment would be "equivalent to eight weeks of kai".

The policy document was unclear on just how much that would be or how it would be administered.

The party's proposal for a wealth tax - 1.5 percent on "net wealth" above $2 million, rising to 2 percent for wealth above $5m, and 2.5 percent for $10m or more - was more moderate than the 2 percent, 4 percent and 8 percent it proposed in 2023.

Te Pāti Māori also doubled its promise for extra funding to tackle tax evasion and fraud, from $500m to $1 billion.

The remaining four policies were exactly the same as the 2023 proposals, including income tax adjustments, returning the company tax rate from 28 percent to 33 percent, and introducing land banking and vacant house taxes, both also at 33 percent.

The party said its proposed rebalancing of income taxes would see 97 percent of New Zealanders paying less income tax, with about 4.2 million people to receive "on average, an additional $4000 a year".

"This is a policy for everyone. Whether you are a cleaner, a nurse, a teacher, a tradie, a pensioner or raising a whānau, we want you to keep more of what you earn," the party said.

"People across Aotearoa are feeling the squeeze. The kai bill is up. Housing costs are up. Power is up. Everything is taking a bigger bite out of the household budget. Our answer is simple: put pūtea back in people's pockets and give Aotearoa some room to breathe."

The party said it was named the "Kiwi tax plan" because it was "a tax policy for everyone".

World.title: 'There is a rot' - Stanford expresses confidence in Blakeley to fix MBIE
World.content:
*This article has been corrected to clarify that this is the first time Blakeley offered his resignation and not the second time.

The ministry chief executive found in contempt for misleading Parliament over a multi-million-dollar IT project has offered his resignation, but it has been rejected.

The Privileges Committee - which rules on and can recommend punishments for rule-breaking at Parliament - has found Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) chief executive Nic Blakeley and former Immigration NZ head Alison McDonald deliberately misled Parliament.

But the committee did not recommend further sanctions - saying essentially that the finding of contempt "will be of sufficient consequence on their own".

The Public Service Commissioner confirmed Blakeley had recently offered his resignation.

"Accountability is fixing what went wrong. Mr Blakeley is responsible for ensuring the failures identified by the committee are addressed. I will hold him accountable for delivering that work - there is no misunderstanding on that point," Commissioner Brian Roche said.

"The committee also said in its report, which is yet to be debated by Parliament, that they didn't recommend any further sanction."

Immigration Minister Erica Stanford had previously refused to say Blakeley had her confidence, but she had now changed tack.

"As it stands, I have confidence in Nic Blakeley, but I want to make it clear that, of course, a report is still pending and so we'll see what happens.

"I'm not downplaying the report. It was very, very serious. But at this stage, I have confidence in him to turn this around to make sure it never happens again."

Asked what had led her to express confidence in him now, she said it was because there were "a whole lot of things in MBIE that need to change".

"There is a rot, and he has committed to make sure that he is going to ensure this never happens again."

The Public Service Commissioner has commissioned a detailed inquiry being carried out by Michael Heron KC.

Finance Minister Nicola Willis said the report findings from the Privileges Committee were "very serious indeed and demonstrate unacceptable conduct".

However, Blakeley had "acknowledged and fully apologised" for that.

"I note that the Privileges Committee did not recommend further sanction. I also note that the Public Services Commission had a resignation offered by Nic Blakeley which they didn't accept given he'd only been in the role six weeks at the time of this."

Like Stanford, Willis also said she would not prejudge the findings of the independent investigation into the matter of the IT project, being carried out by Michael Heron KC on behalf of the commission.

Roche similarly said the position highlighted by the Privileges Committee was "completely unacceptable and must not happen again - all chief executives are now very clear on that expectation".

"Mr Blakeley was only six weeks into the chief executive role when this occurred. That does not excuse what happened, but they are factors I considered in reaching my decision about his position," he said.

Party leaders respond

National's leader and Prime Minister Christopher Luxon pointed to the Privileges ruling.

"That said he'd been in the role for a very short period of time, had been advised poorly by his officials ... and he also fairly admitted, you know, upfront. So I think I'm going to leave it with the privileged committee."

He refused to engage with questions about where the line should be drawn on how long someone needed to have been in the job before facing consequences, saying that was "best left to the Privileges Committee".

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said the situation was "incredibly disappointing".

"Parliament does have a role to ensure that we are acting as a watchdog on those who are administering funds on behalf of the government, taking action on behalf of the government. It's clear that you know they haven't done what they should have been doing in the situation.

"I'm really disappointed at the lack of accountability here. It's happened across multiple governments, and it is right that they are being held to account for that."

He stopped short of calling for further punishment.

"I think the finding in itself will send quite a few reverberations through the public sector, and I think that will be a good thing."

Greens co-leader Marama Davidson said it was "absolutely unacceptable that Ministers and MPs were kept in the dark about the status of the biometric data project and the fact that that biometric information could be shared on with the US."

She said it was important that officials "take accountability and own up and be responsible" for misleadings Parliament, but also said the finding of contempt "will be of huge consequence".

ACT's leader David Seymour said Parliament was the representative of the people, "so if you lie to Parliament you're not lying to people like me, you're lying to all the people who pay taxes and vote".

World.title: Giants star Toby Greene opens up on his AFL future
World.content:
Expecting to make a call on his future in the next two weeks, Greater Western Sydney captain Toby Greene has detailed his plans to meet Geelong and Essendon.

Greene, the greatest player in the Giants' 15-year history, is closely considering finishing his career in Victoria so he has more support for his young family.

Admitting it will be the toughest decision of his career, the 32-year-old denied he had already made up his mind to leave GWS.

"I felt like a lot of people in Melbourne, or friends, maybe even some people at the club, feel like I'm definitely going, which is not true," Greene told the Ausmerican Aces podcast.

"If I was definitely going, I'd say that now. I'd be up front with the Giants and make it easy for them."

Giants not sweating on Greene's future The Giants are keen to retain Toby Greene, but they are happy to wait until the 32-year-old is ready to make a call on his future.

Greene's good friend and former GWS teammate, Jeremy Cameron, looms as a natural attraction at Geelong.

Wooden spooners Essendon are desperate for senior stars to help their young talent develop.

Former Giants assistant Mark McVeigh has just been appointed Bombers coach and wants to talk with Greene.

"I'll meet with Geelong probably this weekend, I'd say," he said.

"I couldn't give a f*** about the tour, to be honest. I couldn't care about what their footy club looks like. They're a bloody good club.

"I'd do weights at Anytime Fitness, if I have to.

"'Spike' (McVeigh) has reached out as well since he got the job and asked to catch up.

"I said I'd catch up with him, but it wasn't exactly what I was thinking all year at all."

GWS missed finals for the first time since 2022, with several experienced players already making an exit.

Coleman medallist in 2024 Jesse Hogan, enigmatic forward Jake Stringer and ruckman Kieren Briggs are confirmed departures.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"If I didn't think the Giants would finish top-four next year, I wouldn't stay," Greene said.

"One thing I want to do with them is win a flag and that's the best thing I could do ever in footy.

"I could win two or three (premierships) somewhere else [but] it wouldn't be as good as one at the Giants."

Greene has played 282 games for GWS, including the club's first AFL game in 2012.

AAP

World.title: Time to 'recalibrate': Olympic figure skating champion Liu to miss season
World.content:
Olympic gold medallist figure skater Alysa Liu has said she will sit ​out the upcoming season to fine-tune her technique but reassured fans she would return to the sport.

Liu became ​the first ‌American woman since 2002 to capture Olympic gold in women's singles at this year's Milano ‌Cortina Games, where she also helped ⁠the United States to gold in ‌the team event.

"I ​always want to ‌challenge myself in new ways, so my artistry and skating can evolve," Liu wrote in a social media post, ​adding ‌that she would take time to "recalibrate".

Loading Instagram content

"It's important to me that my sport ⁠reflects my personal ‌growth.

"So fear not, I'll ‌be back, and in the meantime I'll be ‌rooting for my teammates near and far."

In an interview with ‌NBC ​Sports on Tuesday, ⁠Liu said she was planning to work on her "overall artistry, spins, jumps, everything" during her break from competition and ⁠intended to return in the 2027-28 season.

Winter Olympics live blog Alysa Liu becomes the first American woman to win singles figure skating gold in 24 years, completing her comeback after retiring in 2022 when she was only 16 years old.

"I just felt this ‌was ‌right. So I'm trusting my ​instincts," she said.

The announcement marks the latest change in a roller-coaster career for Liu, who arrived at the 2022 Beijing Winter Olympics and finished sixth.

She won bronze at the world titles a few months later before "retiring" from the sport at the age of 16, saying that skating "takes up your whole life, almost".

When she returned to skating she had a new look, with bleached stripes in her hair and a frenulum piercing — and a new approach and confidence that saw her win the world title in 2025 before gold at Milano Cortina.

Liu said her new approach to her sport and to life was more important than results.

Now she leaves to dream it all up again.

Reuters / ABC

World.title: Hird has chance to finally deliver true unity Essendon seeks
World.content:
When new Essendon coach Mark McVeigh was flanked by president Andrew Welsh and CEO Tim Roberts at his introductory press conference on Wednesday, there was a clear theme emanating from the day: unity.

Unity is the thing Essendon has strived for, and failed to find, for the last two decades as it has cycled through players, coaches and administrators in a bid to end an infamous finals drought.

Welsh hopes that by hiring McVeigh he is able to kill two birds with one stone.

McVeigh to canvass Hird return as icon urges Bombers fans to unite Mark McVeigh and Andrew Welsh are set to approach James Hird about a role at the club after he was overlooked to return as the senior coach for a second time.

The process to find its next coach acted as a litmus test for Essendon to actually show it had changed as a club after years of saying it with no actions to follow.

When Brad Scott was ousted midway through the season and James Hird launched his candidacy on national TV in the same week, the consensus was that Hird's return to the Bombers coaches box was a fait accompli.

The lack of belief or trust in Essendon as a sporting organisation left candidates pulling out, believing the club's trumpeted 'process' was actually a sham designed to deliver Hird the role.

It proved to be anything but, as Hird himself revealed after being beaten by McVeigh, leaving both he and Essendon at a potentially pivotal crossroads.

This rejected bid to be Essendon's coach is completely different to Hird's last rejection, when he finished second behind Brad Scott.

James Hird (centre) was left on the outside looking in when Brad Scott (left) won Essendon's coaching race in 2022. (Getty Images: James Wiltshire)

There was something symbolic in Hird, one of Essendon's favourite sons, being beaten out by Scott, a nemesis of his from the Brisbane Lions heyday.

Scott winning the coaching race was reminiscent another occasion where he'd famously got one over Hird, overpowering the under-cooked then-Essendon skipper on the wing during a key period in the 2001 grand final.

Scott, having arrived from the AFL and being selected by an independent panel, appeared a choice that was an aggressive attempt to get away from the fabric of Essendon.

Scott's regime brought a lot of change, and while his decisions may eventually age well, they left Essendon's diehards feeling more disillusioned with every loss that followed.

Andrew Welsh (left) and Mark McVeigh (right) are keen for Hird to return to the club in an official capacity. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Hird wasn't exactly forbidden from returning to Essendon while Scott was in charge, but he also wasn't welcomed with open arms.

This time around is different as both McVeigh and Welsh prepare to launch full-court presses to get Hird back through the doors, just not as the coach.

While the knock on Hird's coaching bid was his lack of experience in a recent AFL coaches box, what cannot be disputed is his knowledge of the game.

If Hird is able to get past the itch of being the coach, he could prove to be an incredible asset as either a football boss, or as a developmental coach. The opportunities are endless, given Essendon has basically wiped out its entire football department.

James Hird (left), Dean Solomon (centre) and Mark McVeigh (right) have the opportunity to link up under one roof again. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

Having held the belief that McVeigh would have come with him had he been successful, as he also pledged to do in 2022, Hird now has the chance to repay the favour.

Welsh has hinted at Essendon bolstering its football department with key appointments in the coming months as it looks to surround McVeigh with a strong staff. It could do worse than bringing Hird back into the fold.

It is notable that Hird, while not receiving the job he wanted, mentioned he has experienced healing during the process in the form of mending fences with individuals he had fallen out with over the club's supplements scandal.

Hird is smart enough to know what his decision from this point on has the potential to do to his beloved club.

As Essendon desperately seeks unity, Hird's return would guarantee it, and he knows that. It is hard to see him turning his back on Essendon to try and coach elsewhere, even if that means he never gets to coach again.

At the front of Hird's mind will be two scenarios: winning Essendon's next premiership, but not as the coach, or winning a premiership elsewhere as the coach. He must figure out which of those will make him happiest.

The benefits of the McVeigh hire are two-fold for Essendon.

He has spent significant time in the coaches' boxes of two teams that have enjoyed deep September runs, albeit without winning the whole lot.

Loading Instagram content

McVeigh's history of working with both the Allies and the Swans Academy was a major selling point given Essendon's list demographic.

Critics suggesting McVeigh's hire was simply a case of jobs for mates were disrespectful to both his decade of coaching reps as well as Welsh's ability to be a professional.

Contrary to all the hysteria about Essendon only hiring "Essendon people", McVeigh is the first Essendon person to be hired as the club's senior coach since Hird's departure in 2015.

The coaches that have followed Hird — John Worsfold, Ben Rutten and Scott — have all enjoyed success at other clubs like McVeigh has, but lacked an ability to truly connect with the club and its fans.

That is McVeigh's superpower. He connects, and he connects with all generations.

It was not by accident that the club filmed McVeigh being greeted at The Hangar by Ken Fraser, the captain of Essendon's 1965 premiership side.

It was also not by accident that both McVeigh and Welsh continually referenced the goal for Essendon to be "one club", making a pointed note to invest in the club's AFLW program.

McVeigh even appeared on a podcast with some of Essendon's biggest content creators from outside the club, a stark difference from Scott, who gave off the vibe of an untouchable CEO fans could never really connect with, rather than your friendly local head coach.

Matthew Lloyd (centre) has indicated he would potentially join McVeigh (left) and Welsh (right) back at Essendon. (Getty Images: Mark Dadswell)

It is no surprise that McVeigh's arrival has already seemingly caused a change in tune from both Hird and fellow Essendon icon, Matthew Lloyd.

Since his retirement at the end of 2009, Lloyd has mostly stayed away from the club while becoming one of the AFL's most prominent media figures.

Lloyd is uncompromising when it comes to his views on Essendon, annoying segments of the club's fanbase who wonder why he has not stepped in to help fix the problems he keeps highlighting.

As McVeigh's appointment grew closer, Lloyd curiously changed his tune and said he would like to go back to club land.

It would be no surprise to see him in an official role at Essendon in the coming years as McVeigh builds out his staff.

All of this brings us back to Hird and Essendon's seemingly never-ending quest to find unity.

The basic pitch from Hird's supporters is that he is the only one who can truly bring unity back to what has been a broken club.

The pitch just missed one thing.

Who says Hird can only bring unity as Essendon's coach?

World.title: Pogačar's sensational solo attack squeezes Vuelta rivals dry
World.content:
Four days is all it took for Tadej Pogačar to end the Vuelta a España as a meaningful contest, the Slovenian great once again riding away from the peloton to win solo and establish a massive lead over the rest of the field.

It has been 32 years since Tony Rominger led a grand tour from start to finish when he won the 1994 Vuelta.

But with yet another thrilling display of daring, Pogačar put himself in pole position to emulate the Swiss rider and become just the ninth man to lead a three-week race from start to finish.

Superlatives have long been superfluous when writing about this Slovenian superstar.

Things that should not be possible are made to look routine.

When he hits the front of a race as the road goes into the mountains, the rest of the pack knows that their only chance is to ride at their own tempo.

Any attempt to fly too close to this generation's greatest star will surely send their hopes of finishing the race crashing to the ground, like Icarus.

As soon as Tadej Pogačar is in this position, that's likely to be the last the peloton sees of him. (Getty Images: Tim de Waele)

Pogačar took off with just over 50 kilometres remaining of the 104.8km circuit around Andorra la Vella to claim yet another dominant victory.

Decathlon CMA CGM put the power down at the bottom of the Collada de Beixalis climb, the second mountain of the day, and ripped the peloton to shreds.

Australian Jay Vine led the charge in support for the Slovenian's UAE Emirates XRG team, but with the pace already high, Pogačar upped his rate to burst clear.

Decathlon's Austrian leader Felix Gall tried to match Pogačar's pace in the initial throes of his attack.

However, the Austrian, as so many riders have discovered before him, could barely hold the double-world champion's wheel and quickly dropped off before being joined by the rest of the favourites.

"The pace was already super fast on the throttle right from the base [of the climb]," Pogačar told media after the race.

"When Jay let me pass him on Decathlon's wheel, I knew: 'OK, I don't want to get isolated from all those general classification contenders, because otherwise they'll all gang up on me.'

"I tried to attack on the climb. When I saw that I could open up a gap, I just hoped I could hold on until the finish. It worked out.

"It was really tough, but it's a wonderful feeling."

Tadej Pogačar is irresistable. (Getty Images: Alexander Hassenstein)

Pogačar's lead extended to over 3 minutes at one stage before he rolled home to win by 2 minutes and 39 seconds from Jarno Widar, with Gall third.

The 50km attack was his longest in a grand tour, bettering the 43km solo victory he launched in the Pyrenees last month at the Tour de France.

It is another remarkable performance from the Slovenian to add to the extraordinary wins that have become so normal it is expected of him.

Why these people believe in 'freak' Tadej Pogačar's victories As Tadej Pogačar continues to mop up cycling's biggest accolades and most controversial record, one former doper believes he's found the answer to his success: he is just a "freak".

With two key objectives to come this season, the World Championships road race in Canada falls just two weeks after the Vuelta's conclusion, with the Giro di Lombardia a further two weeks after that, Pogačar may now be able to take things easier through the next two-and-a-half weeks of racing in Spain.

The 27-year-old's lead in the general classification now stands at 3 minutes and 21 seconds, with four-time Vuelta winner Primož Roglič sitting second.

"To be honest, any lead is a bonus," Pogačar said.

"This is fantastic, because now I can head into the coming days with peace of mind and a lot of confidence.

"We're taking it day by day and staying focused. Hopefully, after this stage, the pressure will ease up a bit."

Pogačar is also a comprehensive leader in the points and king of the mountains classifications.

Wednesday's fifth stage is a hilly 173.3km ride from Falset Costa Daurada to Terres de l'Ebre in Spain's north east.

World.title: Ex-NBA player who claims to be a woman banned by WNBA team after joust
World.content:
The Chicago Sky has banned Enes Kanter Freedom from its home games after the former NBA centre was ejected from Sunday's (Monday AEST) loss to the Indiana Fever.

Owner Michael Alter made the announcement at a rare news conference on Tuesday, local time. Alter told reporters Kanter Freedom is not allowed inside Wintrust Arena for Sky games "unless sometime in the future, he's able to prove to us that he's able to abide by our rules without being a potential threat".

Kanter Freedom was removed from Sunday's game after a confrontation with Sky guard Natasha Cloud late in the third quarter.

Cunningham's trans stance opens WNBA up to its latest hijacking atempt Sophie Cunningham insists she wants to protect the sanctity of women's sport, but her comments have opened her league up to an unprecedented attack.

Kanter Freedom was sitting along the baseline wearing a black shirt that read "WOMAN noun. adult human female".

The Fever called for a timeout after Cloud scored inside with 1:22 left in the third. Cloud then chest-bumped teammate Aicha Coulibaly before turning and walking in Kanter Freedom's direction.

Cloud, 34, started yelling and pointing at Kanter Freedom, 34, as she approached him. Kanter Freedom, who was standing, held his arms out and stepped onto the court as security and a handful of Sky players moved between the two.

"It was pretty clear to us that his purpose of coming here was trying to be provocative and see how much attention he could get," Alter told reporters from the Chicago Sun-Times and other media outlets.

Kanter Freedom stopped near the basket to plead his case to security as he was escorted from the court area. He spun around while holding his shirt out and encouraged the crowd to respond as he walked toward the front lobby.

He had a conversation with a group of police officers before departing the arena.

"I just got kicked out of a @WNBA game for supporting WOMEN!" Kanter Freedom wrote on social media. "Let that sink in, AMERICA!"

Kanter Freedom and Royce White, another former NBA player, have declared for the WNBA draft, saying they identify as women. But a person familiar with the decision told the AP on Monday, local time, that they are not eligible. The person spoke on condition of anonymity because of the sensitive nature of the situation.

The WNBA has been the subject of recent debates on whether transgender women — people assigned male at birth who transition to align with their gender identity — should be allowed to participate in the league. There has never been such a player in the WNBA.

Although the league's collective bargaining agreement says the WNBA is restricted to women, it contains no more specific language about gender identity or sex assigned at birth.

AP

World.title: CTE study finds 70pc of head impacts happening in sports practice
World.content:
At least one in four former NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 was found to have had chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), according to a new study.

Out of the 878 former players who died during that timeframe 235 donated their brains, researchers said, with 215 of those donated brains found to have CTE.

The study's lead author Daniel Daneshvar, the chair of physical medicine and rehabilitation at Mass General Brigham and an associate professor at Harvard Medical School, said it was difficult to determine how common CTE was as it could only be diagnosed after death.

"People who donate their brains are more likely to donate if they have some concern, some reason for donating, if they think that either they or a loved one is having problems with their memory or thinking or concentration or behaviour changes," he told ABC News Breakfast.

Former NFL players donated their brains to the study and 215 out of 235 were found to have CTE. (Getty Images: Nic Antaya)

"And so you can't just look at the rate of CTE amongst people who donate to get a sense of how common this disease is."

Dr Daneshvar said the "possible prevalence of CTE" among NFL players was "very concerning".

"In the general population, less than 1 per cent of people get this disease pathology in their brain," he said.

" What we found is, at a minimum, 25 per cent of these NFL players died with this disease process. "

The study from Mass General Brigham, Boston University, and the Concussion & CTE Foundation also found dementia was common among brain donors, with researchers urging prevention measures that focus on cutting down on repetitive head impacts across all levels of the sport.

"Similarly, we and others have shown that in NFL players, specifically, there is about a four times higher rate of death from neurodegenerative disease than the general population," Dr Daneshvar said.

"The bulk of the head impacts that these former NFL players experienced didn't occur at the NFL level.

Here's what we know about CTE The brain disease is caused by repeated head injuries. It's most commonly associated with athletes in contact sports, but there's a lot researchers are still trying to learn about it.

"They occurred at the collegiate level ... and at the high school level and in many cases the youth level.

" And all of those cumulative hits to the head added up to result in an increased risk. "

The NFL's 2011 Collective Bargaining Agreement limited the number of contact practices during the season. The Ivy League banned full-contact tackling during practices five years later.

The Supreme Court cleared the way for the NFL's settlement of concussion-related lawsuits with thousands of retired players in 2016.

An NFL spokesperson said the league continuously strives to make the game of football safer, "including by implementing strategies to reduce concussions and head impacts".

"The NFL remains committed to ensuring that the NFL community has access to a robust — and expanding — set of resources to enhance their physical and mental wellbeing," they said.

"We encourage former players to utilise these resources to identify and seek treatment when they are concerned about their health."

Dr Daneshvar urged current and former athletes experiencing cognitive symptoms to seek a neurodegenerative disease expert evaluation.

"If the changes that have been implemented at the NFL level, including reducing the amount of contact in sports practices to less than one per week, were propagated at the collegiate, high school, and youth levels, athletes would be better off," he said.

"We know that nearly 70 per cent of head impacts are occurring in practice.

"So without changing a single minute of game time at any of those levels, we can be substantially reducing the cumulative head impact burden that these individuals are experiencing throughout their lives."

ABC/Reuters

World.title: Tomic's main draw drought continues as Australians struggle at US Open
World.content:
Bernard Tomic's seemingly unending quest to fight his way back into another grand slam main draw has fallen short once again at Flushing Meadows despite one more worthy scrap from the veteran Australian.

The last time the 33-year-old managed to battle into a main draw of a major was at his home Australian Open in 2021.

In the five years since, he has entered 10 more qualifying events in the slams and failed to negotiate his way through any.

Alas for the former teenage wonder boy who got to number 17 in the world a decade ago, that drought continued on Tuesday afternoon, local time, in New York as he fought back in his first-round match against South African Lloyd Harris only to be outplayed in the final stanza.

No-one can possibly fault the effort of world number 179 Tomic, who was once perceived as being a talented but undisciplined figure who did not really care enough about the sport, as he has since battled on in the lower reaches of the game around the world, tirelessly seeking another day in the sun.

Emerson Jones also failed in her bid to advance to the women's main draw despite a valiant fight. (AAP: Darren England)

But Harris, a former world number 31 himself who is still dangerous even if his ranking has fallen to 139, just had a little too much for the Gold Coast veteran, who staged a second-set fightback before going down 6-2, 5-7, 6-2.

It was the same story for a couple of other Australians in first-round action, as teenager Emerson Jones fought valiantly to peg back Dutch world number 164 Suzan Lamens in a tight second-set tiebreak, only to succumb in the decider 7-5, 6-7 (7-9), 6-2 after two hours and 25 minutes.

With another veteran, Alex Bolt, losing 7-6 (7-3), 7-5 to Spain's Pablo Llamas Ruiz, it meant that Australia were still looking for their first winner of the week in qualifying after James McCabe's loss on the opening Monday.

At least one Aussie was guaranteed a place in the second round of qualifying as Storm Hunter took on her friend Maddison Inglis later in the day.

AAP

World.title: Djokovic and Sabalenka stunned in US Open mixed doubles debut
World.content:
Top seeds Novak Djokovic and Aryna Sabalenka have suffered an early exit from the US Open mixed doubles, falling 1-4, 4-2, 10-2 to Henry Patten and Katerina Siniakova in their opening match.

Djokovic, a 24-time grand slam singles champion, and four-time major winner Sabalenka made a strong start by taking the opening set.

However, Patten and doubles specialist Siniakova hit back to claim the second before dominating the tiebreak to secure a place in the quarterfinals.

Siniakova sealed the upset in style with an ace out wide on match point, ending the tournament hopes of the star-studded pairing.

"It wasn't looking very good for a while," Patten said.

"In this format we play one bad game and all of a sudden the first set's gone.

"We knew the same could happen in the second, and we played an amazing tiebreak. Kat acing Novak on match point was great."

The mixed doubles championship is once again being staged in the week before the singles main draw, after organisers revamped the format last year to attract more leading singles players by reducing the field and giving the event a standalone slot on the calendar.

The revamped format proved a commercial success in its debut year, drawing sellout crowds and attracting many of the sport's biggest singles names despite criticism from some doubles specialists, who argued it marginalised established pairings.

Italian duo Sara Errani and Andrea Vavassori went on to retain the title by defeating Iga Świątek and Casper Ruud in last year's final.

No problems for Williams and Alcaraz

Serena Williams (left) and Carlos Alcaraz (right) made a triumphant start to their US Open mixed doubles campaign. (Getty Images: Sarah Stier)

Serena Williams made a triumphant return to the US Open, partnering with Carlos Alcaraz to beat Erin Routliffe and Lloyd Glasspool 5-3, 4-1 in the opening round.

The 23-time major winner had not competed at Arthur Ashe Stadium since her tearful farewell from the sport in 2022.

The crown jewel of American tennis erupted in deafening cheers as their queen took the court again.

The 44-year-old Williams had an easy rapport with Alcaraz, who is 21 years her junior, as the partners grinned and giggled their way into the quarterfinals, where they will meet Belinda Bencic and Flavio Cobolli later on Tuesday.

"It's always such an amazing place to be here," Williams said. "I never expected to be back on this court."

Williams hit a backhand winner the first time she touched the ball, earning uproarious cheers from the packed house a little more than two months after she announced her stunning comeback.

After trading breaks, Williams blasted a 193.1kmh ace on the penultimate point in the seventh game, drawing audible gasps from the crowd. Alcaraz, who has not played since April due to injury, shook off the early rust to close out the set with a forehand winner.

They sprinted through the second set with ease, embracing after the win in their matching royal purple outfits.

"I'm playing next to the one and only Serena Williams," seven-times major winner Alcaraz said. "Trying to do the things she told me to do."

Reuters

Tech.title: Trump is upping the price of Big Tech’s favorite visa
Tech.content:
In the span of a few hours on Monday, the Department of Homeland Security announced that it would be implementing a fee of over $103,000 on H-1B visas, and news broke that the State Department plans on revoking the visas of up to 200,000 asylum seekers — which, according to The Associated Press, would be the largest mass visa revocation in US history.

More than a year into President Donald Trump’s second term, it’s become clear that the only way Trump can get the deportation numbers he wants is by stripping legal immigrants of status. Beyond having ICE arrest, detain, and deport immigrants, the administration is pressuring noncitizens to “self-deport,” in some cases imposing civil fines on them and threatening to seize their assets. It’s creating legal hurdles not only for new legal immigrants but for those already in the country, and in the process, likely hurting businesses and social services nationwide.

H-1B visas are often seen as synonymous with Big Tech, in no small part because Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft are the three biggest employers of H-1B workers. A federal judge struck down Trump’s previous attempt to raise the cost of these high-skilled employment visas in June, but not until over 70 employers paid the $100,000 fee. Now Trump wants to raise the cost to $103,265. Advocates and business leaders are worried Trump will soon come after the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program, which DHS hinted may soon carry a $100,000 fee of its own. OPT lets international students work in their field of study for 12 months, with extensions of up to 24 months for some STEM students and additional extensions for holders of certain graduate degrees.

“Every single other pathway is harder, outlawed, eliminated, more bureaucratic, more difficult across the board.”

“This is clearly unlawful,” said Todd Schulte, the president of FWD.us, an immigration reform organization founded by Mark Zuckerberg and other tech executives in 2013. “We don’t have to guess what this is for. This is to get rid of the OPT and H-1B program, which will have upstream and downstream devastating consequences: companies will be started elsewhere, people will be hired elsewhere.”

This won’t just hurt the tech industry. The previous fee hike exacerbated labor shortages at rural hospitals across the country and Alaska public schools, both of which have increasingly turned to high-skilled immigrant workers in the wake of local population decline. If the $100,000 fee was an inconvenience for Amazon and Meta, it was utterly catastrophic for rural communities already having trouble attracting qualified candidates.

Foreign workers aren’t the only legal immigrants Trump is targeting. According to the AP, which broke the news, the State Department will rescind up to 200,000 business and travel visas issued between 2016 and 2026 to people who applied for asylum after arriving in the US. Beyond limiting their ability to travel outside the country, this move won’t change much for asylum seekers who came to the US on nonimmigrant visas — at least not for now. But Schulte said the visa revocations are part of Trump’s efforts to gut the humanitarian immigration system. “Every single other pathway is harder, outlawed, eliminated, more bureaucratic, more difficult across the board,” he said. “It’s an all-of-government approach.”

The administration is framing this change as a way of closing a loophole in the asylum system: people coming to the country on nonimmigrant visas, ostensibly for work or pleasure, only to ask for asylum upon setting foot in the country.

“We are coordinating with DHS to identify and revoke the nonimmigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the United States claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently,” State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott told the AP.

But the people who applied for asylum this way didn’t break any laws. In fact, a person needs to be present on US soil to apply for asylum; there’s no way to apply from outside the country. And Trump has closed most other avenues for humanitarian migration. There’s an effective “asylum ban” in place at the US-Mexico border. Refugee admissions have dropped to record lows, and the administration is now prioritizing the resettlement of white South Africans and denying almost everyone else.

In his second term, Trump has shown that the only immigrants he wants are those who look a certain way — or who can pay a small fortune for the privilege of working in America.

CD Projekt Red is remastering The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt, the hit RPG that first launched in 2015, and the updated game will be available starting September 29th. The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered will bring improvements to visuals and combat, a “reimagined” skill tree, and more, and it also includes the first two expansions, Hearts of Stone and Blood and Wine.

Remastered will be a free upgrade for players who own the base game on GOG, Steam, Epic Games Store, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X / S. With the launch of Remastered, The Witcher 3 will also be coming to the Nintendo Switch 2.

This remastered version of The Witcher 3 (which follows a next-gen upgrade released in 2022) is the start of a big push for the franchise over the next few years. CDPR is set to launch a brand new Witcher 3 expansion, titled Songs of the Past, in 2027, and it’s aiming to release its next mainline Witcher game, The Witcher 4, in 2028.

Tech.title: Dreame’s dream of a rocket-powered car is dead
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Dreame, the Chinese vacuum company that aspires to be a global technology giant, is reportedly shutting down its automotive project after funding from the government dried up.

According to CarNewsChina, the company’s automotive division called “Project Starry Sky” once employed over 1,000 people, but now only a handful legal and HR staffers remain, charged with winding down the operation. In a statement, Dreame said it “recently adjusted certain operations that were in the exploratory phase,” and that going forward, it would focus on four key business areas: “smart home, outdoor/garden, smart mobility, and embodied AI.” (A spokesperson for the company didn’t respond to a request for comment.)

The news comes after China’s government issued new rules aimed at tightening oversight of the $3.4 trillion private fund industry, singling out Dreame in the process. After becoming one of the world’s largest manufacturer of vacuums, the company quickly moved into a variety of new businesses, spawning nearly a thousand affiliated ventures related to smartphones, robotics, and cars. But much of that expansion was funded by China’s government — and the government is now starting to take a closer look at how Dreame spends that money, according to CNBC.

The NEXT 01 JET Edition Car at the Dreame NEXT event during the Silicon Valley Summit at the Palace of Fine Arts on April 29, 2026 in San Francisco, CA. Photo by Kelsey McClellan / The Verge

Dreame wowed audiences at a San Francisco expo earlier this year with “Nebula Next 01 Jet Edition,” a sleek looking concept car equipped with a pair of rocket engines that theoretically can accelerate from 0 to 60 mph in 0.9 seconds. The vehicle was allegedly equipped with a sulfide-based solid-state battery with a record-breaking energy density exceeding 450 Wh/kg and a purported range of over 550 km (341.7 miles). The company claimed its boosters would deliver 100 kilo-Newtons of force.

But the concept raised a lot of questions, including some basic ones about how Dreame could make a car accelerate so quickly without breaking the laws of physics. Apparently Dreame didn’t have any answers to these questions, as the car itself was fully vaporware. Former employees told China Economy that the concept that was shown off in San Francisco lacked an actual chassis and was driven via remote control. (Concept cars are rarely “real” cars, in the technical sense — but even this is a little shocking in its level of deception.)

The news that Dreame’s vaporware car was totally vaporware will come as little shock to those familiar with the showy, boastful promises of companies that have never actually built a car suddenly deciding to build a car. Faraday Future, another Chinese companies with ambitions to build all manner of electric, autonomous vehicles, ran into this exact problem nearly a decade ago. And it also faced accusations of operating self-driving cars for public demos via offstage remote control.

Tech.title: Bose’s smallest Bluetooth speaker is a great deal at 35 percent off
